# HMPlot documentation

The guide, then the reference: every page of the documentation as Markdown. A reference page is in Python, with its example in Svelte too; Svelte spells the same options in camelCase (fill_scale is fillScale), and its page is at the same address with svelte for python. /reference/api.md has every component's Python signature and Svelte props on one page.

## Html

Page: /reference/svelte/html.md

Anchor ordinary HTML at a numeric 2D frame position; excluded from plot exports.

### Example

```svelte
<script>
  import { Plot, Frame, Points, Html } from "hmplot";
  let count = $state(0);
</script>

<Plot height={300}>
  <Frame x={{ domain: [0, 10] }} y={{ domain: [0, 10] }}>
    <Points x={4} y={6} size={12} />
    <Html x={4} y={6} dx={12} dy={-12}>
      <button onclick={() => count++}>Details opened {count} times</button>
    </Html>
  </Frame>
</Plot>
```

### Options

- `x` (`number`): Scalar x coordinate in the enclosing frame.
- `y` (`number`): Scalar y coordinate in the enclosing frame.
- `dx` (`number`): Horizontal offset in CSS pixels. Default: `0`.
- `dy` (`number`): Vertical offset in CSS pixels. Default: `0`.

`Html` anchors native HTML at a scalar numeric position in the nearest 2D Cartesian
Frame. Its top-left corner follows the displayed scales and camera; `dx` and `dy`
are CSS-pixel offsets. Use CSS on your content for additional alignment.

Attachments preserve Svelte context and state. They do not set domains or reserve
layout space. Use a keyed Svelte loop for a small collection of attachments; use
marks for data-sized collections. Invalid or clipped anchors hide their content
and remove it from keyboard navigation. Content can extend into margins but is
clipped at the canvas boundary.

Native controls retain their normal semantics and events. Provide accessible
names and keyboard behavior for custom controls. If a focused attachment becomes
hidden or is removed, focus returns to the plot canvas. The overlay background is
pointer-transparent, and plot navigation ignores events originating in attachments.
Positions update after resize, navigation and scale animation. Destruction removes
the wrapper and subscription; SSR creates neither.

HTML is excluded from plot PNG/SVG/PDF exports. Browser screenshots include it.
Categorical frames, 3D, and following an animated mark endpoint are not supported.

For external overlays, the Plot and Frame handles expose `getScreenMapping()` and
`subscribeScreenMapping(listener)`. A mapping snapshot has `width`, `height`,
`revision`, `project({x,y})`, and `unproject({x,y})`. Pixel coordinates are local to
the canvas in CSS pixels, independent of device pixel ratio. To convert an event,
subtract the canvas bounding rectangle's `left` and `top` from `clientX/clientY`.
Do not apply CSS transforms to the canvas when using that simple subtraction.

Snapshots describe completed draws and remain unchanged during subsequent updates.
The subscription immediately receives the current mapping, then changed mappings
after draws; its return value unsubscribes. A mapping is null before drawing, after
disposal, or for unsupported geometry. Invalid coordinates map to null. Projected
points outside the visible frame retain their coordinates with `inside: false`;
inverse mapping does not clamp.

## Plot

Page: /reference/python/plot.md

A chart: axes, a camera and the marks inside it, in 2D or 3D.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"x": [1, 2, 3, 4], "y": [3, 1, 4, 2]}
with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True) as plot:
    hm.Points(x="x", y="y")
plot
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Plot, Points } from "hmplot";
  const data = { x: [1, 2, 3, 4], y: [3, 1, 4, 2] };
</script>

<Plot {data} height={300} axes2d>
  <Points x="x" y="y" />
</Plot>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

#### Options

- `animation_group` (`column | column[] | null`): Match animation rows by these columns within each filtered/transformed snapshot; selections keep Data.key. null restores key/position matching. Default: inherited; otherwise Data.key, then position.
- `description` (`string`): Your description of the plot for screen readers and exports; the generated summary of its marks, axes and legend follows it unless describe is false.
- `describe` (`boolean`): Add the generated summary of the plot's marks, axes and legend to its description. Default: `True`.
- `tooltip` (`boolean | field[] | object`): The tooltip of every mark in the plot that sets none: true, a list of fields, or {fields, radius, content, mode}. mode "x" lists every series' value at the pointer's x in one box.
- `nearest` (`boolean | selection | object`): The nearest of every mark in the plot that has rows and sets none: true, a selection(), or {selection, radius}.
- `loading` (`"atomic" | "progressive"`): "atomic" shows the plot once its first frame is complete; "progressive" draws each mark as soon as it is ready. Default: `"atomic"`.
- `background` (`color`): The plot's background: a CSS color, or "transparent". Default: the theme's (white in the default theme).
- `data` (`table`): A table or live pipeline output for the marks in the plot; the same as wrapping them in Data.
- `schema` (`object`): Column types for data, such as {"day": "datetime"}, as on Data.
- `key` (`column | column[]`): The column, or columns, that identify each row of data across updates, as on Data.
- `x` (`{domain, transform, label, ...}`): The x axis: its domain, transform, label, ticks, grid and the rest of an axis definition.
- `y` (`{domain, transform, label, ...}`): The y axis, as x.
- `z` (`{domain, transform, label, ...}`): The z axis of a 3D plot, as x.
- `scale_defaults` (`{color, size, width}`): Defaults for the continuous color, size and width scales the plot's marks make for numeric columns: each {colormap, range, transform, ...}.
- `z_scale` (`number`): The height scale of every surface in the plot (a Heatmap with surface_mode), unless the surface sets its own. Default: each surface's own (0).
- `legend` (`boolean | {position}`): true shows a legend that explains everything the plot's marks map from data (a guide per channel, as a Legend without a channel does), then lists the labeled marks; {position} puts it at the "top", "right", "bottom" (the default) or "left"; false shows none. A channel an explicit Legend explains is left out. Default: a legend at the bottom for each fill, color or outline color mapped from a category column.
- `coordinates` (`"cartesian" | "polar" | "spherical"`): The coordinate system: polar reads x as angle and y as radius; spherical reads x and y as longitude and latitude. Default: `"cartesian"`.
- `polar_axis` (`"X" | "Y" | "Z"`): The axis a 3D polar plot turns around; a 2D polar plot uses "Z". Default: `"Z"`.
- `spherical_view` (`"globe" | "projected"`): How a 3D spherical plot shows the sphere: as a globe, or flat in its map projection. Default: `"globe"`.
- `camera_mode` (`"orbit" | "flyover"`): How the viewer moves a 3D camera: "orbit" turns around a target; "flyover" moves like a map (drag pans the ground, the wheel zooms toward the pointer, right-drag looks, WASD and QE fly). Default: `"orbit"`.
- `camera_position` (`[number, number, number]`): Where the 3D camera is; the plot's box spans -50 to 50. A new value moves it there (easing with animation). Default: [90, 70, 140], scaled to the scene. In world units.
- `camera_target` (`[number, number, number]`): The point the 3D camera looks at. Default: `[0, 0, 0]` world units.
- `camera_up` (`[number, number, number]`): The 3D camera's up direction, overriding the view preset. Default: [0, 0, 1] for 3d; [0, 1, 0] for 3d-y-up.
- `camera_fov` (`number`): The 3D camera's vertical field of view. Default: `50` degrees.
- `camera_near` (`number`): The 3D camera's near clipping distance. Default: from the scene's size. In world units.
- `camera_far` (`number`): The 3D camera's far clipping distance. Default: from the scene's size. In world units.
- `fly_speed` (`number`): A multiplier on flyover's wheel zoom and key travel, from 0.1 to 10. Default: `1`.
- `flyover_momentum` (`boolean`): A flyover ground drag released while moving glides on for a moment, slowing to a stop; false stops the view on release, as reduced motion does. Default: `True`.
- `lights` (`LightSpec[]`): Lights for lit marks: ambient, directional, hemisphere or point. Positions use world units; omitted, no lights are added.
- `effects` (`EffectSpec[]`): Effects over the whole plot: {kind: "sky", ...} (a 3D plot's sky), {kind: "bloom", strength, radius} (how glowing marks bloom), {kind: "fog", near, far, color} (a 3D plot's distance fog) or a registered plugin's kind with its parameters. A kind no plugin registers is skipped with a warning. SVG and PDF exports draw the whole plot as an image while one shows.
- `globe_background` (`color | false`): A color fills the sphere under a 3D globe's marks; false leaves it empty. Default: `False`.
- `angle_unit` (`"degrees" | "radians" | "extent" | "custom"`): The unit of polar and spherical angles: "extent" makes the x domain one turn, "custom" uses angle_period. Default: `"degrees"`.
- `angle_period` (`number`): Angle units in one turn when angle_unit is "custom" (24 for hours). Default: `360`.
- `base_radius` (`number`): The radius at zero: a polar plot's radius is base_radius + radial_scale × y, a globe's base_radius + radial_scale × height. Default: 0 in polar coordinates, 1 in spherical.
- `radial_scale` (`number`): The radius per unit of y in a polar plot, or of height on a globe (see base_radius). Default: `1`.
- `projection` (`"equirectangular" | "mercator" | "equal-area" | "orthographic" | "equal-earth" | "natural-earth" | "albers" | "albers-usa"`): The map projection of a 2D spherical plot (or a projected 3D one). An orthographic globe drags to turn; equal-earth, natural-earth, albers and albers-usa have curved outlines and draw a graticule instead of edge axes. Default: `"equirectangular"`.
- `projection_center` (`[number, number]`): The map's center [longitude, latitude], in angle_unit: the orthographic globe's starting view, and the central meridian of equal-earth, natural-earth and albers (its origin latitude too). Default: `[0, 0]`.
- `parallels` (`[number, number]`): The albers projection's two standard parallels, in angle_unit. Default: `[29.5, 45.5]`.
- `subdivision_tolerance` (`number`): How far a curved line, band or outline may stray from its true shape before it is divided further. Default: `0.5` px.
- `zoom_axis` (`"x" | "xy" | "y"`): Which axes the viewer's 2D zoom changes. Default: `"xy"`.
- `dynamic_margins` (`boolean`): Fit axis margins during navigation. False fits initially, then holds this plot's own margins during pan/zoom; size, font, style and data-domain changes refit. Aligned peers can still reserve space; longer labels may clip. Default: `True`.
- `axis_margin_zoom` (`boolean`): With axes shown, zooming over an axis's margin zooms that axis only. Default: `True`.
- `overview_scale` (`number`): A multiplier on the marks' sizes in the overview. Default: `0.35`.
- `overview_max_instances` (`number | null`): The most rows per mark the overview draws; past it the rows are sampled (null draws them all). Default: `1000`.
- `axis_frame` (`boolean`): Draw a complete rectangular border in 2D Cartesian frames without duplicate ticks or labels. Default: the theme's.
- `axis_mask` (`boolean`): Clip marks and picking to the rectangular 2D Cartesian axes interior, intersecting ancestor masks. Default: the theme's.
- `axes3d` (`boolean | {style, gridPlanes}`): Enable Cartesian 3D guides: true uses theme defaults; an object selects box or triad style and xy/xz/yz grid planes. Default: `False`.
- `aspect` (`"auto" | "equal"`): "equal" keeps one transformed data unit the same length on all Cartesian axes, including 3D; "auto" fills the plot. In 2D an explicit domain is kept: the plot area letterboxes instead of widening it. Polar and spherical plots are always equal. Default: `"auto"`.
- `overview_axes` (`boolean | {x, y}`): Label the overview's axes: true for both, or {x, y} to choose. Default: `False`.
- `rules` (`{axis, value, label, color, width, dash}[]`): Reference lines across the plot at x or y values, each with an optional label, color, width and dash.
- `bands` (`{axis, from, to, label, color, opacity}[]`): Shaded spans of the x or y axis behind the marks and grid lines, labelled like rules.
- `viewport` (`{x, y, zoom, zoomX, zoomY, center}`): The 2D view: its center as a fraction of each axis's domain (x, y) and its zoom. With onviewportchange it controls the view or shares it between plots; with animation, a new value eases there.
- `interactive` (`boolean | "brush"`): Let the viewer pan and zoom a 2D plot or move a 3D camera, and Shift-drag to brush a mark with brush; false fixes the view, and a plain drag brushes. "brush": a plain drag brushes, Shift-drag pans and the wheel zooms. Default: `True`.
- `name` (`string`): The plot's name in its settings and export panels, and its accessible name when it has no title. Default: Plot 1, Plot 2, ....
- `width` (`number`): A fixed width; without one the plot fills its notebook cell or exported page (in a Facet, its cell). hm.export_png, export_svg and export_pdf, with no page to fill, draw it 800 px wide; a view's own export draws it as shown. Default: the container width. In px.
- `height` (`number`): The height of the whole plot: its title, caption and top or bottom legends take their room from it, and the drawing area the rest (at least a quarter of it). Default: `450` px.
- `responsive` (`boolean`): True fills the container even when width is set; false uses width or 800 px. Default: fill the container without width.
- `type` (`"2d" | "3d" | "3d-y-up"`): A 2D plot, a Z-up 3D plot (3d), or a Y-up 3D plot (3d-y-up); camera_up overrides either 3D preset; SVG and PDF exports draw a 3D plot's 2D marks as vectors sorted by depth, and its marks as one image when one has no vector form there (a 3D mark, a Heatmap). Default: `"2d"`.
- `settings` (`{showTrigger, showExport, menu, allowSharedDefaults}`): showTrigger: false hides the settings and export buttons; showExport: false hides the export button and the menu's Export entry; menu: false leaves the browser's own context menu instead of the plot's; allowSharedDefaults: false leaves the shared defaults out of the settings pane. The plot's export and openSettings() methods work whatever these say.
- `tone_mapping` (`number`): The three.js tone mapping the plot renders with: 0 (the default) keeps colors exact, so marks match their legends; 4 is ACES filmic, for a photographic look in lit 3D scenes. Default: `0`.
- `overview` (`boolean`): Show an overview in the corner: a minimap of the whole domain in 2D, an orientation gadget in 3D; exports leave it out. Default: `False`.
- `axes2d` (`boolean`): Draw the 2D axes: lines, ticks, labels and titles; on a 2D orthographic globe, a graticule (every 15°) and the sphere's outline. Default: true for 2D Cartesian plots and 2D orthographic globes; false otherwise.
- `orientation3d` (`boolean`): Show an X/Y/Z orientation indicator in the lower left while a 3D plot is hovered. Default: `False`.
- `axis_tick_labels` (`boolean`): Draw the axes' tick labels. Default: `True`.
- `axis_titles` (`boolean`): Draw the axis titles, in 2D and on the 3D box. Default: `True`.
- `antialias` (`"msaa" | "ssaa8" | "ssaa16" | "smaa" | "off"`): On-screen antialiasing: 4x MSAA (msaa), hybrid 8x/16x sampling (ssaa8/ssaa16: 4x MSAA at 2x/4x the pixel count, then downsampling), SMAA, or off. Hybrid modes cost more GPU work. Exports always use 4x MSAA at their requested resolution. Default: `"msaa"`.
- `auto_bounds` (`boolean`): Fit missing x, y and z domains to the plotted data; an explicit domain always wins. Default: true when the plot has data (its own, an enclosing Data or a Facet); Python's Plot sends true.
- `animation` (`boolean`): Animate changes to the values of every mark in the plot (marks can set their own), and ease a new viewport or camera prop (position, target, up, fov, near, far) to its value, except under reduced motion; the viewer's press or wheel stops the move. Default: `False`.
- `animation_duration` (`number`): How long animated changes take, including setCamera's with animate. Default: `300` ms.
- `animation_easing` (`"linear" | "quad-in" | "quad-out" | "quad-in-out" | "cubic-in" | "cubic-out" | "cubic-in-out" | "sine-in-out"`): The easing of animated changes. Default: `"cubic-in-out"`.
- `animate_bounds` (`boolean`): Animate numeric axis domains and ranges independently of mark animation; structural changes and direction reversals snap. Default: `False`.
- `bounds_duration` (`number`): Duration of scale transitions, independent of mark timing. Default: `300` ms.
- `bounds_easing` (`"linear" | "quad-in" | "quad-out" | "quad-in-out" | "cubic-in" | "cubic-out" | "cubic-in-out" | "sine-in-out"`): Easing of scale transitions, independent of mark timing. Default: `"cubic-in-out"`.
- `title` (`string`): A title above the plot, part of it on screen and in its exports.
- `subtitle` (`string`): A line under the title, smaller and lighter.
- `caption` (`string`): A note under the plot, such as its source, smaller and lighter.
- `filename` (`string`): Save an export to this file when the plot's with block closes; the suffix picks PNG, SVG, PDF or HTML.
- `export_options` (`object`): Options for that export, such as scale for PNG or mode and width for SVG and PDF; needs filename.

#### Map paths

- `interpolation` (`"great-circle" | "angular" | "cartesian"`): How the plot's paths run between two points on a map or a globe: along a great circle, straight in longitude and latitude, or straight in space. Marks can set their own. Default: `"great-circle"`.

#### Axis style

- `axis_font_size` (`number`, setting): The size of the axis labels. Default: the theme's (14 in the default theme). In px.
- `axis_font_family` (`string`, setting): The axis labels' font, a CSS font-family. Default: the theme's.
- `axis_line_width` (`number`, setting): The width of the axis lines and ticks. Default: the theme's (1 in the default theme). In px.
- `axis_tick_size` (`number`, setting): The length of the ticks. Default: the theme's (3 in the default theme). In px.
- `axis_margin_left` (`number | "auto"`, setting): The space left of the plot area: "auto" fits the y axis's labels and title, a number pins it. Default: `"auto"`. In px.
- `axis_margin_right` (`number | "auto"`, setting): The space right of the plot area: "auto" fits what reaches past it (the last x label), a number pins it. Default: `"auto"`. In px.
- `axis_margin_top` (`number | "auto"`, setting): The space above the plot area: "auto" fits what reaches past it (the top y label), a number pins it. Default: `"auto"`. In px.
- `axis_margin_bottom` (`number | "auto"`, setting): The space below the plot area: "auto" fits the x axis's labels and title, a number pins it. Default: `"auto"`. In px.

### Usage

Use Plot for ordinary charts. data supplies a local table; x/y/z configure the implicit frame. Defaults include a white background and atomic initial loading. Handles expose Fit, settlement, settings, selections, and export.

`animateBounds={true}` animates numeric axis domains and ranges independently of mark
updates, using `boundsDuration` and `boundsEasing`. Mark animation keeps its separate
`animation`, `animationDuration`, and `animationEasing` controls. They share one clock; see
[Frame animated scales](frame#animated-scales) for interruptions, exports, and changes that snap.

Axis titles default to the plotted column: an axis is named after the one column its marks plot there (`x={{label}}` and `y={{label}}` override it, and an empty label means automatic); an axis whose marks plot several columns, arrays or expressions has no title (see [Frame axis titles](frame#axis-titles)).

`axes2d` shows the implicit frame's 2D axes (on by default for Cartesian 2D). Given explicitly, it holds whatever the Plot contains. Without it, a child Frame that draws an axis on the plot's side (a twin axis with no range) turns the axes on; ranged or anchored Frames and facet cells, and Frames inside them, draw their axes in their own boxes and never do.

`dynamicMargins={false}` (Python: `dynamic_margins=False`) fits the initial axis labels, then holds this plot's own margins during pan and zoom, including after a gesture ends. Resize, font, axis-style/title and data-domain changes fit again. Longer navigation labels may clip; use a shorter axis format or numeric `Theme.axes.marginLeft`/`marginRight`/`marginTop`/`marginBottom` to reserve predictable space. Aligned plots still share the space their peers need, so this option does not lock the entire plot rectangle against changes elsewhere. The settings pane exposes **Fit margins during navigation**. The default remains true. `axisMarginZoom` separately controls axis-only zoom gestures in the margins.

`type="3d"` uses Z-up, so an x/y terrain grid rises along z. Use `type="3d-y-up"` for scenes whose height is y. `cameraUp` overrides either preset (Python: `camera_up`); the settings pane offers both presets. Switching the preset changes the up direction without remapping data coordinates.

In 3D, `cameraMode` chooses orbit or flyover navigation (flyover is map-style: a drag keeps the ground point under the cursor, the wheel zooms toward the cursor, right-drag or Alt-drag looks, WASD/QE fly, two fingers pinch toward their midpoint on touch, `flySpeed` and Shift scale the wheel and keys). `cameraPosition`, `cameraTarget`, `cameraUp`, and `cameraFov` set the camera; the handle's `getCamera()`, `setCamera(partial, {animate})`, and `fit()` move it programmatically, and `oncamerachange` reports moves.

`flyoverMomentum` (default true; "Flyover momentum" in the settings pane) lets a flyover ground drag released while still moving glide on along the ground for a moment, slowing to a stop within about a second and a half and at most one and a half camera heights away, with the camera's height and direction kept. A drag held still before release does not glide, and only ground drags do (not looking, pinching, the wheel or the keys). Any new input (a press, the wheel, a key, Escape), leaving the page, a programmatic camera change and disabling the controls stop a glide; `whenSettled()` and exports wait for it to stop. `flyoverMomentum={false}`, and the system's reduced-motion setting, stop the view on release.

`lights` lists the [lights](light) used by marks with `lit=true`: ambient, directional,
hemisphere and point. The settings pane edits their color, intensity and position.
Python uses `lights=[hm.light("ambient", intensity=0.3)]`; Svelte uses
`lights={[light("ambient", { intensity: 0.3 })]}`.

`effects` composites [effects](effects) over the whole plot: a 3D plot's sky (`{ kind: "sky", image }` or a gradient) and distance fog (`{ kind: "fog", near: 100, far: 300 }`, distances from the camera in world units; the plot's box spans -50 to 50), how glowing marks bloom (`{ kind: "bloom", strength, radius }`), and [plugins'](plugins) effects. They are drawn after the scene (docs/RENDERING.md "Sky, fog and glow"): picking ignores them, empty background stays clear, and marks that do not write depth, such as labels, take the fog of what is behind them. The settings pane shows fog with the camera settings (3D fog, start, end and color), and bloom's strength and radius.

`antialias` chooses how the screen smooths edges: `"msaa"` (4x multisampling, the default), `"ssaa8"` or `"ssaa16"` (hybrid MSAA + supersampling), `"smaa"` (a post pass: faster when fills are heavy, softer thin lines) or `"off"`. The hybrid modes render 2x/4x as many pixels with native 4x MSAA, then downsample through the presentation compositor: nominal 8x/16x sampling density at greater GPU and memory cost. They preserve CSS mark sizes and picking coordinates. WebGPU's native MSAA is limited to 4x. Points, lines and text smooth their own edges in every mode, and so do 2D [Rects](rect), [Bars](bar), [Histograms](histogram) and [BoxPlot](box-plot) boxes without MSAA (docs/RENDERING.md "Analytic edges"); other fills (Area, Pie and polar sectors, hexagons, GeoJSON, 3D) need MSAA for smooth edges. Exports always render with 4x MSAA at the requested export resolution, whatever the screen uses. Python uses the same values: `hm.Plot(antialias="ssaa16")`.

> **SVG and PDF export**
>
> **Vector, except** a 3D plot's marks (`type="3d"`) when one of them has no vector form there (Points3D, Surface or another 3D mark, a Heatmap or Image, a lit or additive mark, a globe or polar frame): SVG and PDF exports draw them all as one image and keep the axes, titles and legends vector, and `mode="vector"` refuses it. Otherwise a 3D plot's 2D marks (Points, Text, Line, Segments, Arrows, ErrorBars, Area, flat Rects, Histograms, Bars and BoxPlots, Polygon) are vectors, projected through its camera and drawn back to front by depth; where marks intersect or cross closely, which one is in front is approximate, and the export report says so. A sky, fog or plugin [effect](effects), a mark's `glow` or a Frame's `atmosphere` makes the whole plot one image: SVG and PDF exports draw all of the plot's marks, with the effect, as one image (its axes, titles and legends stay vector), and `mode="vector"` refuses it. Each mark's page says when it is an image in a 2D plot. The `overview` gadget is left out of every export. See [what is not exported as vector](/HMPlot/docs/export.md).

### Default size and axes

Without dimensions, a Plot fits its container up to **800 px wide**, and is **450 px** tall;
its title, caption and top or bottom legends take their room from that height. In a Python
notebook view or an exported HTML page it fills the cell or page instead; `hm.export_png`,
`export_svg` and `export_pdf`, with no page to fill, draw it 800 px wide. Set `width` and `height` for fixed dimensions;
set `responsive={true}` (Python: `responsive=True`) for uncapped container width, including
when a width is supplied. `responsive={false}` uses the supplied width or 800 px.
Facet cells continue to fill their allocated space.

Axes and grids are visible by default only in 2D Cartesian plots. Polar, spherical and 3D plots keep them off unless requested.
Use `axes2d={false}` or `axes3d={false}` (Python: `axes2d=False`, `axes3d=False`) to hide them.
For 2D Cartesian plots, the default theme draws subtle major grids; minor grids remain off. Set
`x={{ grid: "off" }}` and `y={{ grid: "off" }}` to hide the grids, or choose another theme.

### Cartesian proportions and 3D guides

`aspect="equal"` makes equal transformed data units equally long on every Cartesian axis,
including 3D. Linear axes preserve ordinary data proportions; log/symlog axes preserve
proportions after their scale transform. User domains, range centers and reversed directions
are retained: in 2D the spare length goes to an axis whose domain is automatic, which shows
more than its data, and where it would fall on a domain you gave, the plot area narrows
(letterboxes) so that domain fills it exactly, leaving at most 45% of the plot on a side. Nested Frames share the root metric; explicit nested placements remain placements.
Changing domains or aspect updates the geometry without resetting camera orientation.
Polar and spherical geometry retains its natural proportions.

```js
<Plot type="3d" aspect="equal" axes3d={{ style: "box", gridPlanes: ["xy", "xz"] }}>
```

`axes3d` defaults to false. True uses `theme.axes.threeD`; an object enables guides with its
overrides. A box shows every edge; a triad shows three incident axes. Labels use near-facing
edges, stay upright and avoid duplicate shared-corner labels; selected grid planes occupy
far faces as the camera moves. Per-axis controls style baselines, ticks, titles, arrows and
grids. Explicit box/triad objects require Cartesian coordinates.

### Borders and data masks

`axisFrame={true}` adds the missing sides of a rectangular Cartesian 2D border, without
opposite-side ticks or labels. `axisMask` clips points, thick lines, fills and data text to
the visible axes interior. Hidden fragments cannot be picked. Nested masks intersect with
ancestor masks; facet cells are supported. Axis guides, titles, legends and brush handles
remain visible. Masks work with hidden baselines and transparent backgrounds, and SVG/PDF
exports use the same boundaries as PNG and the screen.

HMPlot enables masks by default; Minimal leaves them off. A theme's mask is ignored outside
supported Cartesian 2D frames; an explicit unsupported request raises an error. Python spells
the options `axis_frame` and `axis_mask`.

Cartesian 2D `rules` draw above marks, using the theme's axis text color unless a rule supplies
its own `color`. Grid lines and shaded bands stay behind marks. Rule `width`, `dash` and
`color` apply consistently to the canvas and vector exports.

`animationGroup` (`animation_group` in Python) on Data, Plot or Frame matches animated
rows by a column or list of columns independently of Data keys. It inherits through the
tree; a child Frame overrides its branch, and explicit null (Python None) restores
Data-key/position matching. Filter to one row per group before tweening: a country/year
table can keep `key=["country", "year"]` and animate by `"country"` after filtering
to one year. Groups must be unique in each tweened snapshot, and changing the group
column scheme resets motion history. Selection, hover and connections keep Data identity.

### Related examples

- [Data shortcuts](/HMPlot/examples/data-shortcut.md)

## Theme

Page: /reference/python/theme.md

Fonts, colors and mark styles for everything inside it.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"x": [1, 2, 3, 4], "y": [3, 1, 4, 2]}
with hm.Theme(value=hm.themes.dark) as themed:
    with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True):
        hm.Points(x="x", y="y")
themed
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Plot, Points, Theme, themes } from "hmplot";
  const data = { x: [1, 2, 3, 4], y: [3, 1, 4, 2] };
</script>

<Theme value={themes.dark}>
  <Plot {data} height={300} axes2d>
    <Points x="x" y="y" />
  </Plot>
</Theme>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

- `value` (`theme`): The theme: a preset from themes (Python hm.themes), createTheme(...) (Python hm.create_theme), or a definition object. An inner theme changes only what it names.

### Usage

value is a theme definition or shared theme resource. Nested themes merge sections; palettes replace arrays. Explicit mark props and settings keep precedence. Themes do not change data or numerical transforms.

### Inherit from a theme

A definition with `extends` starts from another theme and changes only what it names: `extends` is a preset name (matched ignoring case and punctuation, so `"financeTerminal"` and `"finance-terminal"` both work), a theme definition, or a theme resource. Its own keys deep-merge over the base: objects merge key by key, arrays (a palette) and values replace. Chains work; a cycle is an error.

```js
const desk = createTheme({ extends: "financeTerminal", name: "Desk", palette: ["#00ff88", "#ffd166"] });
const night = createTheme({ extends: desk, axes: { grid: "major" } });
```

```python
desk = hm.create_theme("Desk", extends="finance-terminal", palette=["#00ff88", "#ffd166"])
night = hm.create_theme(extends=desk, axes={"grid": "major"})
```

`update()` cannot change `extends`; `replace({ extends, ... })` rebases a theme.

### Compose themes

`extends` can be a list, merged left to right, with the theme's own keys last: a complete look first, then partial themes that each change one section.

```js
const report = createTheme({ extends: ["paper", "axes/minimal", "legend/inline-top"], name: "Report" });
```

```python
report = hm.create_theme("Report", extends=["paper", "axes/minimal", "legend/inline-top"])
```

The library ships these partial themes (names match ignoring case and punctuation in each part, so `"legend/inlineTop"` works too):

| Partial | Sets |
| --- | --- |
| `axes/minimal` | no grid, baseline or arrows; short outside ticks |
| `axes/grid` | major grid lines, no baseline, ticks or arrows |
| `axes/frame` | a full border with inside ticks, no grid or arrows |
| `legend/inline-top`, `legend/inline-bottom` | the Plot's legend above or below, entries in a row |
| `legend/stacked-right` | the Plot's legend to the right, entries stacked |
| `title/left`, `title/centered` | the title block's alignment |
| `controls/compact`, `controls/large` | inputs' text size, 11 or 15 px |
| `numbers/currency`, `numbers/percent`, `numbers/si` | `numbers.format`: `"$,.0f"`, `".0%"` or `"~s"` |
| `animation/fast`, `animation/slow` | animated changes take 150 or 600 ms |
| `animation/linear` | animated changes ease linearly |
| `animation/fade` | keyed rows fade in and out |
| `title/editorial`, `title/panel`, `title/presentation` | 24, 16 or 32 px title hierarchy with subtitle/caption sizes and spacing; alignment unchanged |
| `axes/quiet-grid`, `axes/print-frame` | thin adaptive major grid, or stronger frame with inside ticks |
| `axes/inside-ticks`, `axes/light-titles` | tick direction alone, or 400-weight axis titles |
| `axes/close-labels`, `axes/comfortable-labels` | axis-title/tick-label offsets of 6/3 or 12/7 px |
| `legend/compact`, `legend/generous` | 12/10 or 16/16 px text/swatch sizing |
| `legend/subdued-heading`, `legend/strong-heading` | heading weight of 400 or 700 |
| `legend/mark-shapes` | swatches follow the encoded mark shape |
| `marks/points-dense` | 4 px points, 0.45 opacity, no outline |
| `marks/points-outlined`, `marks/points-open` | 9 px points with a neutral outline; open also sets transparent fill |
| `marks/points-presentation` | 14 px points with a thin neutral outline |
| `marks/lines-fine`, `marks/lines-medium`, `marks/lines-bold` | Line widths of 1, 2 or 3 px |
| `marks/intervals-crisp` | ErrorBars width 1.25 px, cap size 6 px |
| `marks/areas-subtle` | Area opacity 0.15; does not imply a confidence level |
| `marks/bars-muted` | Bar opacity 0.65 only; bin/category spacing unchanged |

A partial lends only its section, never its name: `["paper", "title/centered"]` is still named Paper. A theme of your own is a partial when its `name` starts with one of the groups `axes/`, `legend/` (the `guides` section), `title/`, `controls/`, `numbers/`, `animation/` or `marks/`: `{ "name": "legend/house", "guides": { "position": "top" } }`. It should set only that section; any other key warns and is ignored wherever the partial is used, in `extends` or as a nested `Theme`. A partial's own `extends` takes only its section from each base, so `{ "name": "axes/paper", "extends": "paper" }` is Paper's axes alone.

The cascade is plain order, with no specificity: the themes in `extends` in list order, the theme's own keys, then a nested `Theme` around part of the page (which changes only what it names), and last a mark's own props. At every step objects merge key by key and lists (a palette, a dash pattern) replace.

`marks/` partials merge only the named mark kinds. They preserve palettes, axes, annotations
and unrelated marks. The point outlines use neutral slate `#64748b`, readable against light
and dark backgrounds; set `outlineColor` explicitly to encode a category or choose another
stroke. Explicit `fill` and `size` channels win over point defaults, including transparent
fill. An open flat point's transparent fill does not hide its solid 3D counterpart: that
counterpart uses the palette unless its own entry overrides it.

### Bars and boxes

A `Rect` or `Prism` with no fill takes the theme's first `palette` color, and so do `Bar` (its bars are Prisms) and `Histogram` (Rects): the color every preset makes stand out on its background (#3478c7 in the default theme). It is the weakest of the theme's defaults: `marks.default`, an entry of the mark's own (`marks: { Rect: { fill: "#e45756" } }`, which a Histogram's bars take too; `Bar` and `Histogram` entries for them alone), the mark's props and its Mapping all win.

`Line`, `Points`, `Area`, `ErrorBars`, `Segments` and `Arrows` also use the first
palette color when their theme entry has no color or fill. HMPlot and Ink use `null` for
these entries, so changing their palette updates ordinary marks too. A `null` color/fill
clears an inherited color; explicit colors and `marks.default` still take precedence.
In Python theme definitions, use `None` for `null`.

### Title block

`title` styles the title block of every Plot and Facet below the theme: their `title`, `subtitle` and `caption`. `align` is `"left"` (the default), `"center"` or `"right"`; `fontSize` (default 1.35 times the theme's text size), `subtitleFontSize` (one pixel larger than the text) and `captionFontSize` (one smaller) are CSS pixels; `fontWeight` is a whole number from 100 to 900 (default 600); `spacing` is the space between the block and the plot (default 8). PNG, SVG and PDF exports draw them as laid out: `{ "title": { "align": "center", "fontSize": 20 } }`.

`"inherit"` as `typography.fontFamily` or `typography.color` takes the font or text color of the element the plot sits in, so an embedded chart matches its page: `{ "extends": "minimal", "typography": { "fontFamily": "inherit", "color": "inherit" } }`. It is the whole theme's text: the axes', legends', titles' and Text marks' fonts and colors, over the ones a preset sets. A section's `fontFamily` or `textColor` (and a mark's `font` or `color`) can be `"inherit"` on its own. In a notebook the font is the notebook's and the color the plot frame's, which keeps text readable on it; exported files and pages use a system sans-serif and dark gray. The host's style is read when the plot mounts.

`guides` styles legends: `fontFamily`, `fontSize` and `textColor` are their text. `position` is where a Plot's own legend sits, `"bottom"` (the default), `"top"`, `"left"` or `"right"`; a Plot's `legend={{ position }}` still wins, and a Facet's grid legend and an explicit `Legend` keep their own defaults. `layout` is how entries flow: `"auto"` (the default) puts them in a row below or above the plot and stacks them beside it, `"inline"` and `"stacked"` always do one. `swatchSize` is a category or series swatch's size in CSS pixels (default 12), and `swatchShape` is `"auto"` (the mark's own shape, the default), `"circle"` or `"square"`; a line or text entry keeps its own, and size and opacity ramps keep theirs. `titleFontSize` (default the text size) and `titleFontWeight` (default 500) style the legend's title: `{ "guides": { "position": "top", "layout": "inline", "swatchShape": "square" } }`.

A page restyles the title block and legends with CSS custom properties, set on the plot or any element around it, over the theme: `--hm-title-font`, `--hm-title-color`, `--hm-title-align`, `--hm-title-spacing`, `--hm-title-font-size`, `--hm-title-font-weight`, `--hm-subtitle-font-size` and `--hm-caption-font-size` (the font, color and alignment are the whole block's, caption included), and `--hm-legend-font`, `--hm-legend-color`, `--hm-legend-font-size`, `--hm-legend-title-font-size` and `--hm-legend-title-font-weight`. Sizes are CSS lengths (`13px`). The plot lays them out as the page shows them, and PNG, SVG and PDF exports from the page draw that layout, overrides included; Python's exports, drawn in a page of their own, use the theme's values. Text inside a legend's graphics (colorbar ticks, size and opacity ramp labels, a text swatch) has a fixed 10 px font: it takes `--hm-legend-color` but not the font or size variables. Axes are drawn by the plot and keep the theme's. The `Title` and `Markdown` marks do not read `--hm-title-*`. The variables inherit, as custom properties do, into nested plots and facets and win over a nested `Theme`; setting them again on an inner wrapper scopes them to it.

```css
.report { --hm-title-font-size: 20px; --hm-title-align: center; --hm-legend-color: #475467; }
```

### Missing values

`missing` is the color a missing value (`NaN` or null) of a colormapped fill or color draws in under the theme, unless its scale sets one (`continuous({ missing })`); the default, `#92989f`, is a neutral gray that reads on light and dark backgrounds. A GeoJSON's features without a value take it too, unless the GeoJSON sets `missingColor`.

### Numbers

Without a format, numbers read as decimals: axis ticks exactly, colorbars to three significant digits, size ramps and tooltips to four (a whole number stays whole), with thousands grouped once a value reaches 10,000 (`12,345`, and `10,000` on a log axis rather than `1e+4`). `numbers.format` is a d3-format string, the language of an axis's `format`, that linear axes' ticks, legends and tooltips use instead: `",.2f"`, `".1%"`, or currency with `"$,.0f"`. An axis's `format`, a mark's `legendTickFormat` and a tooltip field's `format` win over it; dates, durations, log axes and angles (a polar angle, a globe's longitude and latitude) keep theirs.

```python
money = hm.create_theme(extends="hmplot", numbers={"format": "$,.0f"})
```

### Animation

`animation` times animated changes under the theme: `duration` in milliseconds and `easing` (`"linear"`, `"quad-in"`, `"quad-out"`, `"quad-in-out"`, `"cubic-in"`, `"cubic-out"`, `"cubic-in-out"` or `"sine-in-out"`) are every Plot's `animationDuration` and `animationEasing` (300 and `"cubic-in-out"` without a theme), and `enter` and `exit` are every mark's `enterEffect` and `exitEffect`: `true` or `"fade"`, or `{ "effect": "fade", "duration": 200, "easing": "quad-out" }`. A Plot's or mark's own props win. The section does not turn animation on: a Plot's or mark's `animation` does, and `enter` and `exit` reach only marks that animate and whose rows a keyed update stages (Points, Text, Rect, Prism, Segments, Arrows, ErrorBars and their 3D kinds). `false` cancels an enclosing theme's effect: `{ "animation": { "duration": 600, "easing": "linear", "enter": "fade", "exit": "fade" } }`.

### Inputs

Sliders, Selects, Buttons, Checkboxes, Playbacks and the other inputs take their look from the theme around them (the default theme outside any `Theme`): the theme's font (`typography.fontFamily`; `"inherit"` keeps the page's), and a `controls` section. `controls.accentColor` colors a slider's handle and fill, a checked box and the focus ring (default the theme's first `palette` color); `controls.fontSize` is their text size in CSS pixels (default `typography.fontSize`), and the controls' heights and spacing scale with it. Their text color is the page's. Each shows its label first and the control after it (a checkbox's label follows its box); a Slider or Playback shows its value beside it, to its numeric `step`'s decimals (step 0.001 writes `12.345`), else as tooltips write numbers (four significant digits, `12,346`), unless it sets `format`; the theme's `numbers.format` is for data, not controls, and `{$name}` placeholders read the same text: `{ "controls": { "accentColor": "#0f766e", "fontSize": 13 } }`.

A page restyles inputs with the same custom properties as the settings pane, over the theme: `--hm-controls-accent`, `--hm-controls-font`, `--hm-controls-font-size`, `--hm-controls-color` and `--hm-controls-background` (a field's or button's fill, transparent by default). Each input's outer element has the class `hm-input` and one for its kind (`hm-slider`, `hm-range-slider`, `hm-select`, `hm-multi-select`, `hm-button`, `hm-checkbox`, `hm-playback`, `hm-text-input`, `hm-color-picker`, `hm-date-time-input`); its label is `.hm-input-label` and a slider's value `.hm-input-value`.

```css
.dashboard { --hm-controls-accent: #0f766e; --hm-controls-font-size: 12px; }
.dashboard .hm-input-label { font-weight: 600; }
```

### 3D marks

`marks` sets defaults by mark kind. A `Points3D`, `Arrows3D` or `Text3D` with no entry of its own takes only the color of its flat counterpart: the `fill` of `Points`, the `color` of `Arrows` and of `Text`, so a theme recolors 3D plots too (a dark theme's light text reaches Text3D). Symbol names, pixel sizes and outlines stay with the flat marks. An entry such as `marks: { Points3D: { fill: "#e45756" } }` sets a 3D mark apart; a mark's own props and its Mapping still win.

### Basemap schemes

A theme's `vectorTile` section is the color scheme `VectorTile` draws with below it: part → style, with the keys of VectorTile's `styles` (`{ "water": { "fill": "#1e3a5f" }, "buildings": false }`). Every preset has one that matches it. A theme with colors of its own and no `vectorTile` section gets a scheme derived from its background, text color and palette. See docs/VECTOR-TILES.md.

### Settings and export controls

A plot's settings pane, export panel, buttons and context menu take its theme's background and text color, so a dark theme gets dark controls; the rest of their colors are mixed from those two. A page restyles them with CSS custom properties, set on the plot or any element around it: `--hm-controls-background`, `--hm-controls-color`, `--hm-controls-accent` (selection, focus and the Download button) and `--hm-controls-font`.

```css
.dashboard { --hm-controls-accent: #0f766e; --hm-controls-font: "Inter", sans-serif; }
```

### Edit themes as JSON

Built-in theme definitions live in `src/lib/plot/themes/`. Copy one JSON file, edit its presentation fields, and use `createTheme(definition)` in Svelte or `hm.load_theme("my-theme.json")` in Python. A JSON theme can also hold only its differences, with `"extends": "dark"`. The accompanying `theme.schema.json` describes the accepted fields. Python packages include the built-in JSON files.

### Axis titles and tick labels

Themes set axis title position, rotation, placement and spacing with `axes.titlePosition`
(`start`, `middle`, `end`), `titleAngle` (`auto` or degrees), `titlePlacement`
(`inside`, `outside`) and `titleOffset` (CSS pixels). Tick labels have `tickLabelAngle`,
`tickLabelAlign` (`auto`, `start`, `middle`, `end`), `tickLabelPlacement` and `tickLabelOffset`.
These defaults apply to each axis; explicit Plot or Frame axis settings take precedence.
`auto` title rotation follows the axis orientation.

```python
readable = hm.create_theme(extends="hmplot", axes={
    "title_position": "middle", "title_placement": "outside",
    "title_offset": 10, "tick_label_offset": 5,
})
```

JSON and JavaScript use camelCase keys; Python accepts snake_case. The neutral presets use outside axis titles. Notebook and Observable use compact typography;
Presentation enlarges ticks, legends, controls and marks as well as headings. Explicit props win.

### HMPlot's default look

The default preset, **`hmplot`**, pairs a white background and Source Sans 3 with a bright,
contrasting categorical palette: blue, orange, green, rose, violet, gold and cyan. Ordinary
lines use the first palette color. Solid 10 px points have no outlines; bold outside titles,
subtle major grids and small filled arrows provide readable axes. Cartesian data is masked
at the axes interior. It remains suitable for embedding on a white page.

**`minimal`** uses airy spacing, 14 px outside labels, 9 px outlined points and no tick marks,
baselines, arrows, grids, full border or mask. **`ink`** uses outlined points, inside ticks and
charcoal, ink red, blue, green, violet and ochre. The `colorblind` preset is available for a dedicated categorical palette.

### Continuous colors

Every preset supplies both a categorical `palette` and a continuous `colormap`. HMPlot and
Minimal use Viridis; Paper, Journal and Colorblind use Cividis. Ink and Blueprint use custom
sequential maps, and other themes choose a matching built-in map. The colormap applies to
numeric fill/color channels and their legends unless a mark or scale overrides it.

```js
const theme = createTheme({ extends: "hmplot", palette: ["#3478c7", "#df5263"], colormap: "Plasma" });
```

```python
theme = hm.create_theme(extends="hmplot", colormap="Plasma")
```

### Axis defaults

`axes.line`, `ticks`, `tickSize`, `tickDirection`, `titleFontWeight`, `gridColor`, `gridWidth`
and `gridDash` set each axis's default appearance. Omit `gridColor` to adapt it to the
background. `axes.frame` adds a rectangular border and `axes.mask` clips data to its interior.
Journal, Graph and Blueprint use full borders without arrows. Minimal disables masks;
other presets enable them for rectangular Cartesian 2D plots.

`axes.threeD: { style: "box", gridPlanes: [] }` supplies defaults for `axes3d={true}`;
`triad` and plane names `xy`, `xz`, `yz` are also supported. Axes and inherited grids stay off
by default outside 2D Cartesian plots; explicit Plot/Frame settings take precedence.

Themes accept `axes.arrow` (`none`, `start`, `end`, `both`) and `axes.arrowSize` in CSS pixels
(Python: `arrow_size`). Explicit axis settings override them, for example
`x={{ arrow: "none" }}` to remove an x-axis arrow.

### Neutral presentation presets

These are existing presets, with structural differences independent of their palettes:

| Preset | Presentation |
| --- | --- |
| `paper` | centered serif report heading, bottom inline legend, moderate outlined points |
| `journal` | restrained centered heading, full frame and inside ticks, open points, compact side legend |
| `presentation` | 32 px headings, 18 px ticks/legends/controls, 14 px points and 3 px lines |
| `notebook` | 16 px heading, 12 px labels, close offsets and compact top legend |
| `minimal` | generous title spacing, outside labels, no grid or frame, sparse outlined points |
| `ink` | outlined charcoal points, crisp lines, inside ticks and stacked side legend |
| `bureau` | editorial heading, light axis titles, quiet grid and top inline legend |
| `observable` | compact heading, light axis titles, translucent points and bottom inline legend |

The default `hmplot` preset is unchanged. Presets leave axis domains, encodings, category order,
bins, interaction and dynamic-margin policy to the chart. Theme point sizes apply only where
an explicit size or size encoding is absent. Open points use a transparent fill; an explicit
fill encoding takes precedence.

### Presentation recipes and capability boundaries

Start with a full preset and add narrowly scoped partials. A later partial overrides earlier
keys for its named mark kinds; it does not reset other kinds or the palette. A nested Theme
scopes the same merge to a subtree. Explicit mark props and encodings still win. Alignment is
independent of hierarchy: combine `title/editorial` with `title/centered` when desired.

The executable Python recipes in `src/recipes/27_centered_report.py` through
`31_compact_colorbar.py` appear in [the recipe collection](/HMPlot/recipes.md). The matching Svelte
patterns below use the same existing props (imports from `hmplot`, chart templates from
`hmplot/charts`). Here `data` is the table supplied by the corresponding recipe.

Centered report:

```svelte
<Theme value={{ extends: ["paper", "title/centered", "legend/inline-bottom", "marks/lines-medium"] }}>
  <Plot {data} title="Quarterly observations" x={{label:"Month"}} y={{label:"Value"}}>
    <Line x="month" y="value" label="Observed" />
    <Points x="month" y="value" size={9} />
  </Plot>
</Theme>
```

Dense scatter; keep axis preferences on the intended axis:

```svelte
<Theme value={{ extends: ["notebook", "marks/points-dense", "legend/compact"] }}>
  <Plot {data} x={{tickCount:4,grid:"off"}} y={{tickCount:4,grid:"major"}}>
    <Points x="x" y="y" fill="station" />
  </Plot>
</Theme>
```

A supplied interval and local reference rule; the rule does not restyle data Lines:

```svelte
<Theme value={{ extends: ["paper", "marks/lines-fine", "marks/intervals-crisp"] }}>
  <Plot {data}>
    <Area x="x" lower="lo" upper="hi" opacity={0.15} />
    <ErrorBars x="x" lower="lo" upper="hi" />
    <Line x="x" y="y" label="Estimate" />
    <RuleY y={4} color="#64748b" width={1} dash={[5,3]} />
  </Plot>
</Theme>
```

An annotation card uses explicit box and leader props. Leave space for its offset, and use
`box={false}` for an unboxed halo note; these are not theme mark keys:

```svelte
<Callout x={1} y={4} text="Observed response" dx={30} dy={-45} color="#172033"
  box={{fill:"#f8fafc",outlineColor:"#64748b",outlineWidth:1,padding:7,radius:5}}
  leader={{color:"#64748b",width:1}} />
```

Compact colorbar text and horizontal placement; keep exactly the guide the chart needs:

```svelte
<Theme value={{ extends: ["notebook", "legend/compact", "legend/inline-bottom"] }}>
  <Plot legend={false}>
    <Heatmap bind:this={cells} fill={matrix} fillScale={colors} pixelated />
    <Legend for={cells} channel="fill" label="Correlation" position="bottom" />
  </Plot>
</Theme>
```

For axis density use `x={{tickCount:4}}` (Python `tick_count`), value-axis-only grid use
`x={{grid:"off"}}` and `y={{grid:"major"}}`, and categorical rotation use
`x={{tickLabelAngle:30}}`, 45 or 90. These do not rotate the y labels. Short date labels use
`x={{format:"%b %d",tickCount:4}}` on datetime data. Shared outer facet labels belong to the
figure's Facet configuration rather than a global theme.

The development gallery at `/test/theme-comparison` compares the same observations using a
shared palette by default. It includes sparse/dense points, explicit bubble sizes with a
size guide, intervals and rules, grouped bars, histograms, dates, long legends, a matrix,
callouts and inputs. Switch off the shared palette to inspect the original palettes. The
partial selector never changes data encodings; select sparse-points to inspect open interiors,
since an explicit categorical fill in scatter deliberately overrides a transparent default.

| Family | Shipped support and remaining boundary |
| --- | --- |
| Titles | alignment, title size/weight, subtitle/caption sizes, block spacing; separate subtitle weight/color is deferred |
| Axes | existing appearance tokens plus quiet/print/offset partials; tick density, date formats and per-axis rotation use axis props |
| Spacing | automatic text measurement and label-offset partials; no fixed-margin or navigation-policy changes in presets |
| Legends | placement, text/swatch sizing, heading weights and automatic mark shapes; entries flow/wrap with available space, but explicit entry-gap and label-wrap controls are deferred |
| Points | dense, outlined, open and large partials; explicit size/color encodings retain their values |
| Lines and intervals | three Line widths and crisp ErrorBars; fill opacity stays separate from data-line opacity |
| Bars | Bar opacity routes through Prism; Prism does not draw outlines, so outlined bars remain deferred; category spacing uses explicit `bandFraction`, such as 0.72, and never changes histogram bins |
| Rules | RuleX/RuleY already consume color, width and opacity; role-specific dash uses the rule's explicit `dash` prop |
| Bands | explicit BandX/BandY fill/opacity/outline or Area interval bounds; no confidence level is inferred from styling |
| Callouts | themed text only; boxes and leaders use existing explicit props, with anchor and offsets preserved |
| Colorbars | placement changes orientation; current ramps are fixed at 180×18 px horizontally or 18×160 vertically, with fixed 10 px tick text; thickness/length, rounded clips, extension caps and stepped-scale semantics are deferred |
| Matrices | categorical axes and supplied per-cell label colors; no static theme token automatically contrasts every colormap |
| Controls | font and accent tokens only; target sizing, disabled/focus-state redesign and row spacing remain separate follow-ups |
| Print/high contrast | neutral text contrast is tested, but palettes alone do not guarantee distinguishable grayscale series or accessibility; dedicated overlays remain proposals |

The gallery's matrix demonstrates one explicit contrast recipe, not a general automatic-label
API: its declared black-to-white **sRGB** ramp maps each value to `gray=(value+1)/2`. Convert
gray to linear luminance (`gray/12.92` below 0.04045, otherwise `((gray+0.055)/1.055)^2.4`),
then choose black above luminance 0.179 and white otherwise. Supply those colors as an explicit
Text color scale. For a different colormap, sample its actual colors and compare relative
luminance; the threshold on the data value does not transfer. Heatmap SVG output currently
uses an embedded raster (`mode="auto"`), with vector labels and colorbar.

### Related examples

- [Theme presets](/HMPlot/examples/themes.md)

## Facet

Page: /reference/python/facet.md

Small multiples: one cell per category, per field, or per pair of fields (a scatterplot matrix).

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {
    "x": [1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 3, 4],
    "y": [3, 1, 4, 2, 2, 4, 1, 3],
    "group": ["a", "a", "a", "a", "b", "b", "b", "b"],
}
with hm.Facet(data=data, column="group") as facet:
    with hm.Plot(height=300, axes2d=True):
        hm.Points(x="x", y="y")
facet
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Facet, Plot, Points } from "hmplot";
  const data = {
    x: [1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 3, 4],
    y: [3, 1, 4, 2, 2, 4, 1, 3],
    group: ["a", "a", "a", "a", "b", "b", "b", "b"],
  };
</script>

<Facet {data} column="group">
  <Plot height={300} axes2d>
    <Points x="x" y="y" />
  </Plot>
</Facet>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

- `cache_size` (`number`): How many offscreen cells stay mounted besides the visible ones; 0 keeps none. Default: `64`.
- `layout` (`"bands" | "grid"`): In a Facet inside a Plot, how the cells divide the plot: "bands" along the split dimension (the other dimension is the Plot's), or "grid", each cell with its own x and y. Default: "grid" with fields or pairs, else "bands".
- `band_padding` (`number`): The space between bands in the "bands" layout, as a fraction of a band. Default: `0.1`.
- `data` (`table`): A table or live pipeline output for the cells; the same as wrapping the Facet in Data.
- `key` (`column | column[]`): The column, or columns, that identify each row of data across updates, as on Data.
- `name` (`string`): The grid's name in its settings pane. Default: `"Facet"`.
- `settings` (`{showTrigger, showExport, menu}`): showTrigger: false hides the grid's settings and export buttons; showExport: false hides its export button and its cells' Export menu entry; menu: false leaves the browser's own context menu on its cells.
- `row` (`column`): A categorical column: one row of cells per value.
- `column` (`column`): A categorical column: one column of cells per value.
- `wrap` (`number`): The most cells across before the grid wraps, when only one dimension splits the cells.
- `gap` (`number`): Space between the cells. Default: `16` px.
- `row_order` (`category[]`): The rows to show, in order: values of row (a numeric row column needs this), or fields with fields or pairs. Rows with other values are left out. Default: the column's category order.
- `column_order` (`category[]`): The columns to show, in order, as row_order. Default: the column's category order.
- `fields` (`column[] | {row} | {column}`): One cell per field, over the same rows: in each cell the column value is that field and field holds its name. A list lays the cells along columns; {row: [...]} stacks them.
- `pairs` (`column[] | {x, y}`): A scatterplot matrix: each cell's x and y are two of these fields; {x: [...], y: [...]} makes a rectangular one. It cannot combine with row, column or fields.
- `triangle` (`"full" | "upper" | "lower"`): With a list of pairs, the cells of the whole matrix or of its upper or lower triangle. Default: `"full"`.
- `diagonal` (`boolean`): With pairs, whether to draw the cells that pair a field with itself. Default: `True`.
- `as_` (`{value, field} | {x, y}`): New names for the columns the cells alias ({value, field} with fields, {x, y} with pairs), when the table has columns of those names.
- `scales` (`"shared" | "field" | "free-x" | "free-y" | "free-z" | "free"`): How the cells share axis domains: "shared", one per axis; "field", one per plotted column; "free-x", "free-y", "free-z" or "free", each cell its own. Default: "field" with fields or pairs, else "shared".
- `resolve` (`{color, size, width, shape}`): Whether each appearance scale is "shared" across the cells or "independent" in each. Default: "shared" for each.
- `link` (`"auto" | "x" | "xy" | "y" | "none" | "grid"`): Pan and zoom the cells together along x, y or both; "grid" links x down each column and y along each row; "none" keeps each cell's own. "auto" links the axes the cells share (not free in scales), which the grid labels once, on its outer cells. A Facet inside a Plot shares its camera and takes "none" (or "auto"). Default: `"auto"`.
- `legend` (`boolean | {position} | "cell"`): One legend for the whole grid, explaining what the marks map from data and listing the labeled marks: true or {position} shows it, false hides it even when the cells ask for one, "cell" gives each cell its own. Default: the cells' legend around the grid (by default, a legend for each color mapped from a category column).
- `title` (`string`): A title above the grid, part of it on screen and in its exports.
- `subtitle` (`string`): A line under the title, smaller and lighter.
- `caption` (`string`): A note under the grid, such as its source, smaller and lighter.
- `filename` (`string`): Save an export to this file when the Facet's with block closes; the suffix picks PNG, SVG, PDF or HTML.
- `export_options` (`object`): Options for that export, such as scale for PNG or mode and width for SVG and PDF; needs filename.
- `schema` (`object`): Column types for data, such as {"day": "datetime"}, as on Data.

### Usage

row/column choose partition fields; wrap is for single-field layouts. Shared domains are the default for categories, link defaults to auto, linking the shared axes, which the grid labels once on its outer cells. Cells preserve camera and settings by category identity. A transform inside the facet runs per subset.

### Fields and pairs

`fields={["temp", "rain"]}` makes one cell per field over the same rows. Inside a cell, `value` is the cell's field (its identity, metadata and scales: a strip brush on it constrains the field itself) and `field` holds the field's name, one categorical column across the cells. A list lays the cells along columns (`{column: [...]}` says so explicitly); `{row: [...]}` stacks them; a categorical split may take the other dimension (`fields={[...]} row="species"`), and on the same dimension is an error. The order of the fields dimension (`columnOrder` for a list) picks and orders the fields; a name that is not one of them is an empty cell. `pairs={["a", "b", "c"]}` is a scatterplot matrix whose cells alias `x` and `y` to their two fields, with `triangle` ("full", "upper", "lower") and `diagonal`; `pairs={{x: [...], y: [...]}}` is rectangular (columns from x, rows from y). `as` renames the aliases (`{value, field}` or `{x, y}`) when the table has columns of those names, which the aliases otherwise hide inside the cells. With fields or pairs, scales default to `"field"`: a field keeps one domain across the cells (and across x and y in pairs), columns of the table stay shared, and values computed inside a cell follow the cell's field. An embedded Facet with fields or pairs defaults to `layout="grid"`. Every cell shows the same observations, so selection, hover and brushing work by observation across cells and `connect(facet.endpoint("values"))` needs no key. A Facet split by a Fold's key still works and gives the same cells. The grid has one legend: cells add their marks to it, and `legend` (true or `{position}`) shows the automatic legend around the grid. `legend="cell"` restores one legend per cell.

### Related examples

- [Facets & transforms](/HMPlot/examples/facets.md)

## Partition

Page: /reference/python/partition.md

Repeats its children once per group of rows, all in the same frame: one line, fit or density per group.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {
    "x": [1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 3, 4],
    "y": [3, 1, 4, 2, 2, 4, 1, 3],
    "group": ["a", "a", "a", "a", "b", "b", "b", "b"],
}
with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True) as plot:
    with hm.Partition(by="group"):
        hm.Line(x="x", y="y")
plot
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Line, Partition, Plot } from "hmplot";
  const data = {
    x: [1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 3, 4],
    y: [3, 1, 4, 2, 2, 4, 1, 3],
    group: ["a", "a", "a", "a", "b", "b", "b", "b"],
  };
</script>

<Plot {data} height={300} axes2d>
  <Partition by="group">
    <Line x="x" y="y" />
  </Partition>
</Plot>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

- `by` (`column | column[]`): The column, or columns, whose values split the rows into groups; the children repeat once per group, in the column's order. Rows missing a value form a last "(missing)" group.
- `limit` (`number`): The most groups Partition mounts; more is an error. Default: `256`.
- `legend_groups` (`boolean`): One legend entry per group, labelled by its value, instead of one per mark. Default: `False`.
- `name` (`string`): The partition's name in the settings pane, where each group's marks are listed under it. Default: `"Partition"`.

### Usage

`Partition` mounts its children once per distinct value of `by` — a column name, or a list of names for the combinations — with each copy bound to that group's rows. Every group draws in the **same frame**, with the parent's scales, axes, camera, legend, and renderer: there is no layout and no cell. One key makes one group per value that has rows, so a value that disappears from the table (or is filtered out upstream) takes its group with it; a list of keys keeps every combination of those values. Groups follow the key column's order: first appearance for a plain array, dictionary order for a categorical column (every string column from Python), ascending for a numeric one. Rows whose key is missing are not dropped: they form a trailing group labelled `(missing)` whose value is `null`.

Because every group contributes to the inherited domains, the frame looks exactly as it would if the children had been mounted once over the whole table. Transforms inside a Partition run once per group, which is what makes a per-group Density, fit, or summary a two-line change.

Use `Facet` instead when each group should get its own plot; a Facet cannot be nested inside a Partition (partition inside the facet instead). A `Frame` inside a Partition is allowed and gives each group an inset.

`bind:this` gives a `PartitionHandle`: `getGroups()` lists the mounted groups, each a `PartitionGroup` with its `key` (JSON of the key values), `values` by column, display `label` and its marks' legend sources; `whenSettled()` waits for every group; `endpoint(name, {at})` selects the mark named `name` in every group for `connect()`. Python's `await partition.groups()` returns the keys, values, labels and mark labels.

Legends show one entry per authored mark, however many groups there are. `legendGroups` gives each group its own entry, labelled by the key values, for marks whose appearance does not otherwise vary by group; clicking one entry hides only that group.

### Related examples

- [One density per group, one frame](/HMPlot/examples/partition-density.md)

## Panels

Page: /reference/python/panels.md

Stacks Plots over one shared x: one domain, panned and zoomed together, its axis drawn once under the stack.

### Example

```python
import math
import hmplot as hm

days = list(range(120))
data = {"day": days, "price": [100 + 10 * math.sin(d / 8) + d / 6 for d in days],
        "volume": [50 + 30 * abs(math.cos(d / 5)) for d in days]}
## Two Plots over one x: zooming or panning either moves both; the axis is drawn once.
with hm.Scene() as chart:
    with hm.Data(data):
        with hm.Panels(x={"label": "Day"}):
            with hm.Plot(height=220, y={"label": "Price"}):
                hm.Line(x="day", y="price")
            with hm.Plot(height=120, y={"label": "Volume"}):
                hm.charts.Bar(x="day", y="volume", orientation="vertical")
chart
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Data, Panels, Plot, Line } from "hmplot";
  import { Bar } from "hmplot/charts";
  const days = Array.from({ length: 120 }, (_, d) => d);
  const data = { day: days, price: days.map((d) => 100 + 10 * Math.sin(d / 8) + d / 6), volume: days.map((d) => 50 + 30 * Math.abs(Math.cos(d / 5))) };
</script>

<!-- Two Plots over one x: zooming or panning either moves both; the axis is drawn once. -->
<Data value={data}>
  <Panels x={{ label: "Day" }}>
    <Plot height={220} y={{ label: "Price" }}><Line x="day" y="price" /></Plot>
    <Plot height={120} y={{ label: "Volume" }}><Bar x="day" y="volume" orientation="vertical" /></Plot>
  </Panels>
</Data>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

- `x` (`{domain, transform, label, ...}`): Settings for the shared x axis (label, format, domain, ...), under each Plot's own x settings. Only the last Plot draws the axis; the others show their data over the same domain.
- `gap` (`number`): Space between the Plots. Default: `6` px.

### Usage

Panels stacks Plots over one shared x, as matplotlib's `sharex` does: its Plots show one x domain (the union of their data, or the domain given in `x`), pan and zoom together along x, and line up their plot areas, so the panels' data share one time line however wide each one's y labels are. Only the last Plot draws the x axis and its title; `x` holds that axis's settings (label, format, domain, ...), under each Plot's own `x`. Each Plot keeps its own y axis, height, title and marks.

```python
with hm.Data(prices):
    with hm.Panels(x={"label": "Trading day"}):
        with hm.Plot(height=240, y={"label": "Price"}):
            hm.Line(x="day", y="price")
        with hm.Plot(height=140, y={"label": "Volume"}):
            hm.charts.Bar(x="day", y="volume", orientation="vertical")
```

A rule at the same x in each panel ([RuleX](rule-x)) marks one moment across them. Use Panels rather than separate Plots in a Column with LinkViews: those link navigation but repeat the axis and leave the plot areas to their own gutters. For a brush on an overview strip that zooms a chart, use [FocusContext](focus-context).

## TableView

Page: /reference/python/table-view.md

The rows of the data around it as an HTML table, live: a Group's groups, a Sort's top rows, a Filter's kept rows; omitted from image exports.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

cars = {"model": ["Civic", "Corolla", "Golf", "Model 3", "Prius", "Mustang"],
        "mpg": [36.0, 34.0, 31.0, 132.0, 52.0, 18.0], "weight": [1250, 1300, 1350, 1610, 1380, 1700]}
with hm.Scene() as scene:
    with hm.Data(cars):
        with hm.Plot(height=260, axes2d=True):
            hm.Points(x="weight", y="mpg", brush=True)
        with hm.Filter(where="@brushed", inactive="all"):
            with hm.Sort(by="mpg", order="desc"):
                hm.TableView(columns=["model", {"field": "mpg", "format": ".0f"}], limit=5, title="Most efficient")
scene
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Data, Filter, Plot, Points, Sort, TableView } from "hmplot";
  const cars = { model: ["Civic", "Corolla", "Golf", "Model 3", "Prius", "Mustang"],
    mpg: [36, 34, 31, 132, 52, 18], weight: [1250, 1300, 1350, 1610, 1380, 1700] };
</script>

<Data value={cars}>
  <Plot height={260} axes2d>
    <Points x="weight" y="mpg" brush />
  </Plot>
  <Filter where="@brushed" inactive="all">
    <Sort by="mpg" order="desc">
      <TableView columns={["model", { field: "mpg", format: ".0f" }]} limit={5} title="Most efficient" />
    </Sort>
  </Filter>
</Data>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

- `columns` (`(column | {field, label, format})[]`): The columns, in order: names, or {field, label, format} with a header and a d3-format or %-pattern, as tooltip fields take. Default: every column.
- `limit` (`number`): How many rows to show; the rest are counted below the table. A Sort above it gives a top N. Default: `100`.
- `title` (`string`): A caption above the table.
- `select` (`boolean | selection | object`): Click a row: true selects its source rows in the data's selection, or give a selection(); input("root").set("id") writes an input (.set(literal(v)) a constant, .reset() its default), and a second click on that row restores its default.
- `hover` (`boolean | selection | object`): Hover a row: true marks its source rows @hovered, or give a selection(); input("focus").set("id") shows the row's id in an input while the pointer is on it.
- `name` (`string`): A name for the table (its element's data-name attribute).

### Usage

TableView shows the rows of the data around it as an HTML table, and follows them: a Group's groups, a Sort's top rows, a Filter's kept rows, a layout's nodes. It is for the lists and readouts a dashboard shows beside its plots, such as the ten most efficient cars under a brush or each region's total, without reading the rows into your own code. Put it inside the same Data as the plots (or inside the transform whose rows it shows), beside a Plot, never inside one.

```python
with hm.Data(cars):
    with hm.Plot():
        hm.Points(x="weight", y="mpg", brush=True)
    with hm.Filter(where="@brushed", inactive="all"):
        with hm.Sort(by="mpg", order="desc"):
            hm.TableView(columns=["model", {"field": "mpg", "label": "MPG", "format": ".1f"}], limit=10)
```

```svelte
<Data value={cars}>
  <Plot><Points x="weight" y="mpg" brush /></Plot>
  <Filter where="@brushed" inactive="all">
    <Sort by="mpg" order="desc">
      <TableView columns={["model", { field: "mpg", label: "MPG", format: ".1f" }]} limit={10} />
    </Sort>
  </Filter>
</Data>
```

- `columns` lists the columns in order, as names or `{ field, label, format }`; values are written as tooltips write them, numbers right-aligned. The default is every column.
- `limit` (100) is how many rows it shows; the rest are counted below it. The rows are read from the GPU when the data changes (a brush moving, an input), `limit` of them, never on every pointer move.
- `select` on a row: `true` selects its source rows in the data's selection, as a click on a mark does, so plots of the same data that `respond` fade the others. `input("model").set("model")` writes the row's value to an input instead ([select](mark-options) on marks takes the same), and a second click on that row restores the input's default.
- `hover` on a row: `true` marks its source rows `@hovered`; `input("model").set("model")` shows the row's value in an input while the pointer is on it.
- TableViews are omitted from PNG, SVG and PDF exports and kept in standalone HTML pages. For a number inside a plot, use [Text](text) of a Group's column; for a sentence with live values, [Title](title).

## Title

Page: /reference/python/title.md

A heading or note beside plots, drawn as text that stays text in SVG and PDF exports.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"x": [1, 2, 3, 4], "y": [3, 1, 4, 2]}
with hm.Scene() as scene:
    hm.Title("Four measurements")
    with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True):
        hm.Points(x="x", y="y")
scene
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Plot, Points, Title } from "hmplot";
  const data = { x: [1, 2, 3, 4], y: [3, 1, 4, 2] };
</script>

<Title text="Four measurements" />
<Plot {data} height={300} axes2d>
  <Points x="x" y="y" />
</Plot>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

- `text` (`string | (string | expression | {value, format})[]`): The text: "\n" breaks a line and {$name} shows an input's value. Python takes it positionally: hm.Title("..."). A readout shows live values: a list of parts, strings and reductions over the Data around the Title (count(where="@brushed"), mean("fare")), or {value, format} with a d3-format string; in Python an f-string does it, hm.Title(f"Selected: {hm.count(where='@brushed'):,}"). A live value follows the data and its selections, written as tooltips write numbers, "—" when no row has one.
- `size` (`"title" | "subtitle" | "caption" | number`): "title", "subtitle" or "caption", sizes that follow the theme's text size, or pixels. Default: `"title"`.
- `weight` (`number | "normal" | "bold"`): The font weight, as in CSS. Default: 600 for a title, 400 otherwise.
- `align` (`"left" | "right" | "center"`): Where the lines sit across the block. Default: `"left"`.
- `color` (`color`): The text color. Default: the theme's text color.
- `font` (`string`): The font, a CSS font-family. Default: the theme's.
- `wrap` (`boolean`): Wrap words at the block's width; false keeps each line whole. Default: `True`.
- `name` (`string`): A name for the block (its element's data-name attribute).

### Usage

Title is plain text for a layout: a figure's heading, a note between plots, a caption under a grid. Its lines break at `"\n"` and wrap at the block's width in the loaded font, and they are drawn as SVG text, so a scene's SVG and PDF exports carry the same lines as vector, searchable text (in the embedded default font). `size` picks the theme's title, subtitle or caption size, or takes pixels. `{$name}` shows an input's value as the input shows it and follows it: `"Temperature anomaly, {$year}"`.

A Title inside a Data is also a **readout** (a KPI, a live count): its text can hold live values, reductions over that data that follow it and its selections, written as tooltips write numbers or in a d3 format, `"—"` when no row has one. In Python an f-string does it; in Svelte `text` is a list of parts:

```python
with hm.Data(trips):
    hm.Title(f"Selected trips: {hm.count(where='@brushed'):,} · mean fare {hm.mean('fare', where='@brushed'):$.2f}")
    with hm.Plot():
        hm.Points(x="distance", y="fare", brush=True)
```

```svelte
<Title text={["Selected trips: ", count({ where: "@brushed" }), " · mean fare ", { value: mean("fare", { where: "@brushed" }), format: "$.2f" }]} />
```

An expression in an f-string is only a live value in Title's text; elsewhere it is an error. For a number beside the data inside a plot, use [Text](text) of a Group's column.

Use Title for publications; Markdown (Python layouts) is for dashboards and exports as an image. A plot's own heading is its `title`, `subtitle` and `caption`.

### Related examples

- [Titles, bands and callouts](/HMPlot/examples/annotations.md)

## Mapping

Page: /reference/python/mapping.md

Channels (x, y, fill, size, ...) that the marks inside it share.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"x": [1, 2, 3, 4], "y": [3, 1, 4, 2]}
with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True) as plot:
    with hm.Mapping(x="x", y="y"):
        hm.Line()
        hm.Points()
plot
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Line, Mapping, Plot, Points } from "hmplot";
  const data = { x: [1, 2, 3, 4], y: [3, 1, 4, 2] };
</script>

<Plot {data} height={300} axes2d>
  <Mapping x="x" y="y">
    <Line />
    <Points />
  </Mapping>
</Plot>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

#### Position

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `x`, `y`, `z`, `position`.

#### Appearance

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `fill`, `color`, `size`, `width`, `opacity`, `outline_color`, `outline_opacity`, `outline_width`.

#### Scales

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `fill_scale`, `color_scale`, `size_scale`, `width_scale`.

#### Display

- `name` (`string`): The Mapping's name in the settings pane; the marks inside do not take it.

Also these options the marks share (described on Mark options): `visible`, `glow`.

#### Interaction

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `select`, `hover`, `brush`, `respond`, `selection_opacity`, `enter_effect`, `exit_effect`.

#### Animation

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `animation`, `animation_duration`, `animation_easing`.

#### Series
