- `series` (`column | column[] | array`): Split the rows into separate paths, one per value of this column (Line, Area). Without it, a Line colored or an Area filled by a category column splits by that column.

#### Segment ends

- `start` (`channel`): Where each segment starts (Segments, Arrows): a column of positions or an N x 2 (N x 3) array.
- `end` (`channel`): Where each segment ends, as start.

#### Symbol rotation

- `rotation` (`number`): The symbol's rotation. Default: `0` degrees.

#### Symbol

- `shape` (`string | column | string[]`): The point symbol: a shape name, a column of categories mapped to shapes, or one name per row. Default: `"circle"`.
- `shape_scale` (`scale`): A categorical() scale from the shape column's categories to shape names.

### Usage

Explicit mark properties win, then nearest Mapping, outer Mapping, and defaults. Mapped field names resolve in the consuming mark’s Data scope. Event handlers, names, and structural references are not inherited.

### Related examples

- [Shared mappings](/HMPlot/examples/shared-mappings.md)

## Frame

Page: /reference/python/frame.md

A coordinate frame inside a Plot: its own scales for some marks (a second y axis), or a small chart placed within its parent.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"x": [1, 2, 3, 4], "y": [3, 1, 4, 2], "count": [40, 10, 25, 5]}
with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True) as plot:
    hm.Line(x="x", y="y")
    with hm.Frame(y={"domain": "auto", "side": "right"}):
        hm.Line(x="x", y="count")
plot
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Frame, Line, Plot } from "hmplot";
  const data = { x: [1, 2, 3, 4], y: [3, 1, 4, 2], count: [40, 10, 25, 5] };
</script>

<Plot {data} height={300} axes2d>
  <Line x="x" y="y" />
  <Frame y={{ domain: "auto", side: "right" }}>
    <Line x="x" y="count" />
  </Frame>
</Plot>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

- `animation_group` (`column | column[] | null`): Match animation rows by these columns within each filtered/transformed snapshot; selections keep Data.key. null restores key/position matching. Default: inherited; otherwise Data.key, then position.
- `animate_bounds` (`boolean`): Animate numeric domains and ranges independently of mark animation; structural changes and direction reversals snap. Default: the parent frame's (false on Plot).
- `bounds_duration` (`number`): Duration of scale transitions, independent of mark timing. Default: the parent frame's (300). In ms.
- `bounds_easing` (`"linear" | "quad-in" | "quad-out" | "quad-in-out" | "cubic-in" | "cubic-out" | "cubic-in-out" | "sine-in-out"`): Easing of scale transitions, independent of mark timing. Default: the parent frame's (cubic-in-out).
- `axis_frame` (`boolean`): Draw a complete rectangular border in 2D Cartesian frames without duplicate ticks or labels. Default: the theme's.
- `axis_mask` (`boolean`): Clip marks and picking to the rectangular 2D Cartesian axes interior, intersecting ancestor masks. Default: the theme's.
- `placement` (`"fit" | {anchor, size, orientation, rotation}`): Anchors a fixed-size frame at a point of its parent: anchor in parent data coordinates, size in CSS pixels (2D) or world units (3D), and an optional rotation. "fit" centers it in a Cartesian parent's domain, across 90% of the parent's shorter side, and refits it as the parent's view changes. It cannot combine with ranges.
- `rules` (`{axis, value, label, color, width, dash}[]`): Reference lines in this frame's coordinates (a spoke or circle in a polar frame), as on Plot.
- `bands` (`{axis, from, to, label, color, opacity}[]`): Shaded spans of this frame's x or y axis behind its marks, as on Plot.
- `coordinates` (`"cartesian" | "polar" | "spherical"`): This frame's coordinate system. A frame that changes its parent's needs x and y ranges or a placement. Default: the parent's.
- `spherical_view` (`"globe" | "projected"`): How a 3D spherical frame shows the sphere, as on Plot. Default: the parent's.
- `angle_unit` (`"degrees" | "radians" | "extent" | "custom"`): The unit of this frame's polar or spherical angles, as on Plot. Default: the parent's.
- `angle_period` (`number`): Angle units in one turn when angle_unit is "custom", as on Plot. Default: the parent's.
- `base_radius` (`number`): The radius at zero in a polar or spherical frame, as on Plot. Default: the parent's.
- `radial_scale` (`number`): The radius per unit in a polar or spherical frame, as on Plot. Default: the parent's.
- `polar_axis` (`"X" | "Y" | "Z"`): The axis a 3D polar frame turns around, as on Plot. Default: the parent's.
- `projection` (`"equirectangular" | "mercator" | "equal-area" | "orthographic" | "equal-earth" | "natural-earth" | "albers" | "albers-usa"`): The map projection of a spherical frame, as on Plot. A spherical frame with ranges must be a flat orthographic disk (radial_scale 0). Default: the parent's.
- `projection_center` (`[number, number]`): The map's center [longitude, latitude], as on Plot. Default: the parent's.
- `parallels` (`[number, number]`): The albers projection's two standard parallels, as on Plot. Default: the parent's.
- `atmosphere` (`boolean | {color, thickness}`): A glow around a spherical frame's globe in a 3D plot: true, or a CSS color (default "#7fb2ff") and a thickness as a fraction of the radius (default 0.1). It is not picked and has no legend. SVG and PDF exports draw the whole plot as an image. Default: `False`.
- `x` (`{domain, range, transform, label, ...}`): Omit it to share the parent's x scale. A domain (or "auto") gives the frame its own; a range places the frame within its parent, in parent data coordinates, and fits the frame's own data unless a domain is given.
- `y` (`{domain, range, transform, label, ...}`): The frame's y, as x: a domain with side "right" makes a second y axis.
- `z` (`{domain, range, transform, label, ...}`): The frame's z in a 3D plot, as x.
- `scale_defaults` (`{color, size, width}`): Defaults for the continuous color, size and width scales this frame's marks make, as on Plot.
- `name` (`string`): The frame's name in the settings pane. Default: `"Frame"`.
- `auto_bounds` (`boolean`): Fit the frame's missing domains to its marks' data; an explicit domain always wins. Default: `True`.

### Usage

Each dimension inherits its parent's scale unless you give it a domain, "auto", or a range. A dimension with its own domain is linear unless you set `transform`, even inside a log or sqrt parent; a range-only dimension keeps the parent's transform. A range places the child in parent data coordinates, composed through linear, log, and sqrt ancestors. `placement` anchors a fixed-size frame at a parent data position (CSS pixels in 2D, world units in 3D) with optional rotation. Moving a placement moves the frame and re-prepares nothing inside it; in a Python scene its numbers may be expressions of inputs, evaluated as they change (`{"anchor": [8 * hm.cos(hm.input.day / 58), 0, 0], ...}`: the gallery's solar system orbits its planets this way). `placement="fit"` centers the frame in a Cartesian parent's domain (at the middle of each axis as drawn, on log, sqrt and symlog axes too), across 90% of the parent's shorter side, and refits it as the parent pans, zooms or resizes; a Pie places its own polar Frame this way.

Shift-drag on a child frame's tick strip brushes the column its marks plot on that axis, counting the marks of frames inside it that inherit that axis; a twin axis (a child with its own axis and no range) brushes on its own strip too. The band is drawn only on the strip, and a column shared with other strips shows the same band on each; editing any of them edits the one constraint.

A child frame's axis titles follow its own dimensions: one it owns is titled by its own label, else by the column its marks plot on it; one it inherits is titled by the frame it inherits from, where its marks' columns count (see [Frame axis titles](frame#axis-titles)).

Child axes are drawn on the child's own boundary; inherited dimensions do not duplicate their axes. A dimension a child owns draws its axis once it has a domain: one you give, or the extent of the marks that plot on it. Until then it draws no axis, so a range-only child whose marks all sit in a Frame inside it that sets its own x (a Frame in every facet cell, say) shows only its y axis.

### Animated scales

Set `animateBounds={true}` on a Frame to transition numeric `x`, `y`, and `z` domains and
ranges, including inferred domains. `boundsDuration` (milliseconds) and `boundsEasing`
configure scale transitions independently of mark animation. Nested Frames inherit these
scale settings; child marks retain their own `animation`, `animationDuration`, and
`animationEasing` settings. Plot accepts the same bounds controls for its implicit frame.
Python uses `animate_bounds`, `bounds_duration`, and `bounds_easing`.

Transitions start from the layout currently displayed, including when interrupted. Guides,
marks, picking, masks, and PNG/SVG/PDF exports all read that displayed mapping. A frozen
animation clock freezes scales too. Initial layout, categorical scales, changes of transform,
and interval direction reversals arrive immediately instead of interpolating through an
invalid or zero-width scale. Scale endpoints interpolate in data units. Placement and
projection parameters are not animated by this option.

The [Streamgraph example](/HMPlot/examples/streamgraph.md) transitions its inferred scale and areas
together, with equivalent Svelte and Python programs.

```svelte
<Frame animateBounds boundsDuration={700} boundsEasing="cubic-in-out"
  y={{ domain: [0, maximum] }}>
  <Area x="time" upper="value" />
</Frame>
```

### Axis borders and masks

`axisFrame={true}` adds a complete border to a rectangular 2D Cartesian frame. It does not add duplicate ticks or labels on the opposite edges. Set each axis's `line` independently to hide its baseline while retaining ticks, titles, or arrows.

`axisMask={true}` clips data to the axes interior, including parts of large points, thick lines, fills, and data text that cross an edge. The `hmplot` theme enables masking; `minimal` leaves it off. Use `axisMask={false}` to allow overflow from this frame. An enabled ancestor mask still applies, so a child cannot draw outside a masked parent. Nested ranged frames, rotated Cartesian placements, and facet cells use their own boundaries.

Masks work even when axis lines are hidden. They leave guides, titles, legends, brush handles, and controls visible. Hidden fragments cannot be picked, and visible fragments retain their normal interactions. Brushing continues to store constraints in data units; masking does not filter the underlying table or clear an existing selection when you pan.

PNG uses the same fragment mask as the screen; SVG and PDF use matching clip paths, preserving transparent margins. This option supports rectangular 2D Cartesian surfaces. Theme masks are ignored on polar, spherical, and 3D frames; explicitly enabling `axisMask` or `axisFrame` there reports an error. Python uses `axis_mask` and `axis_frame`.

`invert: true` on an axis definition flips its direction on screen — the domain runs top-to-bottom for y, right-to-left for x, near-to-far for z. It is a reversed output range, so automatic domains, log and sqrt transforms, brushing, nearby picking, and ticks all keep working; the settings pane shows it as an Invert checkbox next to the transform. Explicit domains override inference; hidden decorations do not disable the scale. `scaleDefaults` configures automatic appearance mappings for compatible data channels.

> **SVG and PDF export**
>
> **Vector, except** a spherical Frame drawn as a globe, or a Frame in a 3D plot whose view holds a mark with no vector form there (see [Plot](plot)): SVG and PDF exports draw all of that view's marks as one image, and `mode="vector"` refuses it. In other 3D plots a Frame's 2D marks are vectors, drawn back to front by depth. The Frame's axes, `rules` (dashed ones too) and `bands` stay vector. An `atmosphere` makes the whole plot one image: SVG and PDF exports draw all of the plot's marks, with the atmosphere, as one image (its axes, titles and legends stay vector), and `mode="vector"` refuses it. See [what is not exported as vector](/HMPlot/docs/export.md).

### Atmosphere

`atmosphere` on a spherical Frame in a 3D plot draws a glowing rim around its globe: `atmosphere` (true) or `atmosphere={{ color: "#7fb2ff", thickness: 0.1 }}`, the thickness a fraction of the globe's radius. It is a slightly larger sphere seen from inside, added onto what is behind it, brightest at the globe's edge and fading outward; it moves with a placed Frame. It is not a mark: it is not picked, it sets no axis domain and has no legend. The solar system example gives the Earth one. PNG exports include it; SVG and PDF exports draw the whole plot as an image (see the note above).

### Axis titles

An axis is titled by its `label`; without one (an empty label or null means automatic), by a categorical position scale's label (`categorical({label})`), else by the name of the one column its marks plot there. Names follow aliases and transform outputs: a Facet over `fields` titles each cell's axis by its field (the column `value` is that field), a Bin's edges and a Histogram's bars by the binned column, a Histogram's height by its normalization (count, proportion or density), and Bar, BoxPlot, Violin and Lollipop by the columns you give them. Constants (a baseline of 0, a Text at `x={5}`) do not count. An axis whose marks plot several different columns, raw arrays, expressions, or nothing has no title at all; set `label`, or hide every title with `axisTitles={false}`. A Frame that sets its own domain, range, transform or scale for a dimension reads only its own label (a twin y axis is not titled by the Plot's label), and a dimension a Frame inherits is titled by the frame that owns it. The 3D box uses the same titles. Automatic titles are never stored as settings: the settings pane shows them as the label's placeholder, and Reset returns to them.

`animationGroup` (`animation_group` in Python) on Data, Plot or Frame matches animated
rows by a column or list of columns independently of Data keys. It inherits through the
tree; a child Frame overrides its branch, and explicit null (Python None) restores
Data-key/position matching. Filter to one row per group before tweening: a country/year
table can keep `key=["country", "year"]` and animate by `"country"` after filtering
to one year. Groups must be unique in each tweened snapshot, and changing the group
column scheme resets motion history. Selection, hover and connections keep Data identity.

### Related examples

- [Nested scales](/HMPlot/examples/nonlinear-frames.md)

## Markdown

Page: /reference/python/markdown.md

Formatted text (emphasis, lists, tables, math) beside plots in a Python layout.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"x": [1, 2, 3, 4], "y": [3, 1, 4, 2]}
with hm.Scene() as scene:
    hm.Markdown("**Four measurements.** The largest is $y = 4$, at $x = 3$.")
    with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True):
        hm.Points(x="x", y="y")
scene
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

- `text` (`string`): The markdown: CommonMark with tables, task lists and $math$; {$name} shows an input's value. Python takes it positionally: hm.Markdown("...").
- `width` (`number | string`): The block's greatest width: pixels, or a CSS length. Default: the container's.
- `font_size` (`number`): The size of the body text; headings scale with it. Default: the theme's text size + 1. In px.
- `color` (`color`): The text color. Default: the theme's text color.
- `font` (`string`): The font, a CSS font-family. Default: the theme's.
- `align` (`"left" | "right" | "center"`): Where the text sits across the block. Default: `"left"`.
- `name` (`string`): A name for the block, in export reports and as its element's data-name.

### Usage

In a Python scene, `hm.Markdown(text)` sits in a Scene, Row, Column or Grid beside plots: CommonMark with GitHub's tables, strikethrough, task lists, autolinks and footnotes, and `$math$` or `$$math$$` typeset by MathJax. Raw HTML is not rendered, and links keep only http(s), mailto and tel URLs. The block takes the theme's font and text color; `width`, `fontSize`, `color`, `font` and `align` override them. `{$name}` shows an input's value as the input shows it (in an f-string, `{{$name}}`).

> **SVG and PDF export**
>
> **Image.** Scene exports place the block as an image of how it looks, captured at the export's raster DPI, and list it in the report as a raster layer: its text is not searchable, and `mode="vector"` refuses it. For text that must stay vector, use Title. See [what is not exported as vector](/HMPlot/docs/export.md).

## Scene

Page: /reference/python/scene.md

The root of a Python display: it holds plots, layouts and inputs and stacks its children top to bottom.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"x": [1, 2, 3, 4], "y": [3, 1, 4, 2]}
with hm.Scene() as scene:
    with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True):
        hm.Points(x="x", y="y")
    with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True):
        hm.Line(x="x", y="y")
scene
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

- `gap` (`number`): Space between the children. Default: `16` px.
- `theme` (`theme`): A theme for everything in the scene: a preset such as hm.themes.dark, hm.create_theme(...), or a definition dict.

### Usage

Optional for a single Plot or Facet. Use Scene with Row, Column, or Grid(columns=...) for dashboards. Its batch_update coordinates changes and its export methods compose the display. Svelte applications use normal markup/CSS for this layout.

> **SVG and PDF export**
>
> **Partly an image.** A Scene's SVG and PDF exports compose its Plots, Facets, Titles and Legends, each as its reference page says; a Markdown block and a 2D Minimap are images, and inputs and a Minimap of a 3D plot are left out. See [what is not exported as vector](/HMPlot/docs/export.md).

### Related examples

- [Linked views & minimap](/HMPlot/examples/linked.md)

## Row

Page: /reference/python/row.md

Puts its children side by side.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"x": [1, 2, 3, 4], "y": [3, 1, 4, 2]}
with hm.Row() as row:
    with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True):
        hm.Points(x="x", y="y")
    with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True):
        hm.Line(x="x", y="y")
row
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

- `gap` (`number`): Space between the children. Default: `16` px.
- `min_width` (`number`): The width each child starts from (with widths, the narrowest share's; the others start in proportion): with wrap on, a child moves to the next line rather than get narrower. Default: `320` px.
- `widths` (`number[]`): Each child's share of the row's width, in order: [3, 2] gives the first child three fifths and the second two fifths at every width (a child past the list takes 1). Default: equal shares.
- `wrap` (`boolean`): Move children to a new line when they no longer fit at min_width. Default: `False`.

### Usage

gap is in pixels. wrap and min_width make a notebook dashboard responsive. `widths=[3, 2]` gives the first child three fifths of the row and the second two fifths at every width; with `wrap=True` the row stacks once its narrowest share would be narrower than `min_width` (`Row(widths=[3, 2], wrap=True, min_width=286, gap=12)` is three fifths and two fifths, 12 px apart, and one column below about 730 px). In Svelte use a flex or grid container rather than importing Row from hmplot: `flex: 3 1 429px` and `flex: 2 1 286px` on the two children of a wrapping flex row lay them out the same.

For inputs beside plots, use `hm.Row(wrap=True, min_width=0)`: inputs keep their natural widths and wrap as space runs out. This replaces Controls. The row shares its surrounding input context.

### Related examples

- [Linked views & minimap](/HMPlot/examples/linked.md)

## Column

Page: /reference/python/column.md

Stacks its children top to bottom.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"x": [1, 2, 3, 4], "y": [3, 1, 4, 2]}
with hm.Column() as column:
    with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True):
        hm.Points(x="x", y="y")
    with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True):
        hm.Line(x="x", y="y")
column
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

- `gap` (`number`): Space between the children. Default: `16` px.

### Usage

A Python layout container with gap in pixels. Data/transform scopes do not add visible layout boxes. In Svelte use ordinary document layout.

### Related examples

- [Linked views & minimap](/HMPlot/examples/linked.md)

## Grid

Page: /reference/python/grid.md

Lays its children out in rows of equal columns (Python hm.Grid).

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"x": [1, 2, 3, 4], "a": [3, 1, 4, 2], "b": [1, 3, 2, 4], "c": [2, 4, 3, 1], "d": [4, 3, 2, 1]}
with hm.Grid(columns=2) as grid:
    for name in ["a", "b", "c", "d"]:
        with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True):
            hm.Line(x="x", y=name)
grid
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

- `columns` (`number`): How many columns of equal width. Default: `2`.
- `gap` (`number`): Space between the children. Default: `16` px.

### Usage

Python's hm.Grid(columns=2) is a layout grid, beside Row and Column; the scene adapter names that node LayoutGrid. Interpolation is Interpolate. Svelte uses CSS grid.

### Related examples

- [Linked views & minimap](/HMPlot/examples/linked.md)

## LinkViews

Page: /reference/python/link-views.md

Makes 2D plots pan and zoom together, over one shared domain.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"x": [1, 2, 3, 4], "y": [3, 1, 4, 2]}
with hm.Scene() as scene:
    with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True) as top:
        hm.Points(x="x", y="y")
    with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True) as bottom:
        hm.Line(x="x", y="y")
    hm.LinkViews(top, bottom)
scene
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

- `axes` (`"x" | "y" | "xy"`): Which axes follow when one of the plots pans or zooms. The plots are given positionally: hm.LinkViews(first, second). Default: `"xy"`.
- `scales` (`"shared" | "free"`): "shared" shows one domain on the linked axes, the union of the plots' domains (their data, or an explicit domain), so the same value lines up in each; "free" keeps each plot's own. A plot's explicit domain is kept either way. Default: `"shared"`.

### Usage

Pass the Plot handles positionally: hm.LinkViews(first, second, axes='x'). Links compatible 2D dimensions with feedback suppression; 3D cameras remain independent.

The linked axes share one domain: the union of the plots' domains (each one's data, or its
explicit domain), so a value lines up in every plot and panning or zooming one moves the others
over the same range. Stacked panels whose data end at different dates, or whose labels pad their
ends differently, still align. A plot with an explicit domain keeps it, so it lines up with the
others only where its domain is theirs; a plot whose marks draw nothing takes the others'
domain. A plot can be in several LinkViews (one on x, another on y): each shares the domains of its own plots, as it links their views. `scales="free"` keeps each plot's own domain.

A domain can be dates: `x={"domain": [datetime.date(2024, 1, 1), datetime.date(2024, 3, 1)]}`
(or datetime64) draws a time axis over those days.

### Related examples

- [Linked views & minimap](/HMPlot/examples/linked.md)

## Template

Page: /reference/python/template.md

A reusable pattern of components, built by a class or function, with a slot for the caller's children.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

class Panel(hm.Template):
    def build(self, data):
        with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True):
            hm.slot()

data = {"x": [1, 2, 3, 4], "y": [3, 1, 4, 2]}
with Panel(data) as panel:
    hm.Points(x="x", y="y")
panel
```

### Usage

A template packages existing components as a reusable node. Use `@hm.template` for a function,
or subclass `hm.Template` and construct the pattern in `build(self, ...)`. Its signature and
Python defaults are the build's. It can compose marks inside a Plot, or a non-mark pattern
such as Calculate → Plot → slot, placed in a Row. It adds no numerical or rendering operation.

Calling it builds immediately and attaches it to the current context. Create new components
each time; one component cannot belong to two instances. Each instance has independent nodes,
parts, slot and input names. A shared host table still shares its interaction state.

### Parameters, main part and named parts

The template's own marks determine its mark contract; the caller's slot children do not.

| Declaration | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| One mark, no explicit main | That mark is the main part, even below containers. |
| `hm.contract(main=mark, parts={"band": band})` | Declares one main part and names components for `instance.part("band")`. A nested template can be main; its main mark is used. Call contract once during the build. |
| Keywords not taken by `build()` | Forward to the main mark. A `band={...}` keyword overrides the named part's props. Part names must differ from build parameters and main-mark props. A build accepting `**kwargs` handles its own forwarding. |
| Several marks and no main | A group: `visible=` controls its marks; other undeclared props and operations needing one mark raise. Use its named parts instead. |

Mark events, selections, `endpoint()` and `hm.connect()` use the main mark. A declared main
also supplies references such as `Legend(target=instance)`. Without a declared main, references
use the single top-level node, with an only-mark fallback for a Legend. Exports and camera
commands use the single top-level node; expose a specific Plot as a class attribute when a
larger pattern needs that Plot's handles.

### Children and updates

Call `hm.slot()` once in the component scope where children belong. `with instance:`, `add`,
`remove` and `clear` act on that slot; children retain its data/frame scopes and draw position.
`clear()` leaves the template's own components intact. `children` lists the template's own
top-level nodes, and `slot.children` the caller's children. Without a slot, `with` and `add`
raise. There is one unnamed slot, not a separate slot for each named part.

`instance.update(**params)` is supported after its own `with` block closes. It merges parameters
and forwarded properties into the original call and rebuilds in place. Components matched by
kind and position keep IDs, handles and externally registered callbacks; caller children move
to the rebuilt slot. A failed build preserves the previous instance. Parts' direct edits and
settings reset to the new build's declarations. Nested templates rebuild with their parent.

### Settings and legends

Inside a Plot, a mark template has a settings group: with a main part, its controls represent
the template and helper rows are hidden; without a main, parts are listed. View/layout
patterns retain their own settings structure. Build parameters do not automatically create
settings-pane controls; use `update()` or a part's existing controls.

The main mark supplies the legend entry. Helper marks default to `legend=False` and follow
its effective visibility unless they explicitly set their own choices. A group can instead
call `hm.contract(legend_entries=[{"label": "Range", "swatch": band, "parts": [band, points]}])`
to make one entry control several marks; this cannot be combined with `main=`. Slot children
keep their own legend and visibility behavior.

### Portable files and other extensions

Build a fresh instance with explicit `hm.template_param("name", default=...)` markers, an
empty slot and no callbacks, then call `export_template(path)`. `hm.load_template(path)`
returns a callable Template class in Python; [`PortableTemplate`](package-templates) loads
it in Svelte. The tree, parameters and contracts travel; Python methods, arbitrary resources
and build-time branching do not. Reattach host callbacks after loading.

The repository's `docs/PORTABLE-TEMPLATES.md` authoring guide has tested mark and non-mark
examples, file limits and repository-local JavaScript definitions. A template composes
existing operations; a [plug-in](/HMPlot/reference/svelte/plugins.md) adds numerical execution,
layout, effects or shading through its own extension contract.

## slot

Page: /reference/python/slot.md

Where a template's children go: hm.slot() marks the place in its build().

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

@hm.template
def panel(data):
    with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True):
        hm.slot()
        hm.Line(x="x", y="y")

data = {"x": [1, 2, 3, 4], "y": [3, 1, 4, 2]}
with panel(data) as chart:
    hm.Points(x="x", y="y")
chart
```

### Usage

`hm.slot()` marks where a template's caller children go. Call it once inside `build()` or an
`@hm.template` function, in the data and component scope the children should inherit. A helper
called from the build may place it. A Calculate above the slot supplies its output to the
caller's marks; a Plot above it supplies their drawing context.

`with template:`, `template.add(...)`, `remove` and `clear` operate on this slot. The caller's
children stay before anything the build creates after the slot; clearing them keeps the
built-in parts. They do not become the template's main or named parts. Calling slot outside a
build, or twice in one template, raises. A template without one refuses caller children.

There is one unnamed slot. `hm.contract(parts={...})` names existing components for property
edits and handles; it does not create named or replaceable child slots. A rebuild with
`template.update(...)` moves the caller's children to the rebuilt slot. Portable export needs
an empty slot; fill it after loading.

In an ordinary Svelte component, place caller children with `{@render children?.()}`.
[`PortableTemplate`](package-templates) places its Svelte children at the file's exported slot.
See [Template](template) for parameters, updates and contracts.

## AxisDefinition

Page: /reference/python/axis-definition.md

A Plot's or Frame's x, y and z: the domain, scale and transform, and the ticks, labels and title.

### Example

```python
hm.Plot(x={"domain": [0, 10], "label": "Time (s)", "tick_count": 5}, y={"transform": "log"})
```

```svelte
<Plot x={{ domain: [0, 10], label: "Time (s)", tickCount: 5 }} y={{ transform: "log" }}>…</Plot>
```

### Members

- `domain` (`[number, number] | [Date, Date] | [number | Expression | Date, number | Expression | Date] | "auto"`): The data range the axis spans; "auto" (the default) spans the marks' data, widened by padding and, on a 2D linear numeric axis, rounded out to tick values. Two dates make a datetime axis over them. Ends that are reductions (extent(column, {where})) are read from the data and follow it and the selection; automatic while no row matches.
- `transform` (`ScaleTransformName`): How data maps to the axis: "linear" (default), "log", "sqrt" or "symlog"; under log a value at or below zero is missing.
- `range` (`[number, number]`): Where the domain lands in the parent frame's coordinates (a Frame's sub-range of its parent axis).
- `constant` (`number`): symlog's constant c > 0 (default 1): the axis is linear within ±c and logarithmic beyond.
- `invert` (`boolean`): Flip the axis direction on screen (top-to-bottom for y, right-to-left for x, near-to-far for z).
- `scale` (`CategoricalScale`): A categorical scale: the axis becomes one band per category, in the scale's order.
- `label` (`string`): The axis title. Empty (or null) means automatic: the axis is titled by a categorical position scale's label, else by the name of the one column its marks plot there (through a Facet's value/x/y aliases and transform outputs such as a Bin's edges); an axis whose marks plot several columns, only constants, raw arrays or expressions, or nothing has no title. A Frame that sets its own domain, range, transform or scale for this dimension reads only its own label.
- `visible` (`boolean`): false hides the axis (its line, ticks and labels).
- `side` (`"left" | "right" | "top" | "bottom"`): Which side the axis is drawn on; "right" or "top" for a second axis.
- `type` (`"numeric" | "datetime"`): "datetime" labels positions as times counted from origin in timezone; a Date or datetime64 column sets it.
- `origin` (`number | Date`): Datetime axes: the time (a Date, or Unix milliseconds) positions count from.
- `timezone` (`string`): Datetime axes: the IANA time zone labels and calendar intervals use (default UTC).
- `format` (`string`): A d3-format string (".1f", ",") or, on a datetime axis, a time pattern ("%b %d").
- `major_interval` (`string | CalendarInterval`): Datetime axes: the calendar step between major ticks ("1 month", "15 minutes").
- `minor_interval` (`string | CalendarInterval`): Datetime axes: the calendar step between minor ticks.
- `major` (`boolean`): false hides the major ticks and their labels.
- `minor` (`boolean`): Draw minor ticks between the major ones (subdivisions of each step).
- `step` (`number`): The spacing between major ticks, in data units, instead of an automatic choice.
- `tick_count` (`number`): About how many major ticks to draw; the axis picks round values near that count. Automatic: about one per 80 px along a 2D linear numeric x axis and per 45 px along y, else per 90 px.
- `subdivisions` (`number`): How many minor intervals each major step splits into (at least 2; default 5).
- `minor_step` (`number`): The spacing between minor ticks, in data units, instead of subdivisions.
- `padding` (`number`): An automatic domain's margin on each side, as a fraction of its span (default 0.04); on a 2D linear numeric axis the padded ends then round out to tick values, and 0 keeps the data's ends. An explicit domain is not padded.
- `grid` (`"off" | "major" | "major-minor"`): Grid lines at the major ticks ("major") or at major and minor ticks ("major-minor"); "off" draws none.
- `line` (`boolean`): Show the baseline independently of ticks, labels, grids and arrows.
- `ticks` (`boolean`): Show tick marks independently of tick labels.
- `tick_size` (`number`): Tick length in CSS pixels; defaults to the theme's tick size.
- `tick_direction` (`"outside" | "inside" | "both"`): Tick direction relative to the axes interior.
- `title_font_weight` (`number`): Numeric title font weight from 1 to 1000.
- `grid_color` (`string`): Grid stroke color; omitted adapts to the background.
- `grid_width` (`number`): Grid stroke width in CSS pixels.
- `grid_dash` (`number[]`): Alternating dash and gap lengths in CSS pixels; [] draws solid grids.
- `line_width` (`number`): The baseline's stroke width in CSS pixels; 0 hides the baseline and arrow shafts.
- `tick_width` (`number`): The tick marks' stroke width in CSS pixels.
- `arrow` (`"both" | "none" | "start" | "end"`): An arrowhead at the axis's start, end or both ends.
- `arrow_size` (`number`): The arrowhead's size in CSS pixels.
- `label_overlap` (`"hide" | "show"`): "hide" (default) drops tick labels that would overlap their neighbors; "show" keeps them all.
- `tick_label_angle` (`number`): Rotates the tick labels, in degrees.
- `tick_label_align` (`"auto" | "start" | "end" | "middle"`): How tick labels align to their ticks; "auto" chooses by the axis side and angle.
- `tick_label_placement` (`"outside" | "inside"`): Tick labels outside the axes interior (default) or inside it.
- `tick_label_offset` (`number`): Extra distance between tick labels and the axis, in CSS pixels.
- `title_position` (`"start" | "end" | "middle"`): Where the title sits along the axis: at its start, middle or end.
- `title_angle` (`number | "auto"`): The title's rotation in degrees; "auto" reads along a vertical axis.
- `title_placement` (`"outside" | "inside"`): The title outside the axes interior (default) or inside it.
- `title_offset` (`number`): Extra distance between the title and the tick labels, in CSS pixels.
- `context` (`boolean`): Datetime x axes: a second row of labels where the coarser unit changes (the date under hours, the month and year under days); default true.
- `breaks` (`AxisBreak | AxisBreak[]`): Datetime axes: intervals the axis leaves out, in its time zone ("weekends", { hours: [16, 9.5] } every day, { dates: ["2026-12-25"] } whole days, { from, to } one interval).
- `calendar` (`string | { name: string; units: string; }`): A model calendar's axis (set from its column): "360_day", "all_leap" or "noleap", with the column's units ("days since 1850-01-01").

### Usage

A Plot's or a [Frame](frame)'s `x`, `y` and `z` each take one of these objects: how that dimension maps data to the frame, and how its axis is drawn. Set only what you need; the rest keeps its default or the theme's. Python writes the keys in snake_case (`tick_count`, `major_interval`), and an unknown key is an error that names the nearest one.

**The mapping.** `domain` fixes the data range; without it (`"auto"`) the axis spans the marks' data, widened by `padding` (a fraction of the span on each side, 0.04 by default; an explicit domain is not padded). On a 2D linear numeric axis the padded ends then round out to tick values, so both ends carry labeled ticks; an end at a bar's 0 baseline or at the bounds a Heatmap or Image is placed by stays, an end whose padding already reaches past a tick (data from 0, or up to 10) keeps its padding, and `padding: 0` keeps the data's ends. `transform` is linear, log, sqrt or symlog, with `constant` for symlog's linear band around zero. Under log a zero or negative value is missing: it is not drawn and not counted in the automatic domain. `invert` flips the axis on screen and keeps its domain, so zooming and ticks work as before. `scale`, a [categorical](categorical) scale, makes the axis a band per category in the scale's order: along x from the left, along y from the top (`invert` lists a y axis from the bottom). `axisMask` clips marks to the visible axes interior; it is enabled in HMPlot and most themes. Set `axisMask={false}` on Plot/Frame to allow overflow.

**Time.** `type: "datetime"` labels positions as times, counted in milliseconds from `origin` (Unix milliseconds, as [datetimeCoordinates](datetime-coordinates) returns it) and shown in `timezone`. A column of Dates, a datetime schema or a NumPy datetime64 column sets both itself. `majorInterval` and `minorInterval` take calendar steps (`"1 month"`, `"15 minutes"`), an x axis adds a second row of dates under hours (`context`), and `breaks` leaves out weekends, nights or holidays, as in [Market hours](/HMPlot/examples/market-hours.md).

**Ticks, labels and the title.** `tickCount` asks for about that many ticks (automatic: about one per 80 px along a 2D linear numeric x axis and per 45 px along y), `step` fixes their spacing, and `format` is a d3-format string (`".1f"`) or a time pattern (`"%b %d"`). `minor` with `subdivisions` adds minor ticks, and `grid` draws lines at the major (or major and minor) ticks. `label` titles the axis; left empty, it is the name of the one column the marks plot there. `visible: false` hides the line, ticks and labels but keeps the mapping, and `side` moves an axis to the right or the top, as a second y axis needs.

[Axes & datetime](/HMPlot/examples/axes.md) shows a datetime axis in a time zone with minor grids, and [Twin coordinate frames](/HMPlot/examples/twin-axes.md) two y axes over one x.

### Baselines, tick marks, and grids

`line` shows the baseline, independently of `ticks` and tick labels. `tickSize` is the
length in CSS pixels; `tickDirection` is `outside`, `inside`, or `both`. Major/minor
controls still decide which ticks exist. `ticks: false` leaves their labels visible.

```js
x={{ line: false, ticks: true, tickSize: 4, tickDirection: "outside", arrow: "end" }}
y={{ grid: "major", gridColor: "#dde4ed", gridWidth: 1, gridDash: [3, 3] }}
```

A baseline-free arrow has a short shaft twice `arrowSize` long and a filled head.
`lineWidth: 0` suppresses baseline and shaft strokes while arrows remain independent.
`titleFontWeight` sets a numeric weight from 1 to 1000. Grid color defaults to an adaptive
blend with the background; `gridWidth` and `gridDash` affect grids, leaving reference
`rules` independent. Explicit axis settings override matching `theme.axes` values.

`axisFrame` on Plot/Frame draws the missing sides of a rectangular 2D Cartesian border
without repeating ticks or labels. `axisMask` clips data marks and picking to the interior,
including when baselines are hidden. Both have theme defaults (`axes.frame`, `axes.mask`).

### Related examples

- [Twin coordinate frames](/HMPlot/examples/twin-axes.md)
- [Axes & datetime](/HMPlot/examples/axes.md)
- [Market hours: an axis that skips weekends and nights](/HMPlot/examples/market-hours.md)

## rules and bands

Page: /reference/python/bands.md

Reference lines and shaded spans of an axis, behind the marks, on a Plot or a Frame.

### Example

```python
hm.Plot(rules=[{"axis": "y", "value": 0}], bands=[{"axis": "x", "from": 40, "to": 52, "label": "Warm spell"}])
```

```svelte
<Plot rules={[{ axis: "y", value: 0 }]} bands={[{ axis: "x", from: 40, to: 52, label: "Warm spell" }]}>…</Plot>
```

### Members

#### ReferenceRule

- `axis` (`"x" | "y"`): "x" draws a vertical rule at an x value, "y" a horizontal one. Required.
- `value` (`string | number | Date`): Where the rule is, in the axis's units: a number, a Date or an ISO date. Required.
- `label` (`string`): Text at the rule's end.
- `color` (`string`): The rule's color; default the axis text color.
- `width` (`number`): The rule's stroke width in CSS pixels.
- `dash` (`number[]`): Alternating dash and gap lengths in CSS pixels; [] or omitted draws a solid rule.

#### ReferenceBand

- `axis` (`"x" | "y"`): "x" shades a vertical strip (in a polar frame, a wedge of angles), "y" a horizontal one (a ring of radii). Required.
- `from` (`string | number | Date`): One end, in the axis's units: a number, a Date, or an ISO date ("2024-03-01" or "2024-03-01T09:30" in the axis's time zone, or with an offset such as "2024-03-01T12:00:00Z"). Required.
- `to` (`string | number | Date`): The other end (either order). Required.
- `label` (`string`): Text at the band's start, like a rule's label.
- `color` (`string`): A six-digit hex color. Default the axis text color.
- `opacity` (`number`): 0 to 1. Default 0.1.

### Usage

`bands` on a Plot or a Frame shades spans of an axis behind the marks and grid lines: `[{ axis: "x", from: 40, to: 52, label: "Warm spell", color: "#d9824b", opacity: 0.16 }]`. An x band is a vertical strip and a y band a horizontal one; in a polar frame they are a wedge of angles and a ring of radii. Ends are values on the axis (numbers, Dates, or ISO dates: `"2024-03-01"` or `"2024-03-01T09:30"` in the axis's time zone, or with an offset such as `"2024-03-01T12:00:00Z"`), in either order. The label sits at the band's start, as a rule's does.

A Frame takes `rules` and `bands` in its own coordinates. Bands export as vector rectangles or sectors, and the settings pane lists them beside the reference lines.

### Related examples

- [Titles, bands and callouts](/HMPlot/examples/annotations.md)

## Plot (handle)

Page: /reference/python/plot-handle.md

What a bound Plot offers code: fit, settle, selections, the camera, the animation clock and exports.

### Example

```python
with hm.Plot() as plot:
    ...
await plot.when_settled()
await plot.export_png("plot.png", scale=2)
```

```svelte
<script>
  let plot = $state();
  $effect(() => { plot?.whenSettled().then(() => plot.fit()); });
</script>

<Plot bind:this={plot}>…</Plot>
```

### Members

This table describes the JavaScript interface. Python has its own Node and resource methods, listed under “Python members” below; these member names are not Python method names.

- `getFrames` (`() => FrameHandle[]`): Required.
- `getDescription` (`() => string`): The plot's description as screen readers get it (description=, then the generated summary), updated when the plot settles after a change. Required.
- `getTitle` (`() => string`): The plot's title as shown ("" without one). Required.
- `subscribeDescription` (`(listener: (text: string) => void) => () => void`): Called with the description whenever it changes, and once at once; returns a function that stops it. Required.
- `getSelection` (`() => SelectionResource`): Required.
- `getBrush` (`() => SelectionResource`): Required.
- `clearBrush` (`() => void`): Required.
- `getHover` (`() => SelectionResource`): Required.
- `getOffsets` (`() => OffsetLayer`): The table's offsets (dragging). Required.
- `resetOffsets` (`(columns?: string | string[] | undefined) => void`): Clear the table's offsets in `columns` (every column when omitted). Required.
- `applyOffsets` (`() => Record<string, unknown> | Record<string, unknown>[]`): The table as given, with each column that has offsets replaced by its moved values. Required.
- `openSettings` (`(anchorElement?: unknown) => void`): Required.
- `closeSettings` (`() => void`): Required.
- `beginUpdate` (`() => () => Promise<void>`): Required.
- `whenSettled` (`() => Promise<void>`): Resolves once the changes made before the call are drawn; later changes are not waited for. Required.
- `whenAnimationsFinished` (`() => Promise<void>`): Required.
- `exportPNG` (`(options?: { scale?: number | undefined; } | undefined) => Promise<Blob>`): Required.
- `exportSVG` (`(options?: DocumentExportOptions | undefined) => Promise<DocumentExportResult>`): Required.
- `exportPDF` (`(options?: DocumentExportOptions | undefined) => Promise<DocumentExportResult>`): Required.
- `exportVideo` (`(options: { duration: number; fps?: number | undefined; start?: number | undefined; scale?: number | undefined; }) => Promise<Blob>`): The animation as an MP4 (H.264, else VP9) encoded in the browser with WebCodecs: one PNG export per frame at a frozen clock time from `start` for `duration` ms; the clock is restored afterwards. Loads hmplot/video on first use. Required.
- `getRenderError` (`() => string`): Required.
- `setViewport` (`(viewport: Partial<Viewport2D>, axes?: "xy" | "x" | "y" | undefined) => Promise<void>`): Resolves once the viewport is applied, like setCamera. Required.
- `getViewport` (`() => Viewport2D`): Required.
- `getCamera` (`() => CameraState`): The 3D camera state, or undefined for a 2D plot. Required.
- `setCamera` (`(camera: Partial<Omit<CameraState, "mode">>, options?: { animate?: boolean | undefined; } | undefined) => Promise<void>`): Merge a partial 3D camera state; {animate: true} eases over the plot's animationDuration. Required.
- `getAnimationTime` (`() => number`): The clock in milliseconds, shared by the Plots of its scope (an InputContext, a Scene, a standalone Facet or a Simulate; else the Plot's own): 0 when the scope starts, advanced by the frame time while anything in it animates, still while frozen. `@time` and every transition read it. Required.
- `getAnimationTimeFrozen` (`() => boolean`): Whether setAnimationTime froze the clock. Required.
- `setAnimationTime` (`(time: number | null, options?: { freeze?: boolean | undefined; } | undefined) => Promise<void>`): Set the clock of the Plot's scope. With freeze (default) it stops there until setAnimationTime(null) resumes it, so exports capture that moment: transitions and Required.
- `fit` (`() => void`): Reset the view: 2D returns to the full domain; 3D recomputes the camera position. Required.
- `holdAnimations` (`() => () => void`): Required.
- `subscribeSettings` (`(listener: (values: Record<string, unknown>) => void) => () => void`): Required.
- `getScreenMapping` (`() => ScreenMapping | null`): The last completed draw's mapping; null before drawing, after disposal or for unsupported coordinates. Required.
- `subscribeScreenMapping` (`(listener: (mapping: ScreenMapping | null) => void) => () => void`): Receives the current mapping immediately and changes after completed draws. Returns an unsubscribe function. Required.

### Get a handle

In Svelte, use `bind:this={plot}` on Plot. The member table describes that JavaScript handle.
Wait for `whenSettled()` before reading a newly updated plot or exporting it; use
`whenAnimationsFinished()` when the final transition state is required.

### Python members

In Python the node itself is the handle: keep the context manager's result,
`with hm.Plot(...) as plot:`. Its members are of three kinds.

- **sync** members run at once and need no browser. They change the scene, which every view of
  it then shows: a displayed notebook view, or a later standalone export.
- **await** members are coroutines that ask a *displayed* view. They need the plot shown in a
  notebook (JupyterLab, Notebook 7 or VS Code, in a browser with WebGPU) and `await` in a running
  event loop, as a notebook cell's top level has. Without a displayed view they raise
  `hm.SceneError` with code `bridge.missing_view`; with several views of one scene, pass
  `view=`, one of the scene's `views`. Each waits at most `timeout` seconds (default 60), then
  raises `SceneError` with code `bridge.timeout`.
- **property** and **attribute** members are read in Python. A property the browser reports
  (`description`) is `None` until a view has shown the plot.

These are the members of every node (a transform's, a mark's, a Facet's), and `description`
is a Plot's own. Python does not use the JavaScript names in the table above.

| Member | Kind | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | attribute | The node's id in the scene: a string. |
| `kind` | attribute | The component's name, `"Plot"`. |
| `props` | attribute | The props as the scene sends them, camelCase; change them with `update`. |
| `children` | attribute | The child nodes, in draw order. |
| `parent` | attribute | The node that contains this one, or `None`. |
| `description` | property | The description screen readers get (`description=`, else the generated summary), synced from the browser after the plot settles; `None` before a view has shown it. |
| `update(**props)` | sync | Set props, snake_case keywords checked as the constructor checks them, and redraw every view. Returns the node. |
| `add(*children)` | sync | Append components; one already here moves to the end (child order is draw order), one in another container is an error. Returns the node. |
| `remove(child)` | sync | Detach a child; returns it. |
| `clear()` | sync | Remove every child. Returns the node. |
| `batch_update()` | sync | A context manager, `with plot.batch_update():`. The changes inside it reach the views as one update, and none of them stays if the block raises. |
| `on_event(event, callback)` | sync | Call `callback(event)` when a view reports `event`: click, dblclick, pointermove, pointerenter, pointerleave, contextmenu, camerachange, viewportchange, drag or dragend. Returns the callback. Events come only from displayed views. |
| `on_click(callback)` | sync | `on_event("click", callback)`. |
| `on_hover(callback)` | sync | `on_event("pointermove", callback)`. |
| `selection` | property | The selection of the plot's data (`data=`, or the nearest Data above): a [SelectionResource](selection) to read and set. A node without data raises `RuntimeError`. |
| `brush` | property | The data's brush, a SelectionResource. |
| `hover` | property | The data's hover state, a SelectionResource. |
| `nearby` | property | The data's nearby rows, a SelectionResource. |
| `nearest` | property | The data's nearest row, a SelectionResource. |
| `endpoint(name=None, *, at=None)` | sync | This node as an endpoint for `hm.connect`: a mark with an attachment `at`, or the mark `name` that an embedded Facet or a Partition repeats. See [connect](connect). |
| `when_settled(*, view=None, timeout=60)` | await | Returns once the view has drawn every change made before the call, loads in flight included. |
| `when_animations_finished(*, view=None, timeout=60)` | await | Returns once the view's transitions have finished. |
| `fit(*, view=None, timeout=60)` | await | Reset the view: a 2D plot to its full domain, a 3D one to a new camera. |
| `get_camera(*, view=None, timeout=60)` | await | The 3D camera: a dict of position, target, up, fov, near, far, zoom and mode. |
| `set_camera(state=None, *, animate=False, view=None, timeout=60, **fields)` | await | Merge a partial camera (a dict, or keywords: position, target, up, fov, near, far, zoom), easing there with `animate=True`; returns the camera. |
| `get_viewport(*, view=None, timeout=60)` | await | The 2D viewport: x, y, zoom, zoomX and zoomY, and an orthographic globe's center. |
| `set_viewport(state=None, *, view=None, timeout=60, **fields)` | await | Merge a partial viewport (x, y, zoom, zoom_x, zoom_y, center) and return the result. |
| `get_time(*, view=None, timeout=60)` | await | The scene's animation clock, in milliseconds. |
| `set_time(time, *, freeze=True, view=None, timeout=60)` | await | Set the clock (milliseconds), frozen there until `set_time(None)` unless `freeze=False`; returns the clock. |
| `export_png(path=None, *, scale=2, view=None, timeout=60)` | await | This view as PNG bytes, `scale` pixels per CSS pixel, also written to `path` when given. |
| `export_svg(path=None, **options)` | await | This view as SVG bytes. The options are [DocumentExportOptions](document-export-options) in snake_case (width, height, mode, raster_dpi, text, primitive_budget) with view and timeout. |
| `export_pdf(path=None, **options)` | await | The SVG export printed to PDF in a private headless Chrome; bytes. |
| `export_html(path=None, *, snapshot='svg', page=True, view=None, timeout=60, **options)` | await | A standalone page of the scene and this view's camera, showing a snapshot first (`"svg"`, `"png"` or `False`); bytes. `page=` lays the page out: a 24 px margin and the content at most 960 px wide by default, `{"max_width": ..., "margin": ...}` in pixels, or `False` for a bare page. A page over the 10 MiB a notebook can send to the kernel is exported headlessly instead, as `hm.export_html` does, with a warning. Other options are an error. |
| `export_mp4(path, *, duration, fps=30, start=0, scale=2, encoder='ffmpeg', view=None, timeout=60)` | await | The @time animation as an MP4 at `path`: a PNG per frame at a frozen clock, encoded by ffmpeg or, with `encoder="browser"`, by the view's WebCodecs. The clock is restored. Returns the path. |
| `groups(*, view=None, timeout=60)` | await | A Partition's mounted groups: key, values, label and mark labels; other nodes raise. |
| `action(action, *, view=None, timeout=60)` | await | Run an action the node has, such as Force's `"reset"` or a Provider's `"refresh"`. |

### Without a notebook

A script exports with module functions instead. They are synchronous, need no displayed view,
and draw the scene in a private headless Chrome (an installed Chrome, Edge or Chromium, else one
downloaded once; see docs/DOCUMENT-EXPORT.md). Each returns what the matching `await` member
returns, and writes `path` when given. From async code, `hm.export_png_async` and the other
`_async` functions run them in a thread.

| Function | Kind | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `hm.export_png(target, path=None, **options)` | sync | PNG bytes; options `scale` (default 2), and `cells=True` for a Facet's cells one by one. |
| `hm.export_svg(target, path=None, **options)` | sync | SVG bytes, with the DocumentExportOptions in snake_case. |
| `hm.export_pdf(target, path=None, **options)` | sync | PDF bytes, printed from the SVG export. |
| `hm.export_html(target, path=None, **options)` | sync | A page, with its snapshot drawn in the headless Chrome (`snapshot="svg"`, `"png"` or `False`), laid out by `page=` as above. |
| `hm.export_mp4(target, path, *, duration, fps=30, start=0, scale=2, encoder='ffmpeg')` | sync | The @time animation as an MP4; returns the path. |
| `hm.ExportSession()` | sync | `with hm.ExportSession() as session:` reuses one browser for several exports: `session.png`, `session.svg`, `session.pdf`, `session.html` and `session.mp4` take the functions' arguments, and `session.set_time`, `session.get_viewport` and `session.set_viewport` set a plot up first. |

SVG and PDF keep axes, text, legends and most 2D marks as vector shapes and draw the rest as
images at `raster_dpi`; [what is not exported as vector](/HMPlot/docs/export.md) lists what.

### Related examples

- [Linked views & minimap](/HMPlot/examples/linked.md)

## create_theme

Page: /reference/python/themes.md

A theme: fonts, colors, axes and mark defaults, shared and changed live; themes holds the presets.

### Example

```python
paper = hm.create_theme(extends="paper", marks={"Line": {"width": 1.5}})
with hm.Theme(value=paper):
    ...
```

```svelte
const paper = createTheme({ extends: "paper", marks: { Line: { width: 1.5 } } });
<Theme value={paper}>…</Theme>
```

### Members

#### Members

- `name` (`string`): The theme's name, shown in the settings pane. A name that starts with a partial theme's group ("axes/", "legend/", "title/", "controls/", "numbers/", "animation/", "marks/") makes the theme a partial: it should set only that section, and warns when it sets others.
- `extends` (`string | ThemeDefinition | ThemeResource | (string | ThemeDefinition | ThemeResource)[]`): Inherit from themes: a preset name (matched ignoring case and punctuation), a partial theme's name ("axes/minimal", "legend/inline-top", "title/centered", "numbers/currency", ...), a theme definition, a theme resource, or a list of them merged left to right, as in ["paper", "axes/minimal", "legend/inline-top"]. This definition's keys merge over the result: objects merge key by key, lists (a palette) replace.
- `vector_tile` (`Partial<Record<VectorTilePart, boolean | VectorTileStyle>>`): VectorTile's color scheme under this theme: part -> style (or false), as VectorTile's styles.
- `view` (`{ background?: string | undefined; }`): The plot area: background is its color.
- `typography` (`{ fontFamily?: string | undefined; fontSize?: number | undefined; color?: string | undefined; }`): Text everywhere unless a part overrides it: font family, size in CSS pixels and color.
- `axes` (`{ fontFamily?: string | undefined; fontSize?: number | undefined; color?: string | undefined; textColor?: string | undefined; line?: boolean | undefined; ticks?: boolean | undefined; tickDirection?: "outside" | "inside" | "both" | undefined; titleFontWeight?: number | undefined; gridColor?: string | undefined; gridWidth?: number | undefined; gridDash?: number[] | undefined; frame?: boolean | undefined; mask?: boolean | undefined; threeD?: Axes3DConfig | undefined; lineWidth?: number | undefined; tickSize?: number | undefined; grid?: "off" | "major" | "major-minor" | undefined; marginLeft?: number | "auto" | undefined; marginRight?: number | "auto" | undefined; marginTop?: number | "auto" | undefined; marginBottom?: number | "auto" | undefined; arrow?: "both" | "none" | "start" | "end" | undefined; arrowSize?: number | undefined; titlePosition?: "start" | "end" | "middle" | undefined; titleAngle?: number | "auto" | undefined; titlePlacement?: "outside" | "inside" | undefined; titleOffset?: number | undefined; tickLabelAngle?: number | undefined; tickLabelAlign?: "auto" | "start" | "end" | "middle" | undefined; tickLabelPlacement?: "outside" | "inside" | undefined; tickLabelOffset?: number | undefined; }`): Axis lines, ticks, labels, titles, grids and margins (see AxisDefinition for each key).
- `guides` (`{ fontFamily?: string | undefined; fontSize?: number | undefined; textColor?: string | undefined; }`): Legends and colorbars: their fonts, colors and spacing.
- `numbers` (`{ format?: string | undefined; }`): Numbers: format is a d3-format string (",.2f", "$,.0f", ".1%") that linear axis ticks, legends and tooltips use where they set no format of their own; dates keep theirs.
- `controls` (`{ accentColor?: string | undefined; fontSize?: number | undefined; }`): Inputs (Slider, Select, Button, Checkbox, Playback, ...): accentColor colors a slider's handle and fill, a checked box and the focus ring (default palette[0]); font_size is their text size in CSS pixels (default typography.font_size). A page's --hm-controls-* variables win.
- `animation` (`{ duration?: number | undefined; easing?: "linear" | "quad-in" | "quad-out" | "quad-in-out" | "cubic-in" | "cubic-out" | "cubic-in-out" | "sine-in-out" | undefined; enter?: boolean | "fade" | { effect?: "fade" | undefined; duration?: number | undefined; easing?: "linear" | "quad-in" | "quad-out" | "quad-in-out" | "cubic-in" | "cubic-out" | "cubic-in-out" | "sine-in-out" | undefined; } | undefined; exit?: boolean | "fade" | { effect?: "fade" | undefined; duration?: number | undefined; easing?: "linear" | "quad-in" | "quad-out" | "quad-in-out" | "cubic-in" | "cubic-out" | "cubic-in-out" | "sine-in-out" | undefined; } | undefined; }`): Animated changes: duration (milliseconds) and easing are a Plot's animation_duration and animation_easing, enter and exit a mark's enter_effect and exit_effect, where those are not set. It does not turn animation on: a Plot's or mark's `animation` does.
- `marks` (`Record<string, Record<string, string | number | boolean | null>>`): Mark defaults. A null ordinary mark color/fill clears an inherited color and uses palette[0].
- `palette` (`string[]`): The categorical colors, in order, for marks colored by a category.
- `colormap` (`ColormapSpec`): Default colormap for continuous fills and colors without an explicit colormap.
- `missing` (`string`): The color of a missing value (NaN or null) in a colormapped fill or color, unless its scale sets `missing` (default "#92989f", a neutral gray).
- `shapes` (`Record<string, string | [number, number][]>`): Custom point shapes registered when the theme applies: name -> vertices in [-1, 1] or an M/L/Z path.

#### Presets

- `hm.themes` (`Record<name, ThemeDefinition>`): The built-in themes by name, frozen: minimal, paper, presentation, colorblind, dark, 538, financeTerminal, pastel, graph, sea, sunset, ggplot, seabornDark, notebook, graphingCalculator, observable, wesAnderson, ghibli, yellowGlow, 8bit, vaporwave, blueprint, bubblegum, spooky, treasureMap, bureau, journal, bauhaus, risograph and tufte. Pass one to Theme's value, or name it in extends (matched ignoring case and punctuation). Python: hm.themes.paper, hm.themes.five_thirty_eight, hm.themes.eight_bit.

### Usage

JavaScript uses createTheme(definition); Python uses hm.create_theme(**definition). `extends` starts from a preset by name (matched ignoring case and punctuation: `"finance-terminal"` is `financeTerminal`) or from another theme, and the definition's sections override it. `themes` holds the 32 presets listed below as frozen definitions: pass one straight to Theme's `value`, or read its colors. Explicit scale ranges remain independent of a theme palette.

`hmplot` is the default. `minimal` is an airy presentation with quiet outside labels; `ink` uses charcoal-led ink colors. Each preset includes a categorical palette and a continuous colormap. Python discovers the same names through `hm.themes.names()`, including `hm.themes.hmplot` and `hm.themes.ink`.

### Related examples

- [Theme presets](/HMPlot/examples/themes.md)

## connect

Page: /reference/python/connect.md

Connections between marks: Line, Segments, Arrows3D and Arrows draw them between the endpoints' positions.

### Example

```python
before = hm.Points(x="x0", y="y")
after = hm.Points(x="x1", y="y")
hm.Arrows(connections=hm.connect(before, after, key="id"))
```

```svelte
<Points bind:this={before} x="x0" y="y" />
<Points bind:this={after} x="x1" y="y" />
<Arrows connections={connect(before, after, { key: "id" })} />
```

### Members

#### Members

- `key` (`string`): A column matched by exact value in every endpoint; without it, the endpoints must show observations of one table, matched by identity.
- `order` (`"facet"`): "facet" (the default and only order): one endpoint repeated in Facet cells or Partition groups connects its cells in facet order.

#### Endpoints

- `mark.endpoint({at})` (`endpoint`): A mark as an endpoint, with an attachment; passing the mark itself uses its default. Python: mark.endpoint(at="left").
- `facet.endpoint(name, {at})` (`endpoint`): The mark an embedded Facet or a Partition repeats in every cell, by name. Python: the mark itself.
- `at` (`string`): Where on the endpoint: center, anchor, left, right, top, bottom, baseline, value, q1, q3, median, start or end, as its kind offers.

### Usage

`connect()` describes connections between marks, and a Line, Segments, Arrows3D, or Arrows with `connections={connect(...)}` draws them from where those marks are drawn instead of from its own `x`/`y`/`z`, `position`, or `start`/`end`. `connect(before, after, {key: "id"})` pairs the row of `before` and the row of `after` that share an `id`; `connect(a, b, c, {key})` makes three-stop paths; `connect(facet.endpoint("values"), {key: "id"})` connects the mark an embedded Facet or a Partition repeats in every cell, in facet order. One endpoint passed alone must be such a repeated mark (one mark alone has nothing to connect to), and a repeated mark among other endpoints is an error; `{order: "facet"}` names the order and is optional. A Line draws one path per key; Segments, Arrows3D, and Arrows one row per adjacent pair. In Python: `hm.connect(before, after, key="id")`, `mark.endpoint(at="left")`, and `hm.connect(values, key="id")` with `values` the Anchor written inside the Facet (a Python mark is its repeated definition; `facet.endpoint("values")` works too).

Rows match by the exact value of `key` (`"1"` never matches `1`). Without `key`, every endpoint must show observations of one table (a mark, a Sort or Filter of the same data) and rows match by observation. A key missing in one endpoint breaks that connection there; a key that repeats within one endpoint is an error, never a join. Aggregates such as Histogram bins have no single source row, so they need a key.

Endpoints are marks, `mark.endpoint({at})` to choose where a connection attaches (a bound mark that can be an endpoint is an `EndpointHandle`, with `getMark()` and `endpoint()`), or `facet.endpoint(name)` / `partition.endpoint(name)`. Points and Anchors attach at `center`; Text at `anchor`, its data position before any pixel offset; Rect and Prism at `center` or an edge midpoint (`left`, `right`, `bottom`, `top`); Bar and Histogram also at `baseline` and `value`; BoxPlot at `center`, `q1`, `q3`, or `median`; Segments, Arrows3D, and Arrows at `start` or `end`, which they require. Marks without an attachment (a Line's vertices, an Area's boundary, a GeoJSON feature, a Heatmap cell) cannot be endpoints yet: place an Anchor where the connection should attach.

Positions are where each endpoint is drawn, through its own frame, and the connector is drawn in its own frame, which must contain every endpoint (a sibling of the Facet, not a mark inside one of its cells). Color, width, and the other channels resolve per connection: when every endpoint shows one table, unqualified columns come from that table's row and `select`/`hover` act on it; across tables, `source.<column>` and `target.<column>` read the first and last endpoint. Pointer events carry `event.connection` with the key and every endpoint's row. Connectors never animate on their own: they follow their endpoints live, at the same clock time. See docs/CONNECTIONS.md for the matching rules, animation, and the current limitations.

### Related examples

- [Before and after arrows](/HMPlot/examples/before-after-arrows.md)

## light

Page: /reference/python/light.md

An ambient, directional, hemisphere or point light for Plot(lights=[...]).

### Example

```python
hm.Plot(type="3d", lights=[hm.light("ambient", intensity=0.3), hm.light("directional", position=[3, 2, 4])])
```

```svelte
import { light } from "hmplot";
<Plot type="3d" lights={[light("ambient", { intensity: 0.3 }), light("directional", { position: [3, 2, 4] })]}>…</Plot>
```

### Members

- `kind` (`"ambient" | "directional" | "hemisphere" | "point"`): Ambient reaches every surface; directional aims toward the origin; hemisphere blends sky and ground; point shines from a position. Required.
- `color` (`string`): A CSS color, default white.
- `intensity` (`number`): Light strength, at least zero; default 1.
- `position` (`[number, number, number]`): World position for directional and point lights; the up direction for hemisphere. Default [0, 1, 0], or [0, 0, 0] for point.
- `ground_color` (`string`): Hemisphere light's ground color, default white.
- `distance` (`number`): Point light's maximum reach in world units; default 0 means unlimited.
- `decay` (`number`): Point light's distance falloff exponent: default 2 is inverse square, 0 is constant.

### Usage

Lights are settings of a Plot. Set `lit=true` on the marks that should use them.

```python
with hm.Plot(type="3d", lights=[hm.light("ambient", intensity=0.3),
                              hm.light("directional", position=[3, 2, 4], intensity=2)]):
    hm.Points3D(x="x", y="y", z="z", lit=True)
```

In Svelte, pass `lights={[light("ambient", { intensity: 0.3 }),
light("directional", { position: [3, 2, 4], intensity: 2 })]}`. Import `light` from `hmplot`;
plain objects with a `kind` work too. The settings pane can add, remove and adjust individual
lights. Update the Plot's list to change it from code.

| Kind | Behavior | Additional parameters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ambient` | Reaches every surface equally | None |
| `directional` | Parallel light aimed toward the origin | `position`, default `[0, 1, 0]` |
| `hemisphere` | Blends sky and ground colors by surface direction | `groundColor`, `position` (the up direction, default `[0, 1, 0]`) |
| `point` | Shines in every direction from one point | `position`, default `[0, 0, 0]`; `distance`, default `0`; `decay`, default `2` |

Every kind takes `color` (default white) and `intensity` (default 1). Positions and distance
use world units. A point light's distance of zero means unlimited reach; decay 2 dims with the
square of distance, while decay 0 keeps constant intensity. Python spells `ground_color` in
`hm.light()`. Python light parameters can read inputs.

`AmbientLight`, `DirectionalLight`, `HemisphereLight` and `PointLight` scene components were
removed. Move their parameters into `Plot(lights=[hm.light(kind, ...)])`. Existing light
parameter changes update the scene objects; changing their number or kind can rebuild lit
materials. Lighting does not change data, bounds or picking identities.

### Related examples

- [Solar system](/HMPlot/examples/solar-system.md)
- [Earth relief](/HMPlot/examples/earth.md)

## effect

Page: /reference/python/effects.md

Effects over the whole plot: a 3D plot's sky and fog, how glowing marks bloom, and plugins' effects.

### Example

```python
hm.Plot(type="3d", effects=[hm.effect("sky", zenith="#2f5f9e", horizon="#dfe9f3"), hm.effect("fog", near=50, far=200)])
```

```svelte
<Plot type="3d" effects={[{ kind: "sky", zenith: "#2f5f9e", horizon: "#dfe9f3" }, { kind: "fog", near: 50, far: 200 }]}>…</Plot>
```

### Kinds

- `sky` (`{ image } | { zenith, horizon, ground }, rotation, visible`): A 3D plot's sky: an equirectangular image around the camera, or a gradient (zenith default #4a7cc4, horizon #d6e4f2, ground the horizon's); rotation [x, y, z] in degrees; visible false hides it, its image still loaded.
- `bloom` (`{ strength, radius }`): How glowing marks bloom: strength at least 0 (default 1), radius from 0 to 1 (default 0.5).
- `fog` (`{ near, far, color }`): A 3D plot's distance fog from near to far (world units from the camera, 0 <= near < far), toward color (default the plot's background).
- `a plugin's kind` (`its parameters`): An effect a registered plugin declares (registerPlugin), checked against its parameter schema. Unregistered, it is skipped with a warning.

### Usage

A Plot's `effects` are composited over the whole plot after its marks are drawn: each is `{ kind, ...parameters }` (in Python, `hm.effect(kind, ...)`), and a kind appears once. The library's kinds are `sky`, `bloom` and `fog` (the sky is a plugin of the library's own, registered as it loads, built on the same [plugin API](/HMPlot/reference/svelte/plugins.md) as anyone's); any other kind is a [plugin's](/HMPlot/reference/svelte/plugins.md), drawn once its plugin is registered. A kind no plugin registers is a warning (`plugin.missing`), and the plot draws without it.

**sky** (a 3D plot): an `image` (an equirectangular map, longitude across and north up, such as a star map) or a gradient: `zenith` straight up (default `#4a7cc4`), `horizon` at the horizon (default `#d6e4f2`) and `ground` straight down (default the horizon's), blended by the view direction's height. The sky is drawn around the camera, so it turns as the camera turns and does not move as the camera moves; `rotation` ([x, y, z] in degrees) turns it, and its up is the camera's up. It shows its colors as given, not through the plot's tone mapping, and it covers the plot's background. The plot waits for an image to load (`aria-busy` and `whenSettled()`); a failed load is the plot's error, naming the URL. In Svelte, `image` is a URL, an `ImageBitmap`, an `<img>` or a `<canvas>`; in Python a URL, which the browser loads, or a file path, bytes or a PIL image, which go to the browser encoded (a JPEG stays a JPEG). `visible: false` hides the sky with its image still loaded, so a switch (`visible=hm.input.stars` in Python) shows it again at once.

**bloom**: how glowing marks look. A mark glows when its `glow` is above 0: its own color times `glow` blooms around it. `strength` is how bright (at least 0, default 1) and `radius` how far it spreads (0 to 1, default 0.5). Without a bloom effect these defaults apply; a bloom alone does nothing until a mark glows. Only the marks that glow contribute, so an equally bright mark beside a glowing one stays crisp, and an opaque mark in front hides the glow behind it. The glow adds light: it shows best on a dark background or sky. Marks drawn onto a Surface do not glow.

**fog** (a 3D plot): the scene blends toward `color` from `near` to `far`, distances from the camera in world units (`0 <= near < far`, independent of `cameraNear` and `cameraFar`). `color` defaults to the plot's background, or the theme's when the plot is transparent. Fog is blended before the tone mapper; without one, full fog is exactly `color`.

The effects are composited after the scene pass, so picking, the minimap and the axes' automatic domains never see them. A sky or fog in a 2D plot is an error. The settings pane edits fog and bloom; `effects` sets them again when it changes.

```svelte
<Plot type="3d" effects={[{ kind: "sky", image: "/stars_milky_way.jpg" }, { kind: "bloom", strength: 1.2 }]}>
  <Points3D x="x" y="y" z="z" glow={1} />
</Plot>
```

```python
with hm.Plot(type="3d", effects=[hm.effect("sky", image="stars_milky_way.jpg"),  # a local file, sent as a JPEG
                                 hm.effect("bloom", strength=1.2)]):
    hm.Points3D(x="x", y="y", z="z", glow=1)
```

> **SVG and PDF export**
>
> **Image.** While an effect shows (a sky, fog, a plugin's effect, or a mark's glow), SVG and PDF exports draw all of the plot's marks, with the effects, as one image (its axes, titles and legends stay vector), and `mode="vector"` refuses it, naming the effects. A bloom effect alone changes nothing. PNG exports include them. See [what is not exported as vector](/HMPlot/docs/export.md).

### Related examples

- [Solar system](/HMPlot/examples/solar-system.md)
- [Manhattan building flyover](/HMPlot/examples/manhattan-flyover.md)

## registerPlugin

Page: /reference/svelte/plugins.md

Add effects and shades written in TSL: a plugin declares them once, and a Plot's effects and a mark's shade name them.

### Example

```svelte
registerPlugin(vignette);
<Plot effects={[{ kind: "vignette", amount: 0.5 }]}>…</Plot>
```

### Functions

- `registerPlugin(plugin)` (`void`): Registers a plugin from definePlugin: its setup runs once, and plots that name its effects draw them from then on. The same plugin again does nothing; another of the same name, or one declaring a kind already registered, throws.
- `definePlugin({name, apiVersion, setup})` (`plugin`): A checked plugin: a lowercase name ("vignette", "acme.grain"), apiVersion 1 (the plugin API it is written for) and setup(hm), which declares its effects with hm.effect(kind, definition) and its shades with hm.shade(kind, definition). hm.three, hm.tsl and hm.jax are the library's own modules.

### Usage

A plugin adds numerical transforms, graph layouts, effects or shades. Transform and layout
authoring examples appear below; effects and shades are written in [TSL](https://threejs.org/docs/#api/en/nodes/Nodes), three.js's shader language, which a Plot's `effects` and a mark's `shade` then name. It is JavaScript only: `definePlugin({ name, apiVersion: 1, setup })` checks it, and `registerPlugin(plugin)` runs its `setup` once. `setup(hm)` declares each effect with `hm.effect(kind, definition)` and each shade with `hm.shade(kind, definition)`; `hm.three`, `hm.tsl` and `hm.jax` are the library's own modules, which a plugin uses instead of importing its own (two copies of three.js cannot share a shader graph). A plot that names a kind before its plugin registers draws without it, with a warning, and draws it once the plugin arrives.

An effect's definition:

- `stage`: `"linear"`, after the marks are drawn and before tone mapping, in linear color; `"display"`, after tone mapping, in display color (as the sky is drawn); or `"object"`, an object in the plot's scene (below).
- `linear({ rgb, alpha, depth, uv, params, camera })` or `display({ rgb, alpha, uv, params, camera })`: TSL nodes in, `{ rgb, alpha }` nodes out. `rgb` is straight (not premultiplied) color; `depth` is the distance from the camera in world units (linear stage only); `uv` the pixel's position in the plot (0 to 1, down from the top); `camera` the camera's `projectionInverse` and `world` matrices and its `up` vector.
- `parameters`: a schema, by name: `{ type, default, min, max, ... }`, with `type` one of number, color, boolean, select, string, field, expression, vector, image, union, array or object. A Plot's values are checked against it, naming the parameter. Number, color and vector parameters reach `params` as uniforms, so changing one compiles nothing; the rest arrive as plain values (or mark a number `structural: true`), and changing one rebuilds the effect. A vector is a list of `length` (2, 3 or 4) numbers. An image is a URL, an `ImageBitmap`, an `<img>`, a `<canvas>` or a `Blob` (in Python a URL, a file path, bytes or a PIL image): the library loads it, the plot waits for it (`whenSettled()`), and the effect is drawn once it has loaded, with the image in `params` as a texture node sampled as stored (`wrap: "repeat"` filters across its left and right edges, as a panorama needs). A value of `null` is one left out. A parameter without a default that is left out is `null` in `params` (a shade's too); giving it or leaving it out rebuilds the effect.
- `check(values, context)`: optional, what the schema cannot say. It gets the values as given and the Plot's `{ threeD, plot }` (the sky needs a 3D plot) and returns `""`, or a problem that the Plot reports after the effect's name (the sky's `"takes image or the gradient's colors (horizon), not both."`).
- `shown(values)`: optional; false leaves the effect out, not drawn and not exported (the sky's `visible: false`).
