every group in it. Reading a selection on an aggregate's row is 1 while any of its contributors
is a member. Filtering before an aggregate (`Filter` then `Group`) leaves out rows; filtering
after it (`Group` then `Filter(where=hm.col.count > 1)`) leaves out groups; either way a
group's membership is that of the rows it holds. A Filter's, Sort's or Calculate's rows are
members as their source rows are. Every way of reading a selection agrees: `respond`,
`Filter(where=focus)`, an Interaction's `"@focus"` and an expression's operand.

### By a column

`hm.selection(by="gene")` selects values, not rows: the rows picked select their values of the
column, and every row with one of those values is a member, in any table that has the column.
Duplicate values are expected: a gene hovered in a table of genes highlights all of its samples
in another table, and hovering a sample highlights its gene and the gene's other samples.

- Values match exactly and by type: the text `"7"` is not the number `7`; datetimes match as
  instants.
- A missing value (None, NaN) matches nothing, and a value a table lacks matches none of its
  rows.
- Every table that writes or reads the selection needs the column, by that name, with its values
  on the host (an error names the column otherwise). Other names for the column and composite
  keys are not supported; give the tables the same column.
- `by` is not a table's `key` (which keeps rows' state through updates) nor `animation_group`.
- Without `by`, a selection matches rows of the table they were picked in (or its
  [identity](identity)) and none of another table's, whatever its columns.

```python
focus = hm.selection(by="gene")
with hm.Row():
    with hm.Plot(data=genes):
        hm.Points(x="length", y="expression", hover=focus, respond=focus)
    with hm.Plot(data=samples):
        hm.Points(x="sample", y="value", size=hm.where(focus, 8, 4), respond=focus)
```

Hover is transient: leaving the point clears it. A click (`select=focus`) commits until the next
click. See the [gene hover recipe](/HMPlot/recipes.md).

### Python members

`hm.selection()` returns a `SelectionResource`, and a table's own are `table.selection`, `table.brush`, `table.hover`, `table.nearby` and `table.nearest` (a node's `selection` and the others reach its data's). Python keeps the state the browser last reported: the properties read it, and `subscribe` follows it. Changing the selection asks a displayed view, so those members are coroutines: they need the selection used in exactly one displayed Scene (a notebook view; else `RuntimeError`, or `hm.SceneError` with code `bridge.missing_view`) and `await`. `data=` names the owner (a `hm.Table` or an identity) when the selection has none of its own or several: an explicit `hm.selection()` always needs it.

| Member | Kind | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | attribute | The resource's id in the scene. |
| `by` | attribute | The column the selection matches rows by (`hm.selection(by=...)`), or None: the rows themselves. |
| `version` | attribute | Counts the changes Python has received from the browser. |
| `active` | property | Whether any rows are selected, as the browser last reported. |
| `rows` | property | The selected row indices: a tuple for a selection with one owner, else a dict of owner id to tuple. |
| `get_constraints(*, data=None)` | sync | The committed brush constraints: a tuple of dicts, one per brushed column, with its identity, name, type, bounds and categories. |
| `subscribe(callback)` | sync | Call `callback(status)` now and after each change the browser reports; `status` has active, rows and constraints. Returns a function that unsubscribes. |
| `update(rows=(), *, operation='replace', data=None, view=None)` | await | Change the selection in the view: `operation` is replace, add, remove, toggle or clear, and `rows` nonnegative row indices. Returns the view's status: active, count, revision, the owner's rows and constraints. |
| `replace(rows, *, data=None, view=None)` | await | Select exactly `rows`. |
| `add(rows, *, data=None, view=None)` | await | Add `rows` to the selection. |
| `remove(rows, *, data=None, view=None)` | await | Take `rows` out of the selection. |
| `toggle(rows, *, data=None, view=None)` | await | Select the rows of `rows` that are not selected and deselect the others. |
| `clear(*, data=None, view=None)` | await | Select nothing. |
| `clear_columns(*columns, data=None, view=None)` | await | Remove the brush's constraints on `columns`, keeping the others. |

### Related examples

- [Explicit shared selection](/HMPlot/examples/shared-selection.md)

## identity

Page: /reference/python/identity.md

Which rows are the same thing across tables, by key, so selections carry over.

### Example

```python
rows = hm.identity(keys=ids)
hm.Points(position=positions, identity=rows, select=True)
```

```svelte
const rows = identity({ keys: ids });
<Points position={positions} identity={rows} select />
```

### Members

This table describes the JavaScript interface. Python has its own Node and resource methods, listed under “Python members” below; these member names are not Python method names.

- `id` (`string`): Required.
- `length` (`number`): Required.
- `selection` (`SelectionResource`): Required.
- `brush` (`SelectionResource`): Required.
- `hover` (`SelectionResource`): Required.
- `offsets` (`OffsetLayer`): Required.

### Usage

Data and Table normally own identity for you. Explicit identity is useful for raw-array marks. Matching names in separate tables do not imply shared observation identity; use keys when rows reorder.

`identity({ keys })` gives the rows of marks that take raw arrays (`position={...}`) an owner: row i is the observation `keys[i]`, so a selection made on one mark selects the same observations on every mark with that identity, and keyed updates and connections match rows by key. Keys must be unique, present and finite: strings, categories, integers (int64 and uint64 exact) or float32 values. The member table above is the JavaScript object; its `selection`, `brush` and `hover` are [SelectionResources](selection) owned by it.

### Python members

`hm.identity(keys=...)` returns an identity resource with these members, plain attributes fixed when it is made. Its selections' `await` members need a displayed notebook view (see [selection](selection)). Keys that differ only beyond float32 precision are refused, naming the pair; use integer or string keys for large identifiers.

| Member | Kind | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `id` | attribute | The resource's id in the scene. |
| `keys` | attribute | The keys as the column the browser receives (one-dimensional, typed as `hm.typed_column` types them). |
| `selection` | attribute | The SelectionResource of the rows clicked or set from code. |
| `brush` | attribute | The SelectionResource of the brushed rows. |
| `hover` | attribute | The SelectionResource of the hovered rows. |
| `nearby` | attribute | The SelectionResource of the rows near the pointer. |
| `nearest` | attribute | The SelectionResource of the row a tooltip shows (nearest). |

### Related examples

- [Data selections and brushing](/HMPlot/examples/data-selections.md)

## Tooltips

Page: /reference/python/tooltips.md

The nearest row's values in a box by the pointer, set per mark (tooltip=) or for a Plot.

### Example

```python
hm.Points(x="bill", y="mass", fill="species", tooltip=True)
```

```svelte
<Points x="bill" y="mass" fill="species" tooltip />
```

### Members

- `fields` (`TooltipField[]`): The fields to list (default: the columns the mark's channels read).
- `radius` (`number`): How near the pointer a row is found, in CSS pixels (default 16).
- `content` (`Snippet<[{ values: Record<string, unknown>; row: number; mark: string; lines: { label: string; text: string; }[]; }]>`): Svelte only: the box's content, given { values, row, mark, lines }.

### Usage

`tooltip` on a mark shows the nearest row's values in a box beside the pointer. `true` lists the columns the mark's channels read; a list picks the fields, each a column name or `{ field, label, format }`. On a Plot, `tooltip` is the default of its marks, and a mark's `tooltip={false}` opts out. Tooltips are off by default.

The nearest row within `radius` (16 CSS pixels by default) of a mark with a tooltip is shown, so small points are easy to reach: each pick reads a small window of the pick buffer around the pointer, whatever the number of rows. Only what is drawn counts, so a hidden or covered row is never shown, and 3D views work the same way. That row is `@nearest`, which [nearest](interaction) sets without the box; hover and clicks still take the row exactly under the pointer.

`tooltip={{ mode: "x" }}` on a Plot is unified x: one box lists each series' value at the pointer's x, as a time series reads, with a marker on each line; `<Crosshair axes="x" />` draws the rule. In Svelte, `content` replaces the box's table with a snippet given `{ values, row, mark, lines }`.

### Related examples

- [Tooltips](/HMPlot/examples/tooltips.md)

## view

Page: /reference/python/pointer-columns.md

View and interaction state, read in any expression: the pointer, the visible domain, the clock, and each row's interaction flags.

### Example

```python
hm.charts.RuleX(x=hm.view.pointer_x)
hm.Points(x="x", y="y", size=hm.where(hm.view.hovered, 6, 3), hover=True)
```

```svelte
<RuleX x={view.pointer_x} />
<Points x="x" y="y" size={where(view.hovered, 6, 3)} hover />
```

### Parameters

- `selected, brushed, hovered, nearby, nearest, tooltip` (`state`): 1 for the rows in that interaction state, else 0; "@selected" reads the same.
- `any_selected, any_brushed, any_hovered, any_nearby, any_nearest, any_tooltip` (`state`): 1 while any row is in that state.
- `pointer_x, pointer_y` (`state`): The pointer in the frame's data; missing off the frame.
- `view_x_min, view_x_max, view_y_min, view_y_max` (`state`): The frame's visible domain as it pans and zooms.
- `time` (`state`): The animation clock, in milliseconds.
- `dt` (`state`): A Simulate's step, in milliseconds.
- `offset_x, offset_y, offset_z` (`state`): The row's drag offset.

### Usage

`"@pointer_x"` and `"@pointer_y"` are the pointer in the data of the frame that reads them, and `"@view_x_min"`, `"@view_x_max"`, `"@view_y_min"` and `"@view_y_max"` that frame's visible domain. They are view state, as `"@time"` is: a mark channel can name one, and any expression can read one with `view.pointer_x`, in a mark, a Filter, a Calculate or a transform parameter.

The pointer is missing off the frame and before it arrives, so a `where(is_missing("@pointer_x"), ...)` chooses what to show then. Over a band axis it is the category under the pointer, which compares with a categorical column by value. On a datetime axis it counts from the axis's time origin, as the marks on it do.

A mark that reads only the pointer steps as it moves and never on the clock, so a still pointer runs nothing. RuleX, RuleY and Crosshair are built on these values.

### Related examples

- [Crosshair and rules](/HMPlot/examples/crosshair.md)

## Offsets and dragging

Page: /reference/python/offsets-drag.md

Rows dragged with drag= move by offsets that views read through moved() and offset().

### Example

```python
hm.Points(x=hm.moved("x"), y=hm.moved("y"), drag=True)
```

```svelte
<Points x={moved("x")} y={moved("y")} drag />
```

### Functions

- `hm.moved(column)` (`expression`): A numeric table column plus each row's offset: what a view reads to follow drags, as in x={moved("weight")}. Offsets are in the column's units, so log(moved("weight")) moves through a log.
- `hm.offset(column)` (`expression`): Each row's offset in the column alone, 0 where it has none: set by dragging or from code.

### Usage

`drag` on a point mark makes its rows draggable. `true` drags along every numeric axis of the view; `"x"`, `"y"`, `"xy"` or `"xyz"` name the axes, and a categorical axis is never dragged, so a strip plot drags along its numeric axis. A press on a draggable row starts a drag, anywhere else the plot pans, Shift-drag still brushes, and Escape cancels.

A drag never changes the table. It writes **offsets**, per-row deltas in each column's own units, on the table's rows, and every view of the table shares them. A view follows only where it reads them: `moved("weight")` is the column plus its offsets and `offset("weight")` the offsets alone, so `x={moved("weight")}` follows a drag and `x="weight"` does not, the dragged mark included. That is what lets one drag move a row in every cell of a scatterplot matrix: each cell's `x` and `y` stand for its two fields, and `moved("x")` reads the offsets of the field the cell shows.

The drag goes back through the channel's expression and the transforms above the mark, so the row lands under the pointer through `log(moved("w"))`, a polar or map frame, or a Calculate column. A Filter that reads `moved()` hides and shows the row while it is dragged. A row of a Group drags its members: a mean or median moves them all by the change, a sum splits it in proportion to each member. Dragging a selected row moves the selection. Rows being dragged skip their transitions and stay under the pointer; Escape and `resetOffsets()` animate.

`getOffsets()`, `resetOffsets()` and `applyOffsets()` on a Data, Provider or Plot read, clear and apply the offsets; `ondrag` and `ondragend` report the dragged rows' keys and each column's change. In Python, `table.offsets` is a DataFrame of key, column and delta, `table.apply_offsets()` a new Table with the moved values, and `table.set_offsets()` and `table.clear_offsets()` change them. See docs/DATA.md, "Dragging".

### Related examples

- [Dragging points](/HMPlot/examples/drag-matrix.md)
- [Dragging cities on a map](/HMPlot/examples/drag-map.md)

## zoomViewport

Page: /reference/svelte/zoom-viewport.md

A 2D viewport zoomed by a factor along x, y or both, never past the fitted view.

### Example

```svelte
<script>
  import { Plot, Points, zoomViewport } from "hmplot";
  let viewport = $state({ x: 0.5, y: 0.5, zoom: 1 });
</script>

<button onclick={() => (viewport = zoomViewport(viewport, 1.5))}>Zoom in</button>
<button onclick={() => (viewport = zoomViewport(viewport, 1 / 1.5, "x"))}>Zoom x out</button>
<Plot {viewport} onviewportchange={(v) => (viewport = v)} axes2d>…</Plot>
```

### Members

#### Members

- `x` (`number`): Required.
- `y` (`number`): Required.
- `zoom` (`number`): Required.
- `zoomX` (`number`): The horizontal zoom factor, when x and y zoom apart (1 fits the domain).
- `zoomY` (`number`): The vertical zoom factor, when x and y zoom apart.
- `center` (`[number, number]`): Active root longitude and latitude in its angular units.

#### Parameters

- `viewport` (`Viewport2D`): The current viewport: { x, y, zoom }, with zoomX and zoomY when the axes zoom apart (each defaults to zoom).
- `factor` (`number`): The zoom multiplier: above 1 zooms in, below 1 out. Finite and positive, else an error.
- `axis` (`"xy" | "x" | "y"`): Which axes zoom (default "xy"): one axis leaves the other's factor alone.
- `minimum` (`number`): The smallest zoom an axis may reach (default 1, the fitted view). With "xy" the factor is raised so neither axis passes it, keeping their ratio.
- `returns` (`Viewport2D`): A new viewport: the same center, the new zoomX and zoomY, and zoom their geometric mean (center kept for an orthographic globe).

### Usage

A 2D Plot's viewport is `{ x, y, zoom }`: the center in the plot's unit square (0.5 is the middle) and the zoom, 1 being the fitted view; `zoomX` and `zoomY` zoom the axes apart, and each defaults to `zoom`. Pass a viewport to Plot's `viewport` prop and follow the viewer's changes with `onviewportchange`, which reports the same fields. `zoomViewport` gives the next state for a button or a key: it multiplies the zoom along `axis`, never below the fitted view, and keeps the center. Changing `zoom` alone would leave an axis that has its own factor where it was.

The same object is what `getViewport()` and `setViewport()` on the [Plot handle](plot-handle) read and write; Python sets it with `await plot.set_viewport(...)`. An orthographic globe's viewport also has `center`, its longitude and latitude, which `zoomViewport` keeps. See docs/NAVIGATION.md for zooming one axis from its margin.

### Related examples

- [Linked views & minimap](/HMPlot/examples/linked.md)
- [Long time series](/HMPlot/examples/timeseries.md)

## InputContext

Page: /reference/python/input-context.md

A scope for inputs: everything inside it reads the inputs inside it by name (a Python Scene is one already).

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"x": [1, 2, 3, 4], "y": [3, 1, 4, 2]}
with hm.InputContext() as inputs:
    hm.Slider(name="size", min=1, max=10, value=4)
    with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True):
        hm.Points(x="x", y="y", size=hm.input.size)
inputs
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { InputContext, Plot, Points, Slider, input } from "hmplot";
  const data = { x: [1, 2, 3, 4], y: [3, 1, 4, 2] };
</script>

<InputContext>
  <Slider name="size" min={1} max={10} value={4} />
  <Plot {data} height={300} axes2d>
    <Points x="x" y="y" size={input("size")} />
  </Plot>
</InputContext>
```

### Usage

An input sends its value up to the nearest input context (an InputContext, a Python Scene, or a Template instance), and everything in that context reads it by name: `input("name")` in JavaScript, `hm.input.name` in Python, or the string `"$name"` where a string names a column. A read is replaced by the value before its reader sees it, so moving an input re-runs its readers once, and the change animates like any other data change. Inputs go beside Plots (in a Row or Column), not inside them, and are left out of image and PDF exports.

A mark or a Button can write an input too. `input("root", { default: "all" })` reads the input and makes its writes (an `InputExpression`; in Python `hm.input("root", default="all")`):

- `select={root.set("id")}` sets it to the clicked row's `id`, and a click on nothing restores the default.
- `hover={focus.set("series")}` shows the hovered row's `series` until the pointer leaves, then the committed value again.
- `root.set(literal("all"))` (or a number, a boolean, a Date, null) writes a constant, and `root.reset()` the default: a mark's `select`, or a [Button](button)'s `set`, so a press goes back to the top of a drill-down.

```svelte
<script>
  import { InputContext, Button, Plot, GraphData, Treemap, Nodes, Rect, input } from "hmplot";
  let { nodes, edges } = $props();
  const root = input("root", { default: "all" });
</script>

<InputContext>
  <Button label="Top" set={root.reset()} />
  <Plot>
    <GraphData {nodes} {edges} source="parent" target="id">
      <Treemap root={root} value="revenue" levels={1}>
        <Nodes><Rect x0="x0" x1="x1" y0="y0" y1="y1" select={root.set("id")} /></Nodes>
      </Treemap>
    </GraphData>
  </Plot>
</InputContext>
```

The value is visualization state with a default (a drill-down's root, a focused series), where a [selection](selection) is a set of rows. A write works whether a widget declares the input or not: several marks, a [TableView](table-view)'s rows, Buttons and a widget of the same name (a Select named `root`) may write one input, the last write wins, and the widget shows it. Writes made from one `input("root", { default })` carry its default; writers that give different defaults, or write it from columns of different kinds, are an error naming both; so is a hover that writes an input a transform above that mark reads, since each hover would change the rows under the pointer (write it on click). Before any write the value is the default, null when none is given; an expression comparing a column with a null input matches no row. The object form `{ input: "root", column: "id", default: "all" }` (or `value`, or `reset: true`) is the same write.

### Related examples

- [Inputs](/HMPlot/examples/inputs.md)

## TextInput

Page: /reference/python/text-input.md

Text edited by the viewer, updated on each keystroke.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"x": [1, 3, 5, 7, 9], "y": [2, 4, 1, 5, 3]}
with hm.Scene() as scene:
    hm.TextInput(name="caption", value="My observations", placeholder="Plot title")
    with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True, title=hm.input.caption):
        hm.Points(x="x", y="y", size=12)
scene
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { TextInput, InputContext, Plot, Points, input } from "hmplot";
  const data = { x: [1, 3, 5, 7, 9], y: [2, 4, 1, 5, 3] };
</script>

<InputContext>
  <TextInput name="caption" value="My observations" placeholder="Plot title" />
  <Plot {data} height={300} axes2d title={"{$caption}"}>
    <Points x="x" y="y" size={12}  />
  </Plot>
</InputContext>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

- `value` (`string`): The initial text. Default: `""`.
- `placeholder` (`string`): A hint shown while the input is empty.
- `name` (`string`): The name readers use (input("name"), hm.input.name, or "$name" where a string names a column): an identifier, unique in its input context.
- `label` (`string`): The text shown beside the control. Default: the name.

### Usage

Enter a string. The value updates on each keystroke; clearing the box publishes an empty string. `placeholder` supplies a hint while the box is empty and does not become its value. A string used as a mark channel can name a column; the example uses it as a plot title.

Place the control beside the plot in an `InputContext` (JavaScript) or `Scene` (Python). Readers use `input("name")` or `hm.input.name`. The name must be unique in that context.

Static image exports show the plot at the current values and omit the controls.

## ColorPicker

Page: /reference/python/color-picker.md

An opaque RGB color selected with the browser color picker.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"x": [1, 3, 5, 7, 9], "y": [2, 4, 1, 5, 3]}
with hm.Scene() as scene:
    hm.ColorPicker(name="ink", value="#4f7dff")
    with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True):
        hm.Points(x="x", y="y", size=12, fill=hm.input.ink)
scene
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { ColorPicker, InputContext, Plot, Points, input } from "hmplot";
  const data = { x: [1, 3, 5, 7, 9], y: [2, 4, 1, 5, 3] };
</script>

<InputContext>
  <ColorPicker name="ink" value="#4f7dff" />
  <Plot {data} height={300} axes2d >
    <Points x="x" y="y" size={12} fill={input("ink")} />
  </Plot>
</InputContext>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

- `value` (`string`): A six-digit hexadecimal color; the value is lowercase #rrggbb. Default: `"#000000"`.
- `name` (`string`): The name readers use (input("name"), hm.input.name, or "$name" where a string names a column): an identifier, unique in its input context.
- `label` (`string`): The text shown beside the control. Default: the name.

### Usage

Choose an opaque RGB color using the browser's native picker. Supply a six-digit hexadecimal value, such as `#4f7dff`; the control publishes lowercase `#rrggbb`. Use the named input for a mark's `fill` or `color`. Alpha values and CSS color names are not accepted; set the mark's opacity separately.

Place the control beside the plot in an `InputContext` (JavaScript) or `Scene` (Python). Readers use `input("name")` or `hm.input.name`. The name must be unique in that context.

Static image exports show the plot at the current values and omit the controls.

## DateTimeInput

Page: /reference/python/date-time-input.md

A date and time edited in a chosen time zone, held as a Date or null.

### Example

```python
from datetime import datetime, timezone
import hmplot as hm

data = {"x": [1, 3, 5, 7, 9], "y": [2, 4, 1, 5, 3]}
with hm.Scene() as scene:
    hm.DateTimeInput(name="cutoff", value=datetime(2024, 6, 1, 12, tzinfo=timezone.utc), timezone="UTC")
    with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True, title="Cutoff: {$cutoff}"):
        hm.Points(x="x", y="y", size=12)
scene
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { DateTimeInput, InputContext, Plot, Points, input } from "hmplot";
  const data = { x: [1, 3, 5, 7, 9], y: [2, 4, 1, 5, 3] };
</script>

<InputContext>
  <DateTimeInput name="cutoff" value={new Date("2024-06-01T12:00:00Z")} timezone="UTC" />
  <Plot {data} height={300} axes2d title={"Cutoff: {$cutoff}"}>
    <Points x="x" y="y" size={12}  />
  </Plot>
</InputContext>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

- `value` (`Date | null`): The initial instant; omitted or null leaves the input empty.
- `min` (`Date`): The earliest allowed instant.
- `max` (`Date`): The latest allowed instant.
- `step` (`number`): The step in milliseconds. Default: `60000`.
- `timezone` (`string`): The editing time zone: an IANA name, UTC, or Local. Default: `"UTC"`.
- `name` (`string`): The name readers use (input("name"), hm.input.name, or "$name" where a string names a column): an identifier, unique in its input context.
- `label` (`string`): The text shown beside the control. Default: the name.

### Usage

Edit a date and time in `timezone` (UTC by default). The value is a JavaScript `Date` or Python `datetime`, representing an instant; changing the editing zone does not change that instant. Use `min` and `max` to bound the date, and `step` in milliseconds to set its precision (default: one minute). Clearing the input publishes `null` in JavaScript or `None` in Python.

Daylight-saving transitions can make a local time nonexistent or ambiguous. Such edits show an error and keep the last valid value; choose an unambiguous time, or edit in UTC. Timezone-aware Python datetimes make the intended instant explicit.

Place the control beside the plot in an `InputContext` (JavaScript) or `Scene` (Python). Readers use `input("name")` or `hm.input.name`. The name must be unique in that context.

Static image exports show the plot at the current values and omit the controls.

## Slider

Page: /reference/python/slider.md

A number, date or two-endpoint interval the viewer drags between min and max, read by name.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"x": [1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 7]}
with hm.Scene() as scene:
    hm.Slider(name="bins", min=1, max=10, step=1, value=4)
    with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True):
        with hm.stats.Bin(x="x", bins=hm.input.bins):
            hm.Rect(x0="x0", x1="x1", y0=0, y1="count")
scene
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { InputContext, Plot, Rect, Slider, input } from "hmplot";
import { Bin } from "hmplot/stats";
  const data = { x: [1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 7] };
</script>

<InputContext>
  <Slider name="bins" min={1} max={10} step={1} value={4} />
  <Plot {data} height={300} axes2d>
    <Bin x="x" bins={input("bins")}>
      <Rect x0="x0" x1="x1" y0={0} y1="count" />
    </Bin>
  </Plot>
</InputContext>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

- `min` (`number | Date | expression`): The low end of the range: a number, a Date, or an expression such as min("x") over the data around the slider. Default: `0`.
- `max` (`number | Date | expression`): The high end of the range: a number, a Date, or an expression such as max("x"). Default: `1`.
- `step` (`number | string | {unit, step}`): The distance between values; over Dates, a calendar interval such as "1 month" (which lands on month starts) or milliseconds. Default: any value.
- `value` (`number | Date | [number, number] | [Date, Date] | expression`): The initial value, or [lower, upper] for two thumbs selecting an interval. Endpoints are sorted and clamped to min/max; an expression reads the data. Default: min.
- `format` (`string | (value) => string`): How the value is shown: a d3-format string such as ".2f", a %-pattern such as "%b %Y" over Dates, or (in JavaScript) a function. Default: a numeric step's decimals, else 4 significant digits (12,346); over Dates, by the step, as an axis labels them.
- `timezone` (`string`): Over Dates, the time zone its steps and labels are in: an IANA name, "UTC" or "Local". Default: the zone of the datetime column min or max reads, else UTC.
- `name` (`string`): The name readers use (input("name"), hm.input.name, or "$name" where a string names a column): an identifier, unique in its input context.
- `label` (`string`): The text shown beside the control. Default: the name.

### Usage

Use a scalar `value` for one thumb or `[lower, upper]` for two thumbs selecting an interval.
Endpoints are sorted and clamped to `min` and `max`; either numbers or Dates work, including
calendar steps. Both thumbs support keyboard arrows and cannot cross. This replaces RangeSlider.
In Svelte, bind the interval with `bind:value`; in Python, read it with `hm.input.name`,
for example as a plot domain.

An input sends its value up to the nearest input context (an InputContext, a Python Scene, or a Template instance), and everything in that context reads it by name: `input("name")` in JavaScript, `hm.input.name` in Python, or the string `"$name"` where a string names a column. A read is replaced by the value before its reader sees it, so moving an input re-runs its readers once, and the change animates like any other data change. Inputs go beside Plots (in a Row or Column), not inside them.

> **SVG and PDF export**
>
> **Left out.** PNG, SVG and PDF exports leave inputs out, and show the plots at the inputs' current values. See [what is not exported as vector](/HMPlot/docs/export.md).

### Related examples

- [Inputs](/HMPlot/examples/inputs.md)

## Button

Page: /reference/python/button.md

Counts the viewer's presses, so a prop that acts on each change of its value (reset=, refresh=) acts on each press; with set, a press writes other inputs (back to the top of a drill-down).

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"x": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8], "y": [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6]}
## Each press adds one to the button's value, so the Sample draws with a new seed.
with hm.Scene() as scene:
    hm.Button(name="draw")
    with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True):
        with hm.Sample(size=4, seed=hm.input.draw):
            hm.Points(x="x", y="y")
scene
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Button, InputContext, Plot, Points, Sample, input } from "hmplot";
  const data = { x: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8], y: [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6] };
</script>

<!-- Each press adds one to the button's value, so the Sample draws with a new seed. -->
<InputContext>
  <Button name="draw" />
  <Plot {data} height={300} axes2d>
    <Sample size={4} seed={input("draw")}>
      <Points x="x" y="y" />
    </Sample>
  </Plot>
</InputContext>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

- `value` (`number`): The count before the first press. Default: `0`.
- `name` (`string`): The name readers use (input("name"), hm.input.name, or "$name" where a string names a column): an identifier, unique in its input context. Optional with set.
- `label` (`string`): The text shown beside the control (needed with set and no name). Default: the name.
- `set` (`object | array`): Inputs a press writes: input("root").reset() restores root's default, input("root").set(literal("all")) sets a constant; a list writes several.

### Usage

An input sends its value up to the nearest input context (an InputContext, a Python Scene, or a Template instance), and everything in that context reads it by name: `input("name")` in JavaScript, `hm.input.name` in Python, or the string `"$name"` where a string names a column. A read is replaced by the value before its reader sees it, so moving an input re-runs its readers once, and the change animates like any other data change. Inputs go beside Plots (in a Row or Column), not inside them.

A press can also write other inputs: `set={root.reset()}` puts `root` back to its default, and `set={root.set(literal("all"))}` gives it a value, where `const root = input("root", { default: "all" })` (Python `set=hm.input("root", default="all").reset()`). A list writes several. The input need not be a widget's: marks writing it on click (`select={root.set("id")}`) and Buttons together declare it, so a Button goes back to the top of a drill-down a click on a rectangle went into. A Button with `set` needs no `name` (then give it a `label`); with a name it also counts its presses.

> **SVG and PDF export**
>
> **Left out.** PNG, SVG and PDF exports leave inputs out, and show the plots at the inputs' current values. See [what is not exported as vector](/HMPlot/docs/export.md).

### Related examples

- [Inputs](/HMPlot/examples/inputs.md)

## Select

Page: /reference/python/select.md

One or several options, chosen by the viewer and read by name; a Select of column names picks what a channel plots.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"a": [1, 2, 3, 4], "b": [4, 2, 3, 1], "y": [3, 1, 4, 2]}
## "$column" reads the input where a string names a column: x plots the chosen one.
with hm.Scene() as scene:
    hm.Select(name="column", options=["a", "b"])
    with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True):
        hm.Points(x="$column", y="y")
scene
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { InputContext, Plot, Points, Select } from "hmplot";
  const data = { a: [1, 2, 3, 4], b: [4, 2, 3, 1], y: [3, 1, 4, 2] };
</script>

<!-- "$column" reads the input where a string names a column: x plots the chosen one. -->
<InputContext>
  <Select name="column" options={["a", "b"]} />
  <Plot {data} height={300} axes2d>
    <Points x="$column" y="y" />
  </Plot>
</InputContext>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

- `options` (`(string | number | boolean | Date)[] | {label: value} | expression`): The choices: a list of values, labels and their values, or categories("field") or columnNames() read from the data around it.
- `multiple` (`boolean`): Allow several choices; the value is a list usable with is_in(column, input("name")). Default: `False`.
- `value` (`string | number | boolean | Date | (string | number | boolean | Date)[]`): The chosen value, or list of values when multiple is true. Default: the first option, or an empty list when multiple.
- `name` (`string`): The name readers use (input("name"), hm.input.name, or "$name" where a string names a column): an identifier, unique in its input context.
- `label` (`string`): The text shown beside the control. Default: the name.

### Usage

Set `multiple={true}` in Svelte or `multiple=True` in Python to choose several options. The
value is then a list (empty by default), and `is_in(col("species"), input("chosen"))` uses it
to filter rows. When data-derived options change, choices that are no longer present are
removed. This replaces MultiSelect.

An input sends its value up to the nearest input context (an InputContext, a Python Scene, or a Template instance), and everything in that context reads it by name: `input("name")` in JavaScript, `hm.input.name` in Python, or the string `"$name"` where a string names a column. A read is replaced by the value before its reader sees it, so moving an input re-runs its readers once, and the change animates like any other data change. Inputs go beside Plots (in a Row or Column), not inside them.

> **SVG and PDF export**
>
> **Left out.** PNG, SVG and PDF exports leave inputs out, and show the plots at the inputs' current values. See [what is not exported as vector](/HMPlot/docs/export.md).

### Related examples

- [Inputs](/HMPlot/examples/inputs.md)

## Playback

Page: /reference/python/playback.md

A slider with play, pause and reset buttons that moves its value over time, read by name.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"x": [1, 2, 3, 4], "y": [3, 1, 4, 2]}
## Play shows the points up to x = until, one more each second.
with hm.Scene() as scene:
    hm.Playback(name="until", min=1, max=4, step=1)
    with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True, x={"domain": [0, 5]}, y={"domain": [0, 5]}):
        with hm.Filter(where=hm.col.x <= hm.input.until):
            hm.Points(x="x", y="y")
scene
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Filter, InputContext, Playback, Plot, Points, col, input, less_equal } from "hmplot";
  const data = { x: [1, 2, 3, 4], y: [3, 1, 4, 2] };
</script>

<!-- Play shows the points up to x = until, one more each second. -->
<InputContext>
  <Playback name="until" min={1} max={4} step={1} />
  <Plot {data} height={300} axes2d x={{ domain: [0, 5] }} y={{ domain: [0, 5] }}>
    <Filter where={less_equal(col("x"), input("until"))}>
      <Points x="x" y="y" />
    </Filter>
  </Plot>
</InputContext>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

- `rate` (`number | string | {unit, step}`): How fast play moves the value, in value units per second; over Dates, a calendar interval per second ("1 day") or milliseconds per second. Default: `1`.
- `loop` (`boolean`): Wraps back to min at max instead of stopping. Default: `False`.
- `autoplay` (`boolean`): Starts playing when it mounts, unless the viewer prefers reduced motion. Default: `False`.
- `playing` (`boolean`): Plays (true) or pauses (false) it from code; Python has play() and pause().
- `reset` (`number | string`): Each change of its value returns it to its first value (a Button's count works); Python has reset().
- `min` (`number | Date | expression`): The low end of the range: a number, a Date, or an expression such as min("t") over the data around it. Default: `0`.
- `max` (`number | Date | expression`): The high end of the range: a number, a Date, or an expression such as max("t"). Default: `1`.
- `step` (`number | string | {unit, step}`): The distance between values: play moves one step every step/rate seconds, or every frame without one. Over Dates, a calendar interval such as "1 month" or milliseconds. Default: any value.
- `value` (`number | Date | expression`): The first value, where play starts and reset returns; an expression reads it from the data. Default: min.
- `format` (`string | (value) => string`): How the value is shown: a d3-format string such as ".2f", a %-pattern such as "%b %Y" over Dates, or (in JavaScript) a function. Default: a numeric step's decimals, else 4 significant digits (12,346); over Dates, by the step, as an axis labels them.
- `timezone` (`string`): Over Dates, the time zone its steps and labels are in: an IANA name, "UTC" or "Local". Default: the zone of the datetime column min or max reads, else UTC.
- `name` (`string`): The name readers use (input("name"), hm.input.name, or "$name" where a string names a column): an identifier, unique in its input context.
- `label` (`string`): The text shown beside the control. Default: the name.

### Usage

An input sends its value up to the nearest input context (an InputContext, a Python Scene, or a Template instance), and everything in that context reads it by name: `input("name")` in JavaScript, `hm.input.name` in Python, or the string `"$name"` where a string names a column. A read is replaced by the value before its reader sees it, so moving an input re-runs its readers once, and the change animates like any other data change. Inputs go beside Plots (in a Row or Column), not inside them.

> **SVG and PDF export**
>
> **Left out.** PNG, SVG and PDF exports leave inputs out, and show the plots at the inputs' current values. See [what is not exported as vector](/HMPlot/docs/export.md).

### Related examples

- [Inputs](/HMPlot/examples/inputs.md)
- [Calendar functions and a Playback over dates](/HMPlot/examples/calendar.md)

## Simulate

Page: /reference/python/simulate.md

Per-row state, such as positions and velocities, stepped at a fixed interval for the marks inside it to draw.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

radius, speed = hm.row() + 1, 3 - hm.row()
## Each step, a row's angle moves on by its speed (radians per second) times the step.
angle = hm.prev.angle + speed * hm.view.dt / 1000
with hm.Data(rows=3) as table:
    hm.Checkbox(name="running", label="Run simulation", value=False)
    with hm.Simulate(initial={"angle": 0}, update={"angle": angle}, running=hm.input.running):
        with hm.Plot(height=300, axes2d=True, x={"domain": [-4, 4]}, y={"domain": [-4, 4]}):
            hm.Points(x=radius * hm.cos(hm.col.angle), y=radius * hm.sin(hm.col.angle))
table
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Checkbox, InputContext, Data, row, Plot, Points, Simulate, add, cos, divide, multiply, prev, sin, input, subtract } from "hmplot";
  const radius = add(row(), 1), speed = subtract(3, row());
  // Each step, a row's angle moves on by its speed (radians per second) times the step.
  const angle = add(prev("angle"), multiply(speed, divide("@dt", 1000)));
</script>

<InputContext>
<Checkbox name="running" label="Run simulation" value={false} />
<Data rows={3}>
  <Simulate initial={{ angle: 0 }} update={{ angle }} running={input.running}>
    <Plot height={300} axes2d x={{ domain: [-4, 4] }} y={{ domain: [-4, 4] }}>
      <Points x={multiply(radius, cos("angle"))} y={multiply(radius, sin("angle"))} />
    </Plot>
  </Simulate>
</Data>
</InputContext>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

- `name` (`string`): The simulation's name in its status.
- `initial` (`Record<string, string | number | expression>`): Each state column's first value: a column name, a number, or an expression over the data's columns. Rows that arrive later start from it too.
- `update` (`Record<string, string | number | expression>`): Each state column's next value, reading the previous step (prev("x"), Python hm.prev.x), the data's columns, the step ("@dt", Python hm.view.dt) and inputs. Every update reads the previous step, so their order does not matter.
- `step` (`number`): The simulated time one step advances; the state after n steps is the same at any frame rate. Default: `16` ms.
- `max_steps` (`number`): The most steps one frame takes, so a slow device runs behind real time instead of stalling. Default: `8`.
- `stop` (`{tolerance, every, columns}`): Settles once no column in `columns` (default: the updated ones) changes by more than `tolerance` in a step, checked every `every` steps (default 30). New data, inputs, running or reset wake it.
- `running` (`boolean`): Plays or pauses the simulation; running={input("run")} lets a Checkbox do it. Under prefers-reduced-motion one that plays from the start waits until running changes, as a Playback's autoplay does. Default: `True`.
- `reset` (`number | string`): Each change of its value starts again from `initial` (a Button's count works: reset={input("kick")}).

### Usage

Simulate keeps state columns for the rows of the Data scope around it and steps them at a fixed interval of simulated time. `initial` gives each state column's first value and `update` its next one; an update reads the state after the previous step with `prev("x")` (Python `hm.prev.x`), the parent's columns with `col("x")`, the step in milliseconds as `"@dt"` (`hm.view.dt`), [inputs](slider) with `input("name")`, and the Simulate's own rows' `"@selected"`, `"@brushed"` and `"@hovered"`. Every update reads the previous step, so the order of the columns does not matter.

Steps are counted from elapsed time (at most `maxSteps` in one frame), so the motion is the same at 60 and 120 Hz. With `stop`, the simulation settles when nothing moves more than `tolerance` over `every` steps; a change of its data, inputs, selection or `reset` wakes it. `running={input("run")}` with a [Checkbox](checkbox) pauses it, and `reset={input("kick")}` with a [Button](button) starts again from `initial`. Under `prefers-reduced-motion` a Simulate that runs from the start stays at its first state (its exports show that state) until `running` changes; `setAnimationTime` still steps it. A new parent keeps each surviving row's state by key.

### Related examples

- [Springs](/HMPlot/examples/springs.md)

## Options from data

Page: /reference/python/input-options.md

columnNames and categories: an input's options read from the data around it.

### Example

```python
with hm.Scene() as scene:
    with hm.Data(penguins):
        hm.Select(name="species", options=hm.categories("species"))
        hm.Select(name="metric", options=hm.column_names())
        with hm.Filter(where=hm.col.species == hm.input.species):
            with hm.Plot():
                hm.Points(x="$metric", y="body_mass")
```

```svelte
<InputContext>
  <Data value={penguins}>
    <Select name="species" options={categories("species")} />
    <Select name="metric" options={columnNames()} />
    <Filter where={equal(col.species, input("species"))}>
      <Plot><Points x="$metric" y="body_mass" /></Plot>
    </Filter>
  </Data>
</InputContext>
```

### Functions

- `hm.column_names()` (`string[]`): The column names of the Data scope around the input, for a Select of columns.
- `hm.categories(field)` (`category[]`): A categorical column's categories, in order. A numeric column is an error.

### Usage

An input inside a Data scope can take its options from that data: `columnNames()` for a Select that chooses which column to plot (read it as `x="$metric"`), and `categories("species")` for a Select or Select with multiple=true of a categorical column's values. A Slider's `min` and `max`, and any input's first `value`, can be a [reduction](reductions) such as `min("x")` the same way.

They are read once, and again when the data changes, never when the input moves. Until they are read, the input is pending and its readers wait instead of drawing with a stand-in value. When new data changes the options, a Select keeps its value if it is still an option, else takes the first one, and a Select with multiple=true drops the values that are gone. `categories` of a numeric column is an error; type it with a schema or [typedColumn](typed-column) first.

See docs/INPUTS.md, "Options and ranges from the data".

### Related examples

- [Inputs](/HMPlot/examples/inputs.md)
- [Filter and bin inputs](/HMPlot/examples/transform-controls.md)

## Data

Page: /reference/python/data.md

A table whose columns the components inside it read by name.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"x": [1, 2, 3, 4], "y": [3, 1, 4, 2]}
with hm.Data(data) as table:
    with hm.Plot(height=300, axes2d=True):
        hm.Points(x="x", y="y")
table
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Data, Plot, Points } from "hmplot";
  const data = { x: [1, 2, 3, 4], y: [3, 1, 4, 2] };
</script>

<Data value={data}>
  <Plot height={300} axes2d>
    <Points x="x" y="y" />
  </Plot>
</Data>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

- `animation_group` (`column | column[] | null`): Match animation rows by these columns within each filtered/transformed snapshot; selections keep Data.key. null restores key/position matching. Default: inherited; otherwise Data.key, then position.
- `value` (`table | transform`): The table: columns, rows, typed arrays, an Arrow table or a GeoJSON FeatureCollection (Python also takes it as the first argument); or a transform (a Filter, Group, ...: its handle in Svelte, value=node in Python), whose live output the components inside read, computed once wherever it is drawn.
- `rows` (`number`): Number of rows instead of a table: an integer from 0 to 2147483647. Generate columns with row(), random() and Calculate; pass value or rows, not both.
- `key` (`column | column[]`): The column (or columns) whose values identify a row across updates, so selections and animations follow it. Default: the row's index.
- `schema` (`Record<string, type | {type, domain, unit, timezone}>`): Column types, when inference is not enough: numeric, categorical, ordinal, boolean, datetime, duration or geometry.

### Usage

value accepts column tables, row records, and FeatureCollections. Nested Data replaces the active table. Plot and Facet data shortcuts establish the same scope. A key keeps observation identity stable through reorderings.

### A transform's output

`value` can also be a transform: its live output, read where this Data is. A pipeline computed
once can feed several plots in different places, each mark keeping its own Plot or Frame as
its visual parent. In Python pass the transform node, `hm.Data(value=totals)`, or a mark's
`data=totals`; in Svelte its handle, `bind:this={totals}` then `<Data value={totals}>`.

```python
with hm.Scene():
    with hm.Data(sales):
        with hm.Filter(where=hm.col.amount > 20):
            totals = hm.Group(by="region", columns={"orders": hm.count()})
    with hm.Row():
        with hm.Plot():
            hm.Points(data=totals, x="region", y="orders", select=True)
        with hm.Plot():
            with hm.Data(value=totals):
                hm.Points(x="region", y="orders", respond="selected")
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Data, Filter, Group, Plot, Points, count, greater } from "hmplot";
  let { sales } = $props();
  let totals = $state();
</script>

<Data value={sales}>
  <Filter where={greater("amount", 20)}>
    <Group bind:this={totals} by="region" columns={{ orders: count() }} />
  </Filter>
</Data>
{#if totals}
  <Plot data={totals}><Points x="region" y="orders" select /></Plot>
  <Plot><Data value={totals}><Points x="region" y="orders" respond="selected" /></Data></Plot>
{/if}
```

- The pipeline runs once per change of its inputs, however many plots read it, and every
  reader draws the same output; removing one reader leaves the others drawing.
- The connection is fixed: a Data reads the transform it was given for its life. Define the
  transform before its consumers. Python automatically includes a detached pipeline rooted at
  `hm.Data(table)` in each scene that reads it; a transform already parented to another Scene
  cannot be imported this way. A pipeline never reads its own output (an error names the cycle).
- Selections and other interaction state are the source table's: a click on one plot's group
  selects its rows, which every reader of the pipeline sees.
- A transform reading the view (`@time`, the pointer) takes the clock of the plots drawing it.
  Plots with their own clocks are ambiguous and reported; put them in one InputContext.
- An HTML export of the whole scene keeps the references; exporting one plot whose data is a
  pipeline outside it is refused. Put the views in an explicit `with hm.Scene() as chart:` and
  export `chart`; the same rule applies to a Row containing views of a detached chain.
- A positional `hm.Data(node)` adds the node as a child, as for any container: pass
  `value=` to read a transform's output.

### Reading the rows

`read()` on a transform's handle, or on a Data's (`bind:this` gives a `DataHandle`), gives the rows it holds now, on the host:
for a value the page shows outside a plot, such as a total in a sentence, a breadcrumb or a
list. It waits for the current inputs to run, then returns `{ length, version, columns }`:
numbers as `Float64Array` (NaN where missing), times as `Date`, categories as their values
(null where missing). `read({ columns: ["region", "orders"] })` picks and orders the columns;
`read({ rows: true })` gives one object per row instead. In Python, `await totals.read()` in a
displayed scene gives a dict of NumPy arrays (`pandas.DataFrame(await totals.read())`).

```svelte
<script>
  let totals = $state(), top = $state([]);
  // subscribe() says when the output changes; read() fetches it.
  $effect(() => totals?.subscribe(async (status) => {
    if (status.pending || status.error) return;
    const { rows } = await totals.read({ rows: true });
    top = rows.sort((a, b) => b.orders - a.orders).slice(0, 10);
  }));
</script>
```

```python
table = await totals.read(["region", "orders"])
```

- A read copies the columns from the GPU: one wait per call, and its size is bounded by
  `limit.readback` (16 MiB). Marks draw the same output without it; never read on every
  pointer move to redraw what a mark could draw.
- The rows are the visible ones, in the output's order: a Filter's kept rows, a Group's groups.
- `version` names the output it was read from; two reads with the same version hold the same
  rows. A brush or an input that changes the rows publishes a new version.
- A Group of the brushed rows (`Filter where="@brushed"` above it) reads the brushed rows'
  statistics; a selection resource's `rows()` reads which source rows are selected.

Use `rows=N` instead of `value` to generate rows without uploading a table. Pass one or the other.
`row()` (`hm.row()`) gives the zero-based position among visible rows; numeric constants and
seeded `random()` expressions provide generated values. Retain a source index or random draw
in [Calculate] before filtering or sampling when it should follow the original row.
The count is an integer from 0 to 2147483647, subject to device memory for generated arrays.

`animationGroup` (`animation_group` in Python) on Data, Plot or Frame matches animated
rows by a column or list of columns independently of Data keys. It inherits through the
tree; a child Frame overrides its branch, and explicit null (Python None) restores
Data-key/position matching. Filter to one row per group before tweening: a country/year
table can keep `key=["country", "year"]` and animate by `"country"` after filtering
to one year. Groups must be unique in each tweened snapshot, and changing the group
column scheme resets motion history. Selection, hover and connections keep Data identity.

### Related examples

- [Data shortcuts](/HMPlot/examples/data-shortcut.md)
- [Particles without an uploaded table](/HMPlot/examples/constant-data.md)
- [Ten million stars, filtered live](/HMPlot/examples/ten-million-stars.md)

## Provider

Page: /reference/python/provider.md

A table loaded asynchronously, from a URL or a load function, for the components inside it.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

## Palmer penguins, from vega-datasets on a CDN that allows any page to fetch it.
with hm.Provider(url="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/vega-datasets@2/data/penguins.json", format="json") as penguins:
    with hm.Plot(height=300, axes2d=True):
        hm.Points(x="Beak Length (mm)", y="Beak Depth (mm)")
penguins
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Plot, Points, Provider } from "hmplot";
</script>

<!-- Palmer penguins, from vega-datasets on a CDN that allows any page to fetch it. -->
<Provider url="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/vega-datasets@2/data/penguins.json" format="json">
  <Plot height={300} axes2d>
    <Points x="Beak Length (mm)" y="Beak Depth (mm)" />
  </Plot>
</Provider>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

- `url` (`string | (params) => string`): The address to fetch, instead of `source`, with {name} placeholders filled from params. In Svelte markup write it as a string expression: url={"/data/{year}.csv"}.
- `format` (`"json" | "csv" | "arrow" | "parquet"`): How the fetched file is read: JSON rows, CSV, an Arrow IPC file, or Parquet read by byte ranges. Default: `"json"`.
- `path` (`string`): For JSON, a dot path to the rows in the response, such as "data.items".
- `columns` (`column[]`): For Parquet, the columns to read; the others are never downloaded.
- `params` (`object`): The load's inputs, as plain JSON values that fill the url's placeholders; a change that makes a new request loads again.
- `key` (`column | column[]`): The column (or columns) that identify a row, as on Data, so selections follow rows across loads.
- `schema` (`Record<string, type | {type, domain, unit, timezone}>`): Column types, as on Data.
- `initial` (`table`): A table shown until the first load completes, so the components inside mount at once.
- `debounce` (`number`): How long a change of params waits for the next one before loading. Default: `150` ms.
- `refresh_interval` (`number`): Loads again this long after the last load ended; it pauses while the page is hidden. In ms.
- `accumulate` (`boolean | {maxRows}`): Merge each completed load into the table on screen instead of replacing it: with key, a re-sent row updates in place and new keys append; without, rows append in arrival order. {maxRows} keeps the newest rows. New params start a fresh table, and a url's {version} placeholder asks for rows since the result on screen. Default: `False`.
- `refresh` (`number | string`): Each change of its value loads again with the same params (a Button's count works: refresh={input("reload")}).
- `snapshot` (`boolean`): Whether exported HTML embeds the last result and never fetches; false loads when the exported page opens. Default: `True`.
- `name` (`string`): The provider's name in its status.

### Usage

A `Provider` is a `Data` scope whose table is loaded asynchronously. Give it a `source` — a `load(context)` function, or `{ load, requestKey }` — or a `url` with `{name}` placeholders (`fetchJSON` and `fetchCSV` build the same sources), and the explicit `params` the load depends on. It loads when it mounts and whenever `params` change to a new request key, after `debounce` (150 ms) so a dragged slider loads once it pauses. Downstream, a new result is an ordinary Data value change: transforms re-run, keyed updates animate, and selections follow `key`.

While a load runs, the previous result stays on screen, and a newer request aborts the one in flight (its `signal` fires; a result that still arrives is dropped). Going back to the params on screen loads nothing. A failed load keeps the previous result, shows the error and calls `onerror`. `refreshInterval` polls: ticks never overlap a load, pause while the page is hidden, and a result with an unchanged version (an ETag for the fetch helpers) publishes nothing. The children mount with the first result, or at once with `initial`.

`whenSettled()` and every export of a Plot below wait for a load already requested, but not for future refresh ticks, and not for Providers elsewhere on the page. In Python scenes, assigning `provider.params` returns at once and the plot keeps rendering while the browser loads; `when_settled()` and the exports wait for it. Exported HTML embeds the last result (`snapshot`, the default) or loads when opened (`snapshot=False`).

`bind:this` gives a `ProviderHandle`: `refresh()` loads the same params again and resolves once the result is shown (or found unchanged), `whenSettled()` waits for the loads already requested, `subscribe(listener)` reports its status as a transform's (pending while it loads, and its error), and `getResult()` returns the `ProviderResult` on screen: `data` as the load returned it, its `version`, request `key` and `revision`. `getSelection()`, `getBrush()`, `getHover()`, `getOffsets()`, `resetOffsets()` and `applyOffsets()` act on its table as a Data's do. In Python, `await provider.refresh()` loads again.

In Svelte markup, pass a URL template as a JavaScript string, `url={"/data/{year}.csv"}`: in a quoted attribute Svelte would read `{year}` as an expression. See docs/PROVIDERS.md for the lifecycle, static sites, REST APIs and exports.

### Related examples

- [Earthquakes by year, loaded on demand](/HMPlot/examples/provider-earthquakes.md)

## Table

Page: /reference/python/table.md

A table with an identity, so updates and shared views know its rows.

### Example

```python
observations = hm.Table({"x": [1, 2], "y": [3, 4]})
with hm.Plot(data=observations) as plot:
    hm.Points(x="x", y="y")
observations.update_columns(y=[4, 5])
```

```svelte
const observations = table({ id: [1, 2], x: [1, 2], y: [3, 4] }, { key: "id" });
<Plot data={observations}><Points x="x" y="y" /></Plot>
```

### Parameters

- `value` (`table`): Columns or rows (Python: a dict, a DataFrame or an xarray Dataset).
- `key` (`column | column[]`): The column whose values identify a row across updates.
- `update_columns / replace` (`methods`): Python: change some columns, or the whole table, and redraw.

### Usage

Python snapshots numeric columns when updates are queued. update_columns changes named columns; replace replaces the table. In-place array mutations are not observed. Use key for identity across reordering. GPU tensors require explicit host conversion in Python.

### Related examples

- [Data shortcuts](/HMPlot/examples/data-shortcut.md)

## gridTable

Page: /reference/svelte/grid-table.md

A table of every cell of a grid: its dimensions' coordinates and its variables.

### Example

```svelte
const field = gridTable({ dims: { lat, lon }, columns: { temperature } });
<Plot data={field}><Heatmap fill="temperature" /></Plot>
```

### Parameters

- `dims` (`object`): Each dimension's coordinates, in order.
- `columns` (`object`): The variables, one value per cell.
- `edges` (`object`): Optional cell bounds per dimension.
- `positions` (`object`): Optional curvilinear positions.

### Usage

`gridTable({ dims, columns, edges, positions })` is a table of every cell of a grid, for `Data value=` or `Plot data=`: one row per combination of its dimensions' coordinates, the first dimension outermost. The coordinates are columns made when something reads them; only the variables are stored.

Any node reads its rows as a table's: points colored by a variable, a Filter, a Group by a coordinate, a Join on one. Heatmap draws a variable over two of its dimensions, placed by their coordinates (uneven, descending and wrapped ones too, and a curvilinear grid's positions); Image takes band columns as `fill={{ r, g, b }}`; Slice through a dimension blends the two slabs around `at` on the GPU. Calculate keeps the grid for new columns, rewrites a coordinate computed from itself, and drops the grid (saying why) for anything else. See docs/DATA.md, "Grid tables".

### Related examples

- [Bilinear grid](/HMPlot/examples/transform-grid.md)

## datetimeCoordinates

Page: /reference/svelte/datetime-coordinates.md

Turn dates into millisecond offsets from an origin, for a datetime axis.

### Example

```svelte
const { values, origin } = datetimeCoordinates(dates);
<Plot data={{ time: values, value }} x={{ type: "datetime", origin }}>…</Plot>
```

### Parameters

- `values` (`Date[] | number[]`): Dates or Unix milliseconds.
- `origin` (`number`): The epoch the offsets count from (default the first).

### Usage

Returns values and origin. Subtracting an epoch origin preserves float32 precision. Use that same origin in the datetime axis definition. Python can subtract the origin before supplying numerical columns.

### Related examples

- [Long time series](/HMPlot/examples/timeseries.md)

## DictionaryColumn

Page: /reference/python/dictionary-column.md

A category column as integer codes and the categories they stand for.

### Example

```python
hm.Points(x="x", y="y", fill={"codes": [0, 1, 0], "categories": ["A", "B"]})
```

```svelte
<Points x="x" y="y" fill={{ codes: [0, 1, 0], categories: ["A", "B"] }} />
```

### Members

- `codes` (`any`): Required.
- `categories` (`CategoryValue[]`): Required.

### Usage

A dictionary column is a category column already encoded: `codes`, one integer per row, index `categories`, the distinct values in their order. Pass one wherever a column goes (a table's column, or a mark channel directly) when the data comes encoded, or when the codes are computed on the GPU: a jax-js array of codes stays on the GPU, and no step reads it back to find the categories, since they are given. Strings and pandas categoricals are encoded this way for you; Python sends every string column as codes and categories.

The category order is the order of `categories`: it orders a band axis, a legend and the default palette's colors, so `["Low", "Medium", "High"]` keeps that order however the rows are sorted. A code of -1 is a missing category. In JavaScript a code that is out of range, fractional or not finite is unknown too; Python refuses such codes, and codes that are not one-dimensional. Categories must be unique strings, numbers or booleans, and Python refuses integer categories past 2^53 (use strings).

To give a column a category order without encoding it yourself, use a schema's `domain` or [typedColumn](typed-column); to fix colors per category, a [categorical](categorical) scale. [Named data & categories](/HMPlot/examples/categories.md) colors marks by dictionary columns.

### Related examples

- [Named data & categories](/HMPlot/examples/categories.md)

## typed_column

Page: /reference/python/typed-column.md

One column with a logical type (ordinal, datetime, duration, ...), where a schema would type it.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

size = hm.typed_column(["M", "S", "L", "M"], type="ordinal", domain=["S", "M", "L"])
with hm.Plot(data={"price": [4, 2, 7, 5], "size": size}, axes2d=True) as plot:
    hm.Points(x="size", y="price")
plot
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Plot, Points, typedColumn } from "hmplot";
  const size = typedColumn(["M", "S", "L", "M"], { type: "ordinal", domain: ["S", "M", "L"] });
</script>

<Plot data={{ price: [4, 2, 7, 5], size }} axes2d>
  <Points x="size" y="price" />
</Plot>
```

### Parameters

- `value` (`array`): The column's values: numbers, text, Dates, BigInts or a typed array (Python: a list, NumPy array or pandas Series).
- `type` (`"numeric" | "categorical" | "ordinal" | "boolean" | "datetime" | "duration"`): The logical type; required.
- `domain` (`category[]`): Categorical and ordinal: the categories, unique, in order.
- `unit` (`"ns" | "us" | "ms" | "s" | "m" | "h" | "d"`): Datetime and duration: the unit of numeric values (default ms).
- `timezone` (`string`): Datetime only: the zone the times are shown and computed in (an IANA name, "UTC" or "Local").
- `returns` (`typed column`): A frozen column that a table, a Data value or a mark channel takes like any other; Python: an hm Column.

### Usage

A schema types a table's columns for its whole scope (a Data's or a Table's `schema`); `typedColumn` types one column where you make it, for data that has no schema of its own: a list of size labels that sort S, M, L, numbers that are times in seconds, codes that are categories. The type travels with the column to the axis, scale, legend and tooltip that show it, as a schema's would: an ordinal column gets a band axis in its domain's order, a datetime one a time axis.

A categorical or ordinal `domain` fixes the categories and their order; values outside it are missing. A datetime column takes Dates, ISO 8601 text, BigInts or numbers in `unit`, and is shown in `timezone`. Python's `hm.typed_column` also takes NumPy datetime64 and timedelta64 arrays and pandas Series, which carry their own unit. A [cast](casts) types one use of a value inside an expression instead.

See docs/DATA.md, "Logical column types".

### Related examples

- [Categorical and datetime frames](/HMPlot/examples/typed-axes.md)

## Fetch sources

Page: /reference/svelte/fetch-sources.md

fetchJSON, fetchCSV, fetchArrow and fetchParquet: a Provider's source that fetches a URL template.

### Example

```svelte
<script>
  import { Provider, Plot, Points, fetchCSV } from "hmplot";
  // init: fetch's options. A source with init shares its loads with no other source.
  const quakes = fetchCSV("/data/earthquakes/by-year/{year}.csv", { init: { headers: { Accept: "text/csv" } } });
</script>

<Provider source={quakes} params={{ year: 2024 }}>
  <Plot axes2d><Points x="lon" y="lat" /></Plot>
</Provider>
```

### Functions

- `fetchJSON(url, {path, init})` (`ProviderSource`): Fetches JSON: rows, columns or a GeoJSON FeatureCollection; path is a dot path to the rows in the response ("results", "data.items").
- `fetchCSV(url, {init})` (`ProviderSource`): Fetches CSV: a column whose non-empty cells all read as numbers is numeric (unless the Provider's schema says categorical, ordinal or boolean), the others text; an empty cell is missing.
- `fetchArrow(url, {init})` (`ProviderSource`): Fetches an Arrow IPC file or stream as an Arrow Table, whose columns keep their types (apache-arrow, loaded on first use).
- `fetchParquet(url, {columns, init})` (`ProviderSource`): Reads a Parquet file with HTTP range requests: the footer, then only the pages of columns when given (hyparquet, loaded on first use). The server must answer range requests.

### Usage

Each function returns a `source` for a [Provider](provider): an object with an id, a request key and a `load(context)` that fetches the URL with the Provider's `params` filled in and returns what Data reads. A Provider's `url`, `format`, `path` and `columns` props build the same sources, and Python's `hm.Provider(url=..., format=...)` is the only form Python has. Call a helper yourself to pass fetch options, or to share one source object between Providers.

The `url` is a template with `{name}` placeholders, filled from the Provider's `params` (URL-encoded), or a function of the params that returns the URL; the filled URL is the request key, so a param the URL does not use reloads nothing. `init` is fetch's options: headers, credentials, a method and a body. The Provider's own signal aborts the request when a newer one supersedes it.

A response that is not OK is an error naming the status and URL (`HTTP 404 Not Found: /data/2031.csv`). The helpers keep a response's ETag (or Last-Modified) as its version and send `If-None-Match` (or `If-Modified-Since`) when they refresh the result on screen, so an unchanged file publishes nothing; a Parquet source has no version and reads the file again. Two Providers share one load in flight when their sources are equal: the same URL template, format, path and columns, and no `init`. A source with `init` shares only with itself, since its headers can change the response and are never compared or written into a request key.

`fetchArrow` and `fetchParquet` load apache-arrow and hyparquet the first time they run, so a page that never reads those formats does not carry them. See docs/PROVIDERS.md for the load lifecycle, and docs/DATA.md, "Arrow and Parquet", for how their column types arrive.

### Related examples

- [Earthquakes by year, loaded on demand](/HMPlot/examples/provider-earthquakes.md)
- [Earthquakes from a Parquet file](/HMPlot/examples/parquet-earthquakes.md)

## GeoJSON

Page: /reference/python/geojson.md

Maps of GeoJSON regions, lines and points, colored by their properties (choropleths) and optionally extruded.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

def polygon(value, ring):
    return {
        "type": "Feature",
        "properties": {"value": value},
        "geometry": {"type": "Polygon", "coordinates": [ring]},
    }

regions = {
    "type": "FeatureCollection",
    "features": [
        polygon(1, [[-120, 20], [-70, 20], [-70, 55], [-120, 55], [-120, 20]]),
        polygon(2, [[-10, 35], [40, 35], [40, 65], [-10, 65], [-10, 35]]),
        polygon(3, [[110, -40], [155, -40], [130, -10], [110, -40]]),
    ],
}
with hm.Plot(coordinates="spherical", projection="mercator", height=300) as plot:
    hm.GeoJSON(data=regions, fill="value")
plot
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Plot, GeoJSON } from "hmplot";
  const polygon = (value, ring) => ({
    type: "Feature",
    properties: { value },
    geometry: { type: "Polygon", coordinates: [ring] },
  });
  const regions = {
    type: "FeatureCollection",
    features: [
      polygon(1, [[-120, 20], [-70, 20], [-70, 55], [-120, 55], [-120, 20]]),
      polygon(2, [[-10, 35], [40, 35], [40, 65], [-10, 65], [-10, 35]]),
      polygon(3, [[110, -40], [155, -40], [130, -10], [110, -40]]),
    ],
  };
</script>

<Plot coordinates="spherical" projection="mercator" height={300}>
  <GeoJSON data={regions} fill="value" />
</Plot>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

#### Options

- `data` (`object`): The shapes: a GeoJSON Geometry, Feature or FeatureCollection, in longitude and latitude on a map. Feature properties are columns for the channels.
- `geometry` (`column`): A geometry column of the enclosing data, instead of data: a FeatureCollection given as a Plot's or Data's table has one named "geometry".
- `feature_key` (`string`): The feature property that joins each feature to a row of the enclosing table, matched against data_key; "$id" uses feature.id.
- `data_key` (`column`): The column of the enclosing table matched against feature_key; each key may appear once.
- `height` (`channel`): Each feature's extrusion: a number, or a property or column mapped through height_scale. Only polygons extrude, in 3D views. Default: `0`.
- `height_scale` (`scale`): A continuous() scale from heights to extrusions: its domain (by default [0, 1]) maps onto its range (by default [0, 1], nonnegative and increasing); heights outside the domain clamp. The map is linear: a transform, a midpoint or a "symmetric" domain is an error.
- `plane` (`"xy" | "xz"`): In a Cartesian 3D plot, "xz" lays the features on the horizontal ground plane and extrudes them upward. Default: `"xy"`.
- `fit` (`boolean`): On a 2D map, zoom to the features (a city's districts fill the plot, not a speck in a world map); a Plot's own viewport wins. False keeps the whole map. Default: `True`.

#### Appearance

- `fill` (`channel`): The fill of regions and points: a CSS color, or a property or column mapped to colors. null (Python None) draws only lines and polygon boundaries, using color and width. Default: `"#718b9b"`.
- `color` (`channel`): The color of LineString features and, with fill=null, polygon boundaries: a CSS color, or a property or column mapped to colors. Default: the fill.
- `size` (`channel`): The size of Point features: a number, or a property or column mapped to sizes. Default: `8` px.
- `width` (`channel`): The width of LineString features and, with fill=null, polygon boundaries: a number, or a property or column mapped to widths. Default: `1` px.
- `outline_color` (`channel`): The color of region and point outlines. Default: `"#f4f2ed"`.
- `outline_width` (`channel`): The width of region and point outlines; 0 draws none. Default: `0.7` px.

Also these options the marks share (described on Mark options): `opacity`, `outline_opacity`.

#### Scales

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `fill_scale`, `color_scale`, `colormap`, `size_scale`, `width_scale`, `outline_color_scale`, `opacity_scale`.

#### Display

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `label`, `legend`, `visible`, `blend`, `glow`, `shade`, `options`, `name`.

#### Interaction

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `hover`, `tooltip`, `respond`, `selection_opacity`.

#### Animation

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `animation`, `animation_duration`, `animation_easing`.

#### Legend settings

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `legend_font_size`, `legend_font_family`, `legend_text_color`, `legend_tick_format`.

#### Color settings

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `quantize`, `levels`.

#### Limits

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `max_elements`.

#### The mark's own axes

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `x_transform`, `x_invert`, `xbounds`, `xrange`, `y_transform`, `y_invert`, `ybounds`, `yrange`, `z_transform`, `z_invert`, `zbounds`, `zrange`.

#### Shading

- `lit` (`boolean`, setting): Shade the mark with the plot's lights. Default: `False`.
- `transparent` (`boolean`, setting): Draw the mark in the transparent pass, blended in depth order with other transparent marks. Default: `False`.

#### Map settings

- `missing_color` (`color`, setting): The color of the features the data has no value for: no joined row, or a missing (NaN) value. Default: the fill scale's missing, else the theme's (#92989f in the default theme).

### Usage

Accept data as Geometry/Feature/FeatureCollection, or geometry from a Data scope. Feature properties are fields; featureKey/dataKey joins measurements. A numeric `fill` maps through `fillScale` (by default over the values' extent, as on other marks) or the `colormap`; a numeric line `color` through `colorScale`. Height is per feature, mapped through `heightScale`, a `continuous()` scale from its domain (by default [0, 1]) onto its range (by default [0, 1]), clamped at its ends; polygons alone extrude. Longitude/latitude are degrees even when the plot uses other angular units.

Set `fill={null}` (Python `fill=None`) to draw only LineStrings and polygon boundaries,
without filling or triangulating polygons. This replaces GeoJSONLine. `color` and `width`
style all those strokes, including property columns and `colorScale`; the default stroke is
`#425669`, one pixel wide. Feature joins and picking work as for filled regions. Changing
`fill` switches between filled regions and boundaries on the same component.

Set `tooltip` to true or a list of feature-property/joined-column names, as on other marks;
the Plot's tooltip is the default. `hover` marks the whole feature, including every polygon
part, boundary and point. Add `respond="hovered"` to fade other features, with
`selectionOpacity` (Python `selection_opacity`) setting their opacity. Joins and geometry
columns share their enclosing table's row identity, so hover coordinates with other marks;
unmatched features do not mark a table row. Raw GeoJSON owns feature rows of its own.
Brush and drag are not GeoJSON producers.

A `GeoJSONHandle` has `getLegendSource()`, `whenSettled()` (once its geometry is prepared and drawn) and `getDiagnostics()` (features, instances and geometry bytes).

> **SVG and PDF export**
>
> **Partly an image.** SVG and PDF exports draw the filled polygons as an image at the export's raster DPI, and `mode="vector"` refuses them. The boundaries are vector paths in a 2D view, colored by a column too; on a 3D globe they are part of the image. See [what is not exported as vector](/HMPlot/docs/export.md).

### Related examples

- [Globe extrusions](/HMPlot/examples/geojson-globe.md)
- [Earthquakes beneath the globe](/HMPlot/examples/earthquakes.md)

## VectorTile

Page: /reference/python/vector-tile.md

A basemap of land, water, roads, buildings and place names from vector map tiles.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

with hm.Plot(coordinates="spherical", projection="mercator", tone_mapping=0, height=300) as plot:
    hm.VectorTile(tile=[14, 9014, 4818], live=False)
plot
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Plot, VectorTile } from "hmplot";
</script>

<Plot coordinates="spherical" projection="mercator" toneMapping={0} height={300}>
  <VectorTile tile={[14, 9014, 4818]} live={false} />
</Plot>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

- `url` (`string | ({z, x, y}) => string`): Where tiles load from: a URL template with {z}, {x} and {y}, or in JavaScript a function of {z, x, y}. In Svelte markup pass the template as a JavaScript string: url={"https://.../{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf"}. Default: VersaTiles' OpenStreetMap tiles, which need no key and are credited on the plot.
- `tile` (`[number, number, number]`): One tile to load, [z, x, y]: its zoom, its column from the west and its row from the north.
- `tiles` (`[number, number, number][]`): Several tiles to load (at most 16), each clipped to its own square.
- `bounds` (`[number, number, number, number]`): A box [west, south, east, north]: load every tile it touches at zoom (at most 16). In degrees.
- `zoom` (`number`): The zoom at which bounds picks its tiles.
- `data` (`object`): Already decoded tiles to draw instead of loading any: a GeoJSON FeatureCollection whose features name their source layer in properties.layerName.
- `styles` (`object`): Per part (water, roads, buildings, places, ...): false hides it, or {fill, color, width, size, opacity, outline_color, outline_width} changes its look over the scheme.
- `scheme` (`string | object`): The basemap's colors: a theme preset's name ("dark", "sea", ...), "default", or part styles as for styles. Default: the enclosing Theme's basemap colors (derived from its colors when it has none), else "default".
- `source_layers` (`object`): Assign a tileset's source layers to parts, {layer: part}, or hide one with false, before the built-in rules.
- `clip` (`boolean`): End each tile's geometry at the tile's edge (tiles overlap by a buffer). Default: `True`.
