- `fit` (`boolean`): Frame the tiles when they change, in a 2D map. Default: `True`.
- `origin` (`[number, number]`): Draw in a local plane instead of longitude and latitude: meters east and north of this [longitude, latitude], times units_per_meter. For Cartesian and 3D plots. In degrees.
- `units_per_meter` (`number`): The plot units per meter in the local plane that origin sets. Default: `1`.
- `plane` (`"xy" | "xz"`): In a Cartesian 3D plot, "xz" lays the tiles on the horizontal ground plane. Default: `"xy"`.
- `snapshot` (`boolean`): In an HTML export of a scene, embed the tiles on screen as tile_data; false exports only the url, so the page loads its tiles when it opens. Default: `True`.
- `live` (`boolean`): In a 2D view (a Cartesian plot, or a map in any projection, the globe included), and under a 3D flyover camera (with origin and plane="xz"), also load the tiles the camera shows as it moves. Needs opaque styles; not inside nested Frames. Default: `True`.
- `min_zoom` (`number`): The coarsest zoom live tiles load. Default: `0`.
- `max_zoom` (`number`): The finest zoom live tiles load; zoomed in further, those tiles stretch. Default: `14`.
- `zoom_bias` (`number`): Live tile detail offset in zoom levels, between -4 and 4: +1 doubles linear detail at the same view scale or camera height; -1 uses coarser tiles. Zoom limits and the tile budget still apply. Default: `0`.
- `attribution` (`string | false`): A credit line in the plot's lower-left corner, kept in every export (most tile licenses require one); false hides it. Default: the default tiles' credit when there is no url, else none.
- `tile_data` (`object[]`): Embedded tiles instead of loading them: [{tile: [z, x, y], bytes}], bytes as base64 text or a Uint8Array (null for an empty tile). Exported pages carry their tiles this way.
- `extrude_buildings` (`boolean`): Under a 3D flyover camera, stand the tiles' buildings up from their height tags (5 meters when missing) with flat roofs; false draws flat footprints. 2D maps are always flat. Default: `True`.
- `name` (`string`): The name of its group of parts in the settings pane.
- `visible` (`boolean`): Show or hide every part.
- `opacity` (`number`): A multiplier on every part's opacity; live tiles need 1.

### Usage

`VectorTile` loads Mapbox Vector Tiles that you name by their coordinates, `tile={[z, x, y]}`, a list of `tiles`, or a longitude/latitude `bounds` box at a `zoom`, from a `url` template with `{z}`, `{x}` and `{y}`. It decodes them and draws them as a basemap: land and parks, water, buildings, roads, railways, boundaries and place names, each a part with its own style. Put it in a 2D map (`coordinates="spherical" projection="mercator"`); the map frames the tiles, and other marks overlay them in longitude and latitude.

In a 2D view (a Cartesian plot, or a map in any projection, the globe included) the basemap is live by default: as the camera moves, the tiles it shows load at the nearest zoom, over the requested tiles, which stay where live tiles fail. Roads, landuse and place names show by zoom and kind, as VersaTiles' own style shows them, and names that would overlap are left out. Live tiles need opaque styles; `minZoom` and `maxZoom` bound their zoom. Inside nested Frames, in 3D views other than the flyover below, and with `live={false}`, the requested tiles load once and pan and zoom move over them.

Under a 3D flyover camera (`type="3d" cameraMode="flyover"`, the tiles in a local plane with `origin`, `unitsPerMeter` and `plane="xz"`, and linear axes) the basemap lies flat on the ground and is live too: the tiles of a square of about four camera heights around the camera load, at a zoom from the camera's height, and the overview and the plot's `fog` cover the distance a low camera sees past them. The buildings of the tiles that have them stand up (`extrudeBuildings`, default true; "3D buildings" in the settings pane): `height` meters tall above `min_height` as VersaTiles' zoom-14 tiles tag them, 5 meters without a height, flat roofs, the buildings' fill shaded. `extrudeBuildings={false}` draws flat footprints, and `styles={{ buildings: false }}` hides both. With `live={false}` the requested tiles draw the same way and nothing else loads. 2D maps are always flat. See docs/VECTOR-TILES.md, "Live tiles under a 3D flyover". A new tile list loads at once, supersedes a load in flight, and replaces the tiles on screen when it arrives. `attribution` puts a credit line in the plot's lower-left corner, kept in every export. The default tiles' credit is short (OpenStreetMap and ESA WorldCover); ESA's full form, "© ESA WorldCover project 2021 / Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data (2021) processed by ESA WorldCover consortium", belongs in a publication's credits or a page's footer (THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md lists every source's terms). `styles` hides or restyles parts without a reload; `sourceLayers` assigns a custom tileset's layers to parts. In Svelte markup, pass the URL template as a JavaScript string, `url={"https://.../{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf"}`. `bind:this` gives a `VectorTileHandle`: `whenSettled()` resolves once the requested loads are drawn (or failed), `getResult()` returns the tiles on screen and their decoded features (outside live mode), `getTileData()` the tiles' bytes as `tileData` carries them, `getParts()` each part's GeoJSON mark, and `getStatus()` the load state, with the live zoom and tile counts. See docs/VECTOR-TILES.md.

`zoomBias` adjusts live detail at the same view scale or flyover height: `+1` asks for
twice the linear detail, `-1` for coarser tiles, and `0` keeps automatic selection. Pass a
finite number between -4 and 4. `minZoom`, `maxZoom` and the live tile budget still apply,
so increasing detail cannot load unlimited tiles. The settings pane calls this **Tile detail**.
Python uses `zoom_bias`.

> **SVG and PDF export**
>
> **Partly an image.** SVG and PDF exports draw the filled areas (land, water, parks, buildings) as an image at the export's raster DPI, and `mode="vector"` refuses them. Place names stay text. Roads, paths, railways and boundaries are vector paths in a static basemap (`live` off) and part of the image in a live one, the default in a 2D view. In a 3D plot, a flyover's basemap and extruded buildings included, the whole basemap is part of the plot's image. See [what is not exported as vector](/HMPlot/docs/export.md).

### HTML that opens offline and stays live online

Keep `snapshot` enabled (the default) on VectorTile. `live=true` controls fetching new tiles
while navigating; it does not disable embedding. Python's `hm.export_html` normally draws
in headless Chrome and embeds the requested tiles and currently visible live tiles as
`tileData`, while keeping `url` and `live` for online navigation:

```python
with hm.Plot(coordinates="spherical", projection="mercator") as chart:
    hm.VectorTile(tile=[14, 8157, 6111], live=True)  # snapshot=True by default
hm.export_html(chart, "chart.html")
```

The export browser must be able to load the initial tiles. If it cannot reach the service,
provide local MVT bytes with `tile_data=[{"tile": [z, x, y], "bytes": tile_bytes}]` (JavaScript:
`tileData`). Include the requested tiles and any surrounding area needed offline. The
embedded area remains visible offline; navigating beyond it needs the tile service.

`VectorTile(snapshot=False)` deliberately leaves externally loaded tile bytes out of the
page. It requires network access when opened. The separate `hm.export_html(..., snapshot=False)`
skips the headless snapshot/export pass, so externally loaded tiles cannot be captured then
either. Neither option is suitable for making a network-sourced basemap self-contained.
A tile-fetch failure during export means there are no downloaded bytes to embed: keep the
offline requirement, supply local tile bytes or restore service access, and export again.

### Related examples

- [Vector tiles that follow the view](/HMPlot/examples/vector-tiles.md)

## Force

Page: /reference/python/force.md

A force-directed layout of a graph's nodes and edges, simulated live.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"source": ["A", "A", "B", "C", "D"], "target": ["B", "C", "C", "D", "E"]}
with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300) as plot:
    with hm.GraphData(source="source", target="target"):
        with hm.Force(warmup=300):
            with hm.Edges():
                hm.Segments(start="start", end="end")
            with hm.Nodes():
                hm.Points(position="position")
plot
```

```svelte
<script>
  import {
    Plot,
    Force,
    Edges,
    Nodes,
    Segments,
    Points,
    GraphData,
  } from "hmplot";
  const data = {
    source: ["A", "A", "B", "C", "D"],
    target: ["B", "C", "C", "D", "E"],
  };
</script>

<Plot {data} height={300}>
  <GraphData source="source" target="target"
    ><Force warmup={300}>
      <Edges><Segments start="start" end="end" /></Edges>
      <Nodes><Points position="position" /></Nodes>
    </Force></GraphData
  >
</Plot>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

- `name` (`string`): Names the layout, so a Facet's settings and getTransform(name) reach it in every cell.
- `weight` (`column`): An edge column of nonnegative weights, each multiplying its link's spring strength.
- `dimensions` (`2 | 3`): Lays the graph out in two or three dimensions. Default: `2`.
- `seed` (`number`): Seeds the random starting positions, so the same graph lays out the same way. Default: `42`.
- `repulsion` (`number`): How strongly nodes push one another apart. Default: `30`.
- `link_distance` (`number`): The length each link's spring pulls toward. Default: `30` data units.
- `spring_strength` (`number`): How strongly each link pulls its ends toward link_distance. Default: `0.1`.
- `centering` (`number`): How strongly each node is pulled toward the origin. Default: `0.01`.
- `velocity_decay` (`number`): The fraction of each node's velocity lost per tick, like friction. Default: `0.4`.
- `alpha` (`number`): The simulation's heat, which scales every force and cools each tick; it starts at 1, so bind it to read it rather than set it. Default: `1`.
- `alpha_min` (`number`): The layout stops once alpha cools below this. Default: `0.001`.
- `alpha_decay` (`number`): The fraction of the way alpha moves toward alpha_target each tick. Default: 1 - 0.001^(1/300), about 0.0228 (d3's: 300 ticks to cool).
- `alpha_target` (`number`): The alpha the layout cools toward; above alpha_min it keeps running. Default: `0`.
- `forces` (`object`): Named forces, as d3's (center, manyBody, link, collide, x, y, z, radial). An entry named like a default force updates it, one with a type replaces it, and null removes it. Default: charge, link, and x and y (z in 3D), from the options above.
- `fixed` (`{x, y, z}`): Holds nodes at coordinates from nodes-table columns, expressions or numbers (d3's fx, fy, fz); a non-finite value leaves that node free.
- `initial` (`{x, y, z}`): Starting coordinates from nodes-table columns, expressions or numbers; a non-finite value keeps that node's seeded start.
- `ticks` (`number`): Simulation ticks per drawn step. Default: `1`.
- `warmup` (`number`): Ticks run before the layout is first drawn, so it appears already settled. Default: `0`.
- `running` (`boolean`): Plays (true) or pauses (false) the layout, which otherwise starts paused; a Checkbox's input can drive it.
- `reset` (`number | string`): Each change of its value restarts the layout from its starting positions; a Button's input can drive it.
- `reheat` (`number | string`): Each change of its value reheats the layout (alpha back to 1), so it moves again.
- `step` (`number | string`): Each change of its value pauses the layout and advances it one step.
- `release` (`number | string`): Each change of its value frees every pinned node.

### Usage

Provides Nodes and Edges scopes. Initializes paused. `running` plays and pauses it, and each change of `step`, `reset`, `reheat` or `release` runs that action once, so a [Checkbox](checkbox) and [Buttons](button) can drive it: `running={input("run")}`, `reset={input("reset")}`. The handle's action(id) does the same from code. Defaults include seed 42, link distance 30, repulsion 30, and velocity decay 0.4. Supports 2D/3D and node dragging; topology changes reset the layout.

Requires graph data from GraphData. Outputs are visible to children only. Transforms retain the previous complete result while an update prepares. To let the viewer change a setting, read an input in it: `repulsion={input("repulsion")}` (Python `repulsion=hm.input.repulsion`), where `repulsion` is a [Slider](slider).

### Related examples

- [Force layout · 2D](/HMPlot/examples/transform-force.md)
- [Layered forces](/HMPlot/examples/transform-forces.md)

## GraphData

Page: /reference/python/graph-data.md

A graph from edges, with nodes given or inferred from the edges' endpoints; ordinary transforms operate on the selected table.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

edges = {"source": ["A", "A", "B", "C"], "target": ["B", "C", "D", "D"]}
nodes = {"id": ["A", "B", "C", "D"], "column": [0, 1, 1, 2], "lane": [1, 0, 2, 1]}
with hm.GraphData(nodes=nodes, edges=edges) as plot:
    with hm.Nodes():
        with hm.Calculate(x=hm.multiply("column", 2), y="lane"):
            with hm.Plot(height=300):
                with hm.Edges():
                    hm.Segments(start="start", end="end")
                with hm.Nodes():
                    hm.Points(position="position")
plot
```

```svelte
<script>
  import {
    Plot,
    GraphData,
    Edges,
    Nodes,
    Segments,
    Points,
    Calculate,
    multiply,
  } from "hmplot";
  const edges = { source: ["A", "A", "B", "C"], target: ["B", "C", "D", "D"] };
  const nodes = {
    id: ["A", "B", "C", "D"],
    column: [0, 1, 1, 2],
    lane: [1, 0, 2, 1],
  };
</script>

<GraphData {nodes} {edges}>
  <Nodes>
    <Calculate columns={{ x: multiply("column", 2), y: "lane" }}>
      <Plot height={300}>
        <Edges><Segments start="start" end="end" /></Edges>
        <Nodes><Points position="position" /></Nodes>
      </Plot>
    </Calculate>
  </Nodes>
</GraphData>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

- `nodes` (`table`): One row per node with unique IDs, including isolated nodes. Requires edges. Default: inferred from the edges' endpoints.
- `edges` (`table`): Edge rows whose source and target values identify nodes. Default: the surrounding data.
- `node_key` (`column`): The node ID column of nodes, exposed as the canonical id alias. Default: `"id"`.
- `source` (`column`): The edge source ID column. Default: `"source"`.
- `target` (`column`): The edge target ID column. Default: `"target"`.
- `node_from` (`"source" | "target"`): Which endpoint receives each edge row's reduce results. Default: `"source"`.
- `reduce` (`object`): Node columns aggregated from the edge rows, mapped to {field, op}; nodes no edge reaches receive each reducer's empty result. Default: {}.

### Usage

GraphData builds the graph that layouts (Tree, DAG, Force, Pack, Treemap, Sankey) and the Nodes and Edges scopes read. It takes its tables in one of three ways:

- `nodes` and `edges`: an explicit node table and an edge table. `nodeKey` names the unique node ID column.
- `edges` alone: the nodes are inferred from the edges' endpoints, one per distinct ID, in the order the IDs first appear (each edge's source, then its target). Their ID column is `id`.
- Neither: the surrounding data (a Plot's `data`, a Data or a transform above) are the edges, and the nodes are inferred as above. Rows hidden above (a Filter) contribute no nodes.

`source` and `target` name the edge endpoint columns (default `source` and `target`). The default scope is the edges. Use Nodes or Edges to select a relation, then apply ordinary table transforms and marks. Isolated nodes (explicit node tables only), cycles, self-loops and parallel edges are supported; individual layouts may impose stricter requirements.

`reduce` adds node columns aggregated from the edge rows: it maps each output name to a reducer, `{op, field}` (`op` one of count, sum, mean, min, max, first, last, variance, std, any, all). `nodeFrom="source"` (the default) groups edge rows by source ID; `"target"` groups by target ID. A reduced column replaces a same-named node attribute; nodes without matching rows receive the reducer's empty value. Changes to numerical attributes reuse the endpoint grouping plan; endpoint identity changes rebuild it.

The graph relationship is a capability of the data, like a grid descriptor. Marks and ordinary transforms see a table. Filtering nodes induces the remaining edges; changes in one branch do not affect sibling branches. Transforms that discard identity produce ordinary tables and cannot subsequently feed a graph layout.

An existing table retains its own observation key and interaction resources. `nodeKey` maps graph endpoints independently; it does not rekey a shared table. In Python, marks and containers under Nodes expose the supplied node Table's selection, brush and hover resources, while Edges and the default graph scope expose the edge Table's (or, without `edges`, the surrounding data's). Inferred nodes are computed in the browser and have no Python host Table: pass `nodes` when Python needs their selection. Browser interactions still work on them.

GraphData does not position nodes. Provide a two- or three-dimensional `position` column, or `x`/`y` and optional `z`. Calculate can create these inside Nodes. Edge `start`/`end` columns gather current node coordinates lazily when consumed, including after node transforms. Layouts accept this graph directly and publish their own geometry.

### Migration

FromEdges is part of GraphData: replace `FromEdges` with `GraphData`, keeping its `source`, `target`, `nodeFrom` and `reduce`. A FromEdges under a GraphData that enriched its nodes becomes that GraphData's `reduce` and `nodeFrom`.

Replace the old Graph with GraphData and ordinary node coordinate columns. Move `nodes`, `nodeKey`, `source` and `target` from Force, Tree, DAG, Pack, Treemap or Sankey to GraphData.

### Related examples

- [Positioned graph](/HMPlot/examples/positioned-graph.md)
- [Rooted tree](/HMPlot/examples/rooted-tree.md)

## DAG

Page: /reference/python/dag.md

A layered layout of a directed acyclic graph, with edges routed around the nodes.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"source": ["a", "a", "b", "c", "a"], "target": ["b", "c", "d", "d", "d"]}
with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300) as plot:
    with hm.GraphData(source="source", target="target"):
        with hm.DAG():
            with hm.Edges():
                hm.Routes()
            with hm.Nodes():
                hm.Points(position="position")
plot
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Plot, DAG, Edges, Nodes, Routes, Points, GraphData } from "hmplot";
  const data = {
    source: ["a", "a", "b", "c", "a"],
    target: ["b", "c", "d", "d", "d"],
  };
</script>

<Plot {data} height={300}>
  <GraphData source="source" target="target"
    ><DAG>
      <Edges><Routes /></Edges>
      <Nodes><Points position="position" /></Nodes>
    </DAG></GraphData
  >
</Plot>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

- `orientation` (`"left" | "right" | "down" | "up"`): The direction the layers run, from sources to sinks. Default: `"down"`.
- `node_width` (`number | column | expression`): Each node's width, which the layout keeps clear: a number, or a nodes-table column or expression. Default: `1` data units.
- `node_height` (`number | column | expression`): Each node's height, which the layout keeps clear: a number, or a nodes-table column or expression. Default: `1` data units.
- `node_gap` (`number`): The space between neighboring nodes in a layer. Default: `1` data units.
- `layer_gap` (`number`): The space between layers. Default: `1` data units.

### Usage

DAG consumes GraphData and uses d3-dag's Sugiyama layout to place an acyclic directed graph. It exposes node positions and bounds, edge endpoints, and complete routed paths. `Routes` draws the paths; ordinary edge marks can use `start` and `end`. The layout runs when input changes.

### Related examples

- [Layered DAG](/HMPlot/examples/layered-dag.md)

## Pack

Page: /reference/python/pack.md

A hierarchy drawn as nested circles, each leaf's area set by its value.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"source": ["root", "root", "a", "a", "a", "b", "b"],
        "target": ["a", "b", "a1", "a2", "a3", "b1", "b2"]}
with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, aspect="equal") as plot:
    with hm.GraphData(source="source", target="target"):
        with hm.Pack(root="root"):
            with hm.Nodes():
                hm.Points(position="position", size=hm.col.r * 2, size_units="data", fill="depth")
plot
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Plot, Pack, Nodes, Points, multiply, GraphData } from "hmplot";
  const data = {
    source: ["root", "root", "a", "a", "a", "b", "b"],
    target: ["a", "b", "a1", "a2", "a3", "b1", "b2"],
  };
</script>

<Plot {data} height={300} aspect="equal">
  <GraphData source="source" target="target"
    ><Pack root="root">
      <Nodes
        ><Points
          position="position"
          size={multiply("r", 2)}
          sizeUnits="data"
          fill="depth"
        /></Nodes
      >
    </Pack></GraphData
  >
</Plot>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

- `root` (`string | number | boolean`): The ID of the node whose subtree the layout divides: the hierarchy's root, or any node below it (a drill-down), or an input a Select or a click sets. Nodes outside its subtree stay rows of the nodes table, hidden; depth counts from it (0).
- `levels` (`number`): How many levels below root to show (1: its children only); root itself is then left out, as its area is the whole layout. Default: every level.
- `value` (`column | expression`): Each leaf's nonnegative weight, which sets its circle's area: a nodes-table column or an expression over it. A parent holds the sum of its leaves. Default: `1`.
- `width` (`number`): The width of the area the circles fill. Default: `1` data units.
- `height` (`number`): The height of the area the circles fill. Default: `1` data units.
- `padding` (`number`): The gap between circles. Default: `0` data units.

### Usage

`Pack` uses d3-hierarchy to place one connected, directed hierarchy in nested circles. Supply the edges (and nodes, or let it infer them) and endpoint mapping through GraphData; set `root` on Pack. `value` evaluates on node columns; leaf values determine area and default to 1. `width` and `height` default to 1, and `padding` separates circles.

Inside `<Nodes>`, use `x`, `y`, `position`, and `r` to draw circles: Points with `size={multiply("r", 2)}` and `sizeUnits="data"` in a Plot with `aspect="equal"`, so a data unit is as long on y as on x and each circle stays round and inside its parent (the automatic domain holds every whole circle). `x0`, `x1`, `y0`, and `y1` enclose each circle. `parent`, `depth`, `degree`, and node attributes are also available. `<Edges>` retains source rows and exposes center-to-center `start` and `end`.

`root` may be any node, and `levels` shows that many levels below it, as on [Treemap](treemap): a drill-down. Each node's `total` is its summed value.

### Related examples

- [Circle packing](/HMPlot/examples/packed-hierarchy.md)

## Treemap

Page: /reference/python/treemap.md

A hierarchy drawn as nested rectangles, each leaf's area set by its value.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"source": ["root", "root", "a", "a", "a", "b", "b"],
        "target": ["a", "b", "a1", "a2", "a3", "b1", "b2"]}
with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300) as plot:
    with hm.GraphData(source="source", target="target"):
        with hm.Treemap(root="root", padding=0.02):
            with hm.Nodes():
                hm.Rect(x0="x0", x1="x1", y0="y0", y1="y1", fill="depth")
plot
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Plot, Treemap, Nodes, Rect, GraphData } from "hmplot";
  const data = {
    source: ["root", "root", "a", "a", "a", "b", "b"],
    target: ["a", "b", "a1", "a2", "a3", "b1", "b2"],
  };
</script>

<Plot {data} height={300}>
  <GraphData source="source" target="target"
    ><Treemap root="root" padding={0.02}>
      <Nodes><Rect x0="x0" x1="x1" y0="y0" y1="y1" fill="depth" /></Nodes>
    </Treemap></GraphData
  >
</Plot>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

- `padding_inner` (`number`): The gap between sibling rectangles. Default: padding. In data units.
- `padding_outer` (`number`): The gap between a parent's edges and its children. Default: padding. In data units.
- `tile` (`"squarify" | "resquarify" | "binary" | "slice" | "dice" | "sliceDice"`): How each rectangle is split among its children, by d3's tiling methods. Default: `"squarify"`.
- `root` (`string | number | boolean`): The ID of the node whose subtree the layout divides: the hierarchy's root, or any node below it (a drill-down), or an input a Select or a click sets. Nodes outside its subtree stay rows of the nodes table, hidden; depth counts from it (0).
- `levels` (`number`): How many levels below root to show (1: its children only); root itself is then left out, as its area is the whole layout. Default: every level.
- `value` (`column | expression`): Each leaf's nonnegative weight, which sets its rectangle's area: a nodes-table column or an expression over it. A parent holds the sum of its leaves. Default: `1`.
- `width` (`number`): The width of the rectangle the layout divides. Default: `1` data units.
- `height` (`number`): The height of the rectangle the layout divides. Default: `1` data units.
- `padding` (`number`): The gap around and between rectangles, where padding_inner and padding_outer do not set their own. Default: `0` data units.

### Usage

`Treemap` uses d3-hierarchy to subdivide one connected, directed hierarchy. Supply the edges (and nodes, or let it infer them) and endpoint mapping through GraphData; set `root` on Treemap. `value` evaluates on node columns; leaf values determine area and default to 1. `width` and `height` default to 1. `padding`, `paddingInner`, and `paddingOuter` control gaps. `tile` selects `squarify` (default), `resquarify`, `binary`, `slice`, `dice`, or `sliceDice`.

Inside `<Nodes>`, `x0`, `x1`, `y0`, and `y1` give rectangles; `x`, `y`, and `position` give centers. `parent`, `depth`, `degree`, and node attributes are also available. `<Edges>` retains source rows and exposes center-to-center `start` and `end`.

### Drilling down

`root` may be any node, not only the hierarchy's: the layout divides that node's subtree to fill the whole area, and the other nodes stay rows of the nodes table, hidden, so marks draw only the subtree. `depth` counts from `root` (0), and `levels={1}` shows its children only (root itself is then left out, as its rectangle is the whole area). Each node's `total` is its summed value, for labels and lists; `parent` is its parent's ID, for an Up control. With `const root = input("root", { default: "all" })` and `root={root}`, a click on a rectangle can set the input: `select={root.set("id")}` on the Rect writes the clicked node's ID, a click on nothing restores the default, a [Button](button) with `set={root.reset()}` goes back to the top, and a Select named `root` shows and edits the same value. A node table may not have a column named `total`.

```svelte
<script>
  const root = input("root", { default: "all" });
</script>

<InputContext>
  <Select name="root" options={["all", ...divisions]} />
  <Button label="Top" set={root.reset()} />
  <Plot>
    <GraphData {nodes} {edges} source="parent" target="id">
      <Treemap root={root} value="revenue" levels={1} padding={0.004}>
        <Nodes bind:this={shown}>
          <Rect x0="x0" x1="x1" y0="y0" y1="y1" fill="division" select={root.set("id")} />
          <Text x="x" y="y" text="id" />
        </Nodes>
      </Treemap>
    </GraphData>
  </Plot>
</InputContext>
```

```python
root = hm.input("root", default="all")
with hm.Scene() as scene:
    hm.Select(name="root", options=["all", *divisions])
    hm.Button(label="Top", set=root.reset())
    with hm.Plot():
        with hm.GraphData(nodes=nodes, edges=edges, source="parent", target="id"):
            with hm.Treemap(root=root, value="revenue", levels=1):
                with hm.Nodes():
                    hm.Rect(x0="x0", x1="x1", y0="y0", y1="y1", fill="division", select=root.set("id"))
```

`await shown.read({ columns: ["id", "total"] })` gives the shown nodes for a breadcrumb or a list, or put a [TableView](table-view) inside the Nodes, after a [Sort](sort) for a top ten.

### Related examples

- [Treemap](/HMPlot/examples/treemap-hierarchy.md)

## Sankey

Page: /reference/python/sankey.md

A flow diagram layout, with nodes in columns and links as thick as their values.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"source": ["in", "in", "a", "b"], "target": ["a", "b", "out", "out"], "value": [3, 2, 3, 2]}
with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300) as plot:
    with hm.GraphData(source="source", target="target"):
        with hm.Sankey(value="value"):
            with hm.Edges():
                hm.Flow(start_lower="startLower", end_lower="endLower",
                        start_upper="startUpper", end_upper="endUpper")
            with hm.Nodes():
                hm.Rect(x0="x0", x1="x1", y0="y0", y1="y1")
plot
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Plot, Sankey, Edges, Nodes, Flow, Rect, GraphData } from "hmplot";
  const data = {
    source: ["in", "in", "a", "b"],
    target: ["a", "b", "out", "out"],
    value: [3, 2, 3, 2],
  };
</script>

<Plot {data} height={300}>
  <GraphData source="source" target="target"
    ><Sankey value="value">
      <Edges>
        <Flow
          startLower="startLower"
          endLower="endLower"
          startUpper="startUpper"
          endUpper="endUpper"
        />
      </Edges>
      <Nodes><Rect x0="x0" x1="x1" y0="y0" y1="y1" /></Nodes>
    </Sankey></GraphData
  >
</Plot>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

- `value` (`column`): The edge table's column of nonnegative flows, which set the links' thickness.
- `orientation` (`"left" | "right" | "down" | "up"`): The direction the flow runs. Default: `"right"`.
- `node_width` (`number`): The thickness of each node's bar along the flow; the layout spans 0 to 1. Default: `0.025` data units.
- `node_padding` (`number`): The gap between neighboring nodes in a column; the layout spans 0 to 1. Default: `0.02` data units.
- `iterations` (`number`): Relaxation passes that straighten the links. Default: `8`.
- `align` (`"left" | "right" | "center" | "justify"`): Which column each node takes: its depth from the sources (left), its distance to the sinks (right), beside its targets for a source (center), or left with every sink in the last column (justify). Default: `"justify"`.

### Usage

Sankey consumes GraphData and lays out nonnegative flows in an acyclic directed graph. Nodes expose `x0`, `x1`, `y0`, `y1`, `x`, `y`, `position`, `depth`, and `throughput`. Edges expose four attachment corners for `Flow`, plus the original edge columns. Explicit GraphData node tables can include isolated nodes.

### Related examples

- [Sankey flow](/HMPlot/examples/sankey-flow.md)

## Flow

Page: /reference/python/flow.md

A Sankey's links drawn as bands, one per edge.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"source": ["in", "in", "a", "b"], "target": ["a", "b", "out", "out"], "value": [3, 2, 3, 2]}
with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300) as plot:
    with hm.GraphData(source="source", target="target"):
        with hm.Sankey(value="value"):
            with hm.Edges():
                hm.Flow(start_lower="startLower", end_lower="endLower",
                        start_upper="startUpper", end_upper="endUpper")
plot
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Plot, Sankey, Edges, Flow, GraphData } from "hmplot";
  const data = {
    source: ["in", "in", "a", "b"],
    target: ["a", "b", "out", "out"],
    value: [3, 2, 3, 2],
  };
</script>

<Plot {data} height={300}>
  <GraphData source="source" target="target"
    ><Sankey value="value">
      <Edges>
        <Flow
          startLower="startLower"
          endLower="endLower"
          startUpper="startUpper"
          endUpper="endUpper"
        />
      </Edges>
    </Sankey></GraphData
  >
</Plot>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

#### Options

- `start_lower` (`channel`): Where one side of each band starts, at its source node: a column of positions, Sankey's start_lower.
- `end_lower` (`channel`): Where that side ends, at the target node: a column of positions, Sankey's end_lower.
- `start_upper` (`channel`): Where the other side of each band starts: a column of positions, Sankey's start_upper.
- `end_upper` (`channel`): Where the other side ends: a column of positions, Sankey's end_upper.

#### Appearance

- `fill` (`channel`): The fill color: a CSS color, or a column of numbers or categories mapped to colors.
- `color` (`channel`): The line or text color: a CSS color, or a column mapped to colors.
- `size` (`channel`): The size of each point or label: a number, or a column mapped to sizes. In px.
- `width` (`channel`): The line width: a number, or a column mapped to widths. In px.
- `opacity` (`channel`): The opacity, 0 to 1: a number, or a column (categories map through opacity_scale). Default: `0.2`.
- `outline_color` (`channel`): The outline's color: a CSS color, or a column of categories mapped through outline_color_scale.
- `outline_opacity` (`channel`): Border opacity from 0 to 1: a number, numeric column, array or expression. Fades the border over the fill; mark opacity still applies to both. Missing values hide the border. Default: `1`.
- `outline_width` (`channel`): The outline's width in CSS pixels, drawn inside the mark's edge (a point's at most its radius). Default: `0`.

#### Scales

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `fill_scale`, `color_scale`, `colormap`, `size_scale`, `width_scale`, `outline_color_scale`, `opacity_scale`.

#### Display

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `label`, `legend`, `visible`, `domains`, `rows`, `blend`, `glow`, `shade`, `options`, `name`.

#### Interaction

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `identity`, `select`, `hover`, `tooltip`, `nearest`, `respond`, `selection_opacity`, `enter_effect`, `exit_effect`.

#### Animation

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `animation`, `animation_duration`, `animation_easing`.

#### Map paths

- `interpolation` (`"great-circle" | "angular" | "cartesian"`): How a path between two points runs on a map or a globe: along a great circle, straight in longitude and latitude, or straight in space. Default: `"great-circle"`.

#### Symbol rotation

- `rotation` (`number`): The symbol's rotation. Default: `0` degrees.

#### Symbol

- `shape` (`string | column | string[]`): The point symbol: a shape name, a column of categories mapped to shapes, or one name per row. Default: `"circle"`.
- `shape_scale` (`scale`): A categorical() scale from the shape column's categories to shape names.

#### Legend settings

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `legend_font_size`, `legend_font_family`, `legend_text_color`, `legend_tick_format`.

#### Color settings

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `quantize`, `levels`.

#### Limits

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `max_elements`.

#### The mark's own axes

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `x_transform`, `x_invert`, `xbounds`, `xrange`, `y_transform`, `y_invert`, `ybounds`, `yrange`, `z_transform`, `z_invert`, `zbounds`, `zrange`.

#### Shading

- `transparent` (`boolean`, setting): Draw the mark in the transparent pass, blended in depth order with other transparent marks. Default: `False`.

#### Advanced renderer options

- `max_instances` (`number | null`): The most rows drawn; past it the rows are sampled (null draws them all), though SVG and PDF exports draw every row. Default: `None`.

### Usage

Place `Flow` inside Sankey's `Edges` scope and bind its four attachment channels. Each original edge draws as one filled band that retains its source row for picking and export.

### Related examples

- [Sankey flow](/HMPlot/examples/sankey-flow.md)

## Routes

Page: /reference/python/routes.md

A DAG's edges drawn along their routed paths, bends included.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"source": ["a", "a", "b", "c", "a"], "target": ["b", "c", "d", "d", "d"]}
with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300) as plot:
    with hm.GraphData(source="source", target="target"):
        with hm.DAG():
            with hm.Edges():
                hm.Routes()
plot
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Plot, DAG, Edges, Routes, GraphData } from "hmplot";
  const data = {
    source: ["a", "a", "b", "c", "a"],
    target: ["b", "c", "d", "d", "d"],
  };
</script>

<Plot {data} height={300}>
  <GraphData source="source" target="target"
    ><DAG>
      <Edges><Routes /></Edges>
    </DAG></GraphData
  >
</Plot>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

#### Options

- `dash` (`number | boolean | [number, number]`): Dashes the lines: true (4 px dashes and gaps), a dash length (gaps as long), or [dash, gap], measured along the drawn path. In px.
- `curve` (`"linear" | "step" | "step-before" | "step-after" | "link-horizontal" | "link-vertical" | "quadratic" | "cubic"`): How each piece of a route runs between its two points. Default: `"linear"`.

#### Appearance

- `color` (`channel`): The line or text color: a CSS color, or a column mapped to colors.
- `width` (`channel`): The line width: a number, or a column mapped to widths. In px.
- `opacity` (`channel`): The opacity, 0 to 1: a number, or a column (categories map through opacity_scale). Default: `1`.

#### Scales

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `color_scale`, `colormap`, `width_scale`, `opacity_scale`.

#### Display

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `label`, `legend`, `visible`, `domains`, `rows`, `blend`, `glow`, `shade`, `options`, `name`.

#### Interaction

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `identity`, `select`, `hover`, `tooltip`, `nearest`, `respond`, `selection_opacity`, `enter_effect`, `exit_effect`.

#### Animation

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `animation`, `animation_duration`, `animation_easing`.

#### Map paths

- `interpolation` (`"great-circle" | "angular" | "cartesian"`): How a path between two points runs on a map or a globe: along a great circle, straight in longitude and latitude, or straight in space. Default: `"great-circle"`.

#### Legend settings

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `legend_font_size`, `legend_font_family`, `legend_text_color`, `legend_tick_format`.

#### Color settings

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `quantize`, `levels`.

#### Limits

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `max_elements`.

#### The mark's own axes

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `x_transform`, `x_invert`, `xbounds`, `xrange`, `y_transform`, `y_invert`, `ybounds`, `yrange`, `z_transform`, `z_invert`, `zbounds`, `zrange`.

#### Shading

- `transparent` (`boolean`, setting): Draw the mark in the transparent pass, blended in depth order with other transparent marks. Default: `False`.

#### Advanced renderer options

- `max_instances` (`number | null`): The most rows drawn; past it the rows are sampled (null draws them all), though SVG and PDF exports draw every row. Default: `None`.

### Usage

Place `Routes` inside a DAG `Edges` scope. It expands each edge's ordered route points into visible segments, retaining the original edge row for styling and picking.

> **SVG and PDF export**
>
> **Vector, except** in a 3D view that holds a mark with no vector form there (Points3D, Surface or another 3D mark, a Heatmap or Image, a lit or additive mark, a globe or polar frame): then SVG and PDF exports draw all of that view's marks as one image, and `mode="vector"` refuses it. In other 3D views the routes are vectors too, drawn back to front by depth (approximate where marks cross closely). `dash` and a `color` column stay vector. See [what is not exported as vector](/HMPlot/docs/export.md).

### Related examples

- [Layered DAG](/HMPlot/examples/layered-dag.md)

## Nodes

Page: /reference/python/nodes.md

A graph's nodes, one row each, for the marks inside to draw.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"source": ["root", "root", "a", "a", "b"], "target": ["a", "b", "a1", "a2", "b1"]}
with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300) as plot:
    with hm.GraphData(source="source", target="target"):
        with hm.Tree(root="root"):
            with hm.Nodes():
                hm.Text(position="position", text="id")
plot
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Plot, Tree, Nodes, Text, GraphData } from "hmplot";
  const data = {
    source: ["root", "root", "a", "a", "b"],
    target: ["a", "b", "a1", "a2", "b1"],
  };
</script>

<Plot {data} height={300}>
  <GraphData source="source" target="target"
    ><Tree root="root">
      <Nodes><Text position="position" text="id" /></Nodes>
    </Tree></GraphData
  >
</Plot>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

- `drag` (`boolean`): Lets the viewer drag nodes with the pointer, in a Force layout. Default: `False`.

### Usage

Nodes selects the node relation from graph data. It works before or after a layout and supplies an ordinary table to its children. Apply Calculate, Filter, Sort or Join inside it to transform nodes; use a nested Edges to switch back to the corresponding edge relation. Filtering nodes induces edges with both endpoints still present.

GraphData owns the node table and its `nodeKey`. To add attributes, supply them there, aggregate them from the edges with its `reduce`, or use the ordinary Join transform inside Nodes. Nodes has no separate data/key join API.

Layout columns include `id`, `position`, `x`/`y`/`z` and degree. Tree, Pack and Treemap also provide parent and depth; Pack adds `r`, and Treemap adds rectangle bounds. Tree exposes parent coordinates and partition bounds for animation. `drag=true` opts into Force dragging; static layouts do not simulate.

### Related examples

- [Rooted tree](/HMPlot/examples/rooted-tree.md)

## Edges

Page: /reference/python/edges.md

A graph layout's edges, one row each with start and end positions, for the marks inside to draw.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"source": ["root", "root", "a", "a", "b"], "target": ["a", "b", "a1", "a2", "b1"]}
with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300) as plot:
    with hm.GraphData(source="source", target="target"):
        with hm.Tree(root="root"):
            with hm.Edges():
                hm.Segments(start="start", end="end")
plot
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Plot, Tree, Edges, Segments, GraphData } from "hmplot";
  const data = {
    source: ["root", "root", "a", "a", "b"],
    target: ["a", "b", "a1", "a2", "b1"],
  };
</script>

<Plot {data} height={300}>
  <GraphData source="source" target="target"
    ><Tree root="root">
      <Edges><Segments start="start" end="end" /></Edges>
    </Tree></GraphData
  >
</Plot>
```

### Usage

Edges selects the edge relation from graph data, before or after a layout. Its children receive an ordinary table with the original edge attributes. Calculate, Filter and other table transforms can operate on it without coupling marks to the graph structure.

When node geometry is available, `start` and `end` lazily gather the current endpoint positions; `sourceIndex` and `targetIndex` identify the corresponding node rows. Filtering nodes induces only edges whose endpoints remain. Tree publishes its chosen spanning-tree edges; other layouts retain their documented edge mappings.

### Related examples

- [Rooted tree](/HMPlot/examples/rooted-tree.md)

## Tree

Page: /reference/python/tree.md

A rooted tree layout of an edge table, as a tidy tree, an icicle or a dendrogram.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"source": ["root", "root", "a", "a", "b"], "target": ["a", "b", "a1", "a2", "b1"]}
with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300) as plot:
    with hm.GraphData(source="source", target="target"):
        with hm.Tree(root="root"):
            with hm.Edges():
                hm.Segments(start="start", end="end")
            with hm.Nodes():
                hm.Points(position="position")
plot
```

```svelte
<script>
  import {
    Plot,
    Tree,
    Edges,
    Nodes,
    Segments,
    Points,
    GraphData,
  } from "hmplot";
  const data = {
    source: ["root", "root", "a", "a", "b"],
    target: ["a", "b", "a1", "a2", "b1"],
  };
</script>

<Plot {data} height={300}>
  <GraphData source="source" target="target"
    ><Tree root="root">
      <Edges><Segments start="start" end="end" /></Edges>
      <Nodes><Points position="position" /></Nodes>
    </Tree></GraphData
  >
</Plot>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

- `root` (`string | number | boolean | expression`): The starting node's ID, or a scalar reduction over node columns and selection. Its depth is zero; every mode keeps only reachable nodes.
- `directed` (`boolean`): Follows edges only from source to target, instead of both ways, in every mode. Default: `False`.
- `orientation` (`"left" | "right" | "down" | "up"`): The direction the tree grows from its root. Default: `"down"`.
- `sibling_spacing` (`number`): The distance between neighboring leaves, across the tree (tidy and cluster modes). Default: `1` data units.
- `depth_spacing` (`number`): The distance between levels, along the tree (tidy and cluster modes). Default: `1` data units.
- `mode` (`"tidy" | "tidy-approx" | "partition" | "cluster"`): A compact CPU tidy tree, a GPU approximation reserving subtree intervals (tidy-approx), a GPU icicle of nested rectangles with x0, x1, y0 and y1 (partition), or a dendrogram with every leaf on one level (cluster). Every mode gives the leaves an order column, their place from left to right. Default: `"tidy"`.
- `layer_height` (`number | column | expression`): Partition mode: nonnegative band thickness per node. Children start at their parent's end; zero collapses a layer. tween() runs before layout. Default: `1` data units.
- `node_width` (`number | column | expression`): Each node's width, as a number or a nodes-table column or expression. Partition and tidy modes allow zero widths for collapsing branches; incoming tween() is evaluated before geometry. Default: `1` data units.
- `child_align` (`"left" | "right" | "center"`): Partition mode with width_mode "fixed": where the children sit in a parent wider than they are. Default: `"center"`.
- `width_mode` (`"proportional" | "fixed"`): Partition mode: a parent spans its children's total width (proportional), or at least its own node_width (fixed). Default: `"proportional"`.
- `visual_margin` (`number`): Partition mode: a gap between neighboring rectangles, inset from each node's bounds without moving its center. Default: `0` data units.
- `height` (`column | expression`): Cluster mode: a nodes-table column of merge heights, which places each node that far from the leaves, drawn to scale as scipy's dendrogram does.
- `edge_length` (`number | column | expression`): Tidy modes: nonnegative incoming edge lengths read from the edge table, accumulated along root paths and multiplied by depth_spacing. Default: `1`.
- `where` (`boolean | column | expression`): Node-table predicate; hidden nodes disconnect descendants. The root remains present. Layout entry/exit retains departing branches until they shrink.
- `enter` (`{ nodeWidth?: number; layerHeight?: number; edgeLength?: number }`): Starting numeric contributions for entering branches. Omitted endpoints are zero; initial mounting rests at the target.
- `exit` (`{ nodeWidth?: number; layerHeight?: number; edgeLength?: number }`): Departing branch contributions, reached before removal. Omitted endpoints are zero.
- `animation_duration` (`number`): Duration of layout-owned entry and exit; incoming tweens keep their own timing. Default: `300` ms.
- `animation_easing` (`"linear" | "quad-in" | "quad-out" | "quad-in-out" | "cubic-in" | "cubic-out" | "cubic-in-out" | "sine-in-out"`): Easing of layout-owned entry and exit. Default: `"cubic-in-out"`.
- `name` (`string`): The layout's name in the status its handle reports.

### Usage

Provides Nodes and Edges scopes with parent, depth, degree, order, positions, and endpoints. Drops unreachable nodes and non-tree edges. Default traversal is undirected, orientation down, and spacing 1. directed follows source-to-target edges. A missing root is an error.

All modes honor `directed`: true follows outgoing edges and shows a subtree, false traverses either way and reroots the reachable component. The root has depth zero, and Edges publish the child node's `depth`, even when an original edge points toward the root. Explicit node tables retain selection and keyed animation identity while unreachable nodes are omitted. Automatic bounds update when layout geometry changes; explicit domains remain fixed.

Nodes also publish `parentPosition`, `parentX` and `parentY`, plus `parentX0`/`parentX1`/`parentY0`/`parentY1` in partition mode. Roots have NaN parent coordinates. These support enter/exit animation: `x={animate(col.x, {enter: col.parentX, exit: col.parentX})}`. New rows read their new parent's coordinates; departing rows read their previous parent's coordinates.

`root` can be a scalar reduction expression over the original node table, including its selection. See [Zoomable sunburst](/HMPlot/examples/sunburst.md) for declarative focus and [Expandable tree](/HMPlot/examples/expandable-tree.md) for collapse, depth filtering and layout-owned transitions.

In `mode="partition"`, `visualMargin` insets the published node bounds to create visible gaps between sibling rectangles and depth bands. It defaults to zero, and the node `x`/`y` centers stay fixed.

Every mode publishes `order` on its nodes: each leaf's place among the leaves, left to right (0, 1, 2, ...), and NaN for inner nodes, so marks placed by it skip them. A nodes table may not have its own `order` column.

Requires graph data from GraphData. Outputs are visible to children only. Transforms retain the previous complete result while an update prepares. To let the viewer change a setting, read an input in it: `orientation={input("orientation")}` (Python `orientation=hm.input.orientation`), where `orientation` is a [Select](select) of `"down"`, `"up"`, `"left"` and `"right"`.

### Dendrograms

Partition widths and heights can be zero. `layerHeight` accepts a number, node-table column or expression, with each child's band starting at its parent's end. `tween()` in `nodeWidth` and `layerHeight` runs **before** layout on the plot clock. With a stable topology, tweening unwanted subtree weights and ancestor heights to zero shrinks them coherently; restoring the values grows them. Filter zero-area nodes after layout and draw the moving geometry directly, without another mark transition. See [Zoomable sunburst](/HMPlot/examples/sunburst.md).

`mode="cluster"` lays a tree out as d3.cluster does: every leaf at the same level, one `siblingSpacing` apart in `order` (leaf k at k), and each parent centered over its children (their mean). The leaves sit at 0 along the tree and the root at the far end. Without `height`, a node sits 1 + its tallest child from the leaves (times `depthSpacing`). With `height`, a column of the nodes table (or an expression over it), each node sits at its merge height, drawn to scale as scipy's dendrogram draws it: y is the height in `"down"`, -height in `"up"`, x is the height in `"left"` and -height in `"right"`. Leaves take height 0 (a missing value reads as 0); a merge needs a finite height, at least its children's, and Tree names the node otherwise. Only nodes reachable from the root are published.

Draw the links with Segments and a step curve for right-angle elbows: `curve="step-after"` (across, then along) for `"down"` and `"up"`, and `curve="step-before"` for `"left"` and `"right"`. In a polar Plot or Frame, `"up"` with `step-after` draws arcs, then radial lines; a `baseRadius` equal to the root's height puts the root at the center.

A clustered heatmap sorts its rows (or columns) in the order of the leaves, one unit per leaf, and puts each dendrogram in a Frame beside it whose leaf axis has the domain [-0.5, n - 0.5] over the heatmap's n rows, so leaf k sits at the center of row k. Nodes can label the leaves with `y="order"` (or `x="order"`).

Tree takes precomputed trees; it does not cluster. In Python, `hm.linkage_table(Z, labels)` turns a scipy linkage matrix into the tables below, and `scipy.cluster.hierarchy.leaves_list(Z)` is the leaf order. In JavaScript, turn merge rows `[a, b, height]` (scipy's convention: leaves 0 to n - 1, merge i makes node n + i) into an edge table and a nodes table:

```js
function linkageTable(merges, labels) {
  const n = labels.length, edges = { source: [], target: [] };
  const nodes = { id: labels.map((_, i) => i), label: [...labels], height: labels.map(() => 0) };
  merges.forEach(([a, b, height], i) => {
    edges.source.push(n + i, n + i); edges.target.push(a, b);
    nodes.id.push(n + i); nodes.label.push(null); nodes.height.push(height);
  });
  // The leaves left to right, as mode="cluster" places them (its order column).
  const leaves = [], stack = [2 * n - 2];
  while (stack.length) {
    const node = stack.pop();
    if (node < n) leaves.push(node); else stack.push(merges[node - n][1], merges[node - n][0]);
  }
  return { edges, nodes, root: 2 * n - 2, leaves };
}
```

```svelte
<GraphData nodes={rows.nodes} edges={rows.edges}>
  <Tree root={rows.root}
    mode="cluster" height="height" orientation="down">
    <Edges><Segments start="start" end="end" curve="step-after" /></Edges>
  </Tree>
</GraphData>
```

A d3 hierarchy converts the same way: `root.links()` lists each parent with its children, in order, for the edge table, and the nodes table takes each node's merge height from its data.

See the [complete example](/HMPlot/examples/clustermap.md).

### Tree layout animation

Tree offers compact CPU `tidy`, GPU `tidy-approx` (horizontal intervals per subtree),
GPU `partition`, and CPU `cluster`. GPU modes cache topology by node IDs/order, source/target
columns, root and direction. Width/height changes reuse structural buffers. Partition uses
leaf prefix sums; root-path accumulation uses logarithmic pointer-jumping passes. Approximate
and fixed-width subtree sizing uses ordered depth passes, so very deep trees cost more.
CPU tidy can consume moving inputs too, but reads numeric values and lays out on the host.

`edgeLength` (Python `edge_length`) reads a nonnegative edge-table column or expression.
Tidy modes accumulate lengths along root paths, multiplied by `depthSpacing`; siblings can
have unequal lengths. Partition uses per-node `layerHeight`; cluster uses merge heights.

Put visibility on Tree's `where`, not a Filter after Nodes, when branches should reflow.
It reads the node table and disconnects descendants of hidden nodes; the root remains present.
Tree's `enter` and `exit` specify nonnegative numeric `nodeWidth`, `layerHeight`, and
`edgeLength` contributions (omitted endpoints are zero). `animationDuration` and
`animationEasing` control these lifecycle transitions. Initial mounting rests at the target.
In Python, nested keys are `node_width`, `layer_height`, and `edge_length`.

Departing nodes and edges remain until their contributions land; new rows start at enter
values. Interrupted membership transitions continue from their current contribution.
`presence` on Nodes and Edges ranges from zero to one, so `opacity="presence"` fades marks
with their branch. Incoming `tween()` expressions remain ordinary numeric inputs with their
own timing; they do not declare layout entry/exit. Draw moving geometry directly without
another mark animation or bounds animation. Cluster does not support layout lifecycle.
Changing the root or reparenting a surviving node switches topology discretely; it does not
retain both parents. Use a fixed root with tweened weights/heights for continuous zoom, as in
the sunburst example. Structural changes may compile a new GPU plan.

Source validation and membership updates may read data once; GPU numeric layout does not
read coordinates back each frame. Rendering, bounds, picking and export retain their existing
readbacks. See [Expandable tree](/HMPlot/examples/expandable-tree.md) and [Sunburst](/HMPlot/examples/sunburst.md).

### Related examples

- [Rooted tree](/HMPlot/examples/rooted-tree.md)
- [Tree icicle](/HMPlot/examples/tree-icicle.md)
- [Clustered heatmap](/HMPlot/examples/clustermap.md)

## DocumentExportOptions

Page: /reference/python/document-export-options.md

How exportSVG and exportPDF draw: size, vector or raster, and text.

### Example

```python
await plot.export_svg("figure.svg", width="160mm", mode="vector")
```

```svelte
const { blob, report } = await plot.exportSVG({ width: "160mm", mode: "vector" });
```

### Members

- `width` (`string | number`): The page width: CSS pixels, or a CSS length ("20cm").
- `height` (`string | number`): The page height: CSS pixels, or a CSS length.
- `mode` (`"auto" | "vector" | "raster"`): "auto" (default) draws what has no vector form as images, "vector" refuses it, "raster" draws the whole plot as one image.
- `raster_dpi` (`number`): The images' resolution (default 300).
- `text` (`"embedded" | "outlines"`): "embedded" keeps text selectable with its fonts embedded; "outlines" draws it as paths, so it looks the same without the fonts.
- `primitive_budget` (`number`): The most vector pieces one export draws (default 100,000): a mark past it is drawn as an image, or refused in "vector" mode.

### Usage

Export SVG or PDF for print and publication, where lines and text should stay sharp at any size and a journal asks for vector figures; export PNG (`exportPNG({ scale })`) for slides, the web and plots that are mostly images anyway. The options are the same for a Plot, a Facet and a Python Scene.

`width` and `height` set the document's size, as a number of CSS pixels or a length with a unit: `"160mm"`, `"7in"`, `"12cm"`, `"300pt"`. The plot as it is drawn on screen is scaled to that size, not laid out again, so fonts and line widths scale with it: give the plot the on-screen size you want at print size, and only one of the two lengths, so the other follows its aspect (both stretch it to that box). Without either, the document is the plot's size on screen.

`mode` decides what happens to content that has no vector form ([what is not exported as vector](/HMPlot/docs/export.md)): `"auto"` (the default) draws it as an image at `rasterDpi` (`raster_dpi` in Python; 300 by default), in its place among the vector shapes; `"vector"` refuses the export and names it; `"raster"` draws the whole plot as one image. Use `"vector"` to make sure a figure has no images in it, and `"raster"` for a dense plot whose vector form would be too large to open. `primitiveBudget` (`primitive_budget`; 100,000 by default) caps the vector pieces of one export: a mark that would pass it is drawn as an image, or refused in `"vector"` mode. `text: "outlines"` is not implemented yet: the text stays text, and the report says so.

The result's `report` lists what happened to each mark (`markOutcomes`: vector or raster), the image layers and their DPI (`rasterLayers`), and warnings. Read it to find which mark became an image, then change that mark or accept the image.

Python takes the same options as keywords. `await plot.export_svg("figure.svg", width="160mm")` and `export_pdf` export a displayed notebook view; `hm.export_svg(plot, "figure.svg", width="160mm")` and `hm.export_pdf` export without a notebook, in a private headless Chrome. Python's PDFs are printed from the SVG export by Chrome, keep text as text and embed the fonts; prefer them to the handle's `exportPDF()`, whose in-browser conversion mishandles some SVG. See the [Plot handle](plot-handle) for the export methods, and docs/DOCUMENT-EXPORT.md for what each mark exports as.

### Related examples

- [Legends & uncertainty](/HMPlot/examples/guides.md)

## check

Page: /reference/python/check.md

Draw a plot headlessly and say what it drew: errors, each mark's rows and columns, the axes, and a PNG.

### Example

```python
with hm.Plot(data={"x": [1, 2, 3], "y": [3, 1, 2]}, axes2d=True) as plot:
    hm.Points(x="x", y="y")
result = hm.check(plot)
print(result)
result.save_png("plot.png")
```

### Parameters

- `target` (`Node`): A Plot, Facet, Scene or layout (or a mark with data=); the check draws the scene that holds it.
- `scale` (`number`): The PNG's pixel ratio. Default: 1.
- `vector` (`boolean`): Also make the SVG export, for its report of what it draws as images. Default: true.
- `timeout` (`number`): Seconds to wait for the scene to draw. Default: 60.
- `session` (`ExportSession`): A session whose browser to reuse, for several checks.
- `returns` (`CheckResult`): ok, errors, warnings, plots (each plot's marks with their rows and columns, its axes, size and description), png (bytes), save_png(path), summary() (also str(result)) and to_dict().

### Usage

`hm.check(plot)` draws the scene that holds `plot` in a private headless Chrome, as `hm.export_png` does, and returns what it drew, so a program (or an agent writing one) can see its result and fix its own mistakes without a notebook:

- `errors`: Python's validation errors and every error the browser showed (a missing column, a failed transform), each naming the component and what to pass instead. `ok` is true without any.
- `plots`: each plot's marks with their row counts and the columns they draw, its axes' ranges (or categories), its size in CSS pixels and its description (the summary screen readers get).
- `warnings`: marks that drew no rows, a legend whose mark has not bound yet, and what SVG and PDF exports draw as images rather than vectors (the export report; `vector=False` skips it).
- `lints`: what runs but does nothing or looks wrong, each naming the component and the fix: a Legend that explains nothing (no mark maps its channel), a Filter on `"@brushed"` over data no mark brushes, a color mapped from data with no legend to say which color is which (a color repeating the x or y column needs none), an explicit `x` or `y` domain at least 20 times wider than the data, or one holding none of it (in 3D, data past the domain, which draws outside the axes), category labels hidden where they would overlap, and points at least half the plot across (a size drawn as pixels). `strict=True` lists each lint as an error instead, so `ok` is false while any is left.
- `png`: the scene as drawn, `scale` times its CSS pixels (a fixed-width Plot at its own width); `save_png(path)` writes it.

`str(result)` (or `result.summary()`) is all of it as text; `result.to_dict()` is the same as JSON-ready data. In a notebook the result shows the PNG with the summary. A scene that fails before its plots draw has its errors and no PNG.

`timeout=60` gives each wait for component preparation or first-frame readiness 60 seconds, including the initial mount. Increase it for large scenes on software WebGPU. It is not an overall deadline for resource loading and image export.

```text
check: 1 plot drawn, no errors.
Plot 1, 1200 x 400 px, 2d:
  Points: 3 rows; x: x, y: y
  axes: x 0.9 to 3.1; y 0.9 to 3.1
  description: Scatter plot of y against x. x from 0.9 to 3.1, y from 0.9 to 3.1. 3 points.
png: 1200 x 400 px
```

### From the command line

`hmplot check plot.py` (or `python -m hmplot check plot.py`) runs a program as a notebook cell runs, in its own folder, and checks what it shows: its last line when that is a component (as a notebook displays it), else each component it leaves at top level, else each plot it exported (a plot built and exported inside `main()`). It prints the summary, saves the PNG beside the program as `plot.check.png` (`--png PATH` elsewhere, `--no-png` not at all) and exits with 0 when every check passed, 1 when the program raised (with the line: `plot.py:3: TypeError: Points: unknown property 'colr'. Did you mean 'color'?`) or a check found errors, and 2 when there was nothing to check or no browser could draw. `--json` prints the result as JSON, `--scale` sets the PNG's pixel ratio, and `--strict` counts lints as errors.

The browser is the exports' (`hm.install_chrome`): an installed Chrome, Edge or Chromium, else Chrome for Testing, downloaded once; WebGPU on the machine's GPU, or on SwiftShader's software adapter where there is none. Reuse one `hm.ExportSession()` as `session=` for many checks.

An MCP server can offer the check to an agent as one tool: take a program's path, run `hmplot check PATH --json`, and return the JSON with the saved PNG as an image.

## hmplot/check

Page: /reference/svelte/package-check.md

Inspect mounted Svelte plots for readiness, diagnostics and export omissions.

### Example

```svelte
import { inspect } from "hmplot/check";
const report = await inspect({ timeout: 30000 });
```

### Members

#### InspectionOptions

- `root` (`ParentNode`): Document, plot container or application subtree. Defaults to document.
- `timeout` (`number`): Total readiness/settling budget in milliseconds; defaults to 30000.

#### PlotInspection

- `title` (`string`): Required.
- `description` (`string`): Required.
- `ready` (`boolean`): Required.
- `completedFrame` (`number`): Required.
- `pendingPreparations` (`number`): Required.
- `model` (`unknown`): Required.
- `animation` (`unknown`): Required.
- `work` (`{ markPreparations: number; transformRuns: Record<string, number>; }`): What the plot did to get here (2026-10-22): mark preparations and transform runs by cause. Required.
- `diagnostics` (`Diagnostic[]`): Required.
- `exportOmissions` (`string[]`): Required.

#### InspectionReport

- `schema` (`1`): Required.
- `ready` (`boolean`): Required.
- `plots` (`PlotInspection[]`): Required.
- `errors` (`Diagnostic[]`): Required.
- `warnings` (`Diagnostic[]`): Required.
- `lints` (`Diagnostic[]`): Required.

#### Exports

- `inspect` (`(options?: InspectionOptions) => Promise<InspectionReport>`): Wait for completed draws and collect serializable diagnostics; screenshots and interaction assertions belong to the caller.

`inspect()` checks mounted Svelte plots. Import it explicitly in browser tests;
HMPlot installs no global testing hook. It returns an `InspectionReport` containing
`PlotInspection` records and structured errors, warnings and lints. `InspectionOptions`
selects a DOM root and a total timeout, defaulting to 30 seconds.

Wait for application data to finish loading before calling it. Inspection waits
for mounted plots' first visible draws, then the work already started by each plot.
An ongoing animation does not need to finish. A timeout is reported as an error,
never as successful settling. Visible application alerts in the inspection root are included as errors.
Reports include mark summaries and axis descriptions
in `model`, completed-frame counters, pending preparations and export omissions.

```js
import { inspect } from "hmplot/check";
const report = await inspect({ root: document.querySelector("main") });
console.log(JSON.stringify(report));
```

For Playwright, expose the imported function from a test-only application entry
point, then use `await page.evaluate(() => window.inspectPlot())`. Save its JSON
and a `page.screenshot()` at device pixel ratio 2. Check values, exported geometry,
or DOM after interactions; a changed screenshot alone does not establish correct
selection, aggregation, or filtering. See the web authoring guide for a complete
checking workflow.

## Package entry points

Page: /reference/svelte/package-entries.md

What each import path of the npm package offers, and how stable it is.

### Example

```svelte
import { Plot, Points } from "hmplot";          // components and functions
import { numpy as np } from "hmplot/jax";        // the bundled jax-js
import { tileAt } from "hmplot/tiles";           // vector-tile helpers
import { composition } from "hmplot/compound";   // experimental
```

### Entry points

The npm package `hmplot` has one main entry point and ten subpaths, the `exports` of its package.json. Import only from these; a file's path inside `dist/` is internal and may change in any release.

| Import | Stability | What it offers |
|---|---|---|
| `hmplot` | Public | Core components and functions, and their TypeScript types. |
| [`hmplot/charts`](package-charts) | Public | Chart patterns such as Bar, Histogram, Arrows and ErrorBars. |
| [`hmplot/stats`](package-stats) | Public | Statistical patterns: Bin, Hexbin, Normalize, Window and Summary. |
| [`hmplot/jax`](package-jax) | Public | The jax-js that hmplot runs on, for GPU arrays that plots read without a copy. |
| [`hmplot/vite`](package-vite) | Public | A Vite plugin that makes an app's own `@jax-js/jax` hmplot's. |
| [`hmplot/tiles`](package-tiles) | Public | Vector-tile helpers: the tile at a point, a tile's box, loading and decoding tiles. |
| [`hmplot/video`](package-video) | Public | MP4 encoding in the browser, which Plot's `exportVideo()` loads on first use. |
| [`hmplot/scene`](package-scene) | Public | The runtime that draws Python's declarative scenes in a Svelte app. |
| [`hmplot/templates`](package-templates) | Public | Renders portable, code-free Python templates inside Svelte contexts. |
| [`hmplot/types`](package-types) | Public | Option types for the settings a component registers. |
| [`hmplot/compound`](package-compound) | Experimental, in part | The built-in templates also offered by `hmplot/charts`, and `composition`, the experimental surface for writing a pattern in Svelte. |

**Public** names follow the version rules in docs/STABILITY.md: at 0.x a minor release may change them, and every change is listed in CHANGELOG.md. **Experimental** names may change in any release. `api/hmplot.api.md` in the repository lists every name each entry point exports, with its type; a change to it needs a CHANGELOG entry.

In Python, `import hmplot as hm` exposes core components and helpers; chart patterns use `hm.charts` (`from hmplot.charts import Bar`) and statistical patterns use `hm.stats` (`from hmplot.stats import Bin`). Other modules, and names that start with an underscore, are internal.

### Requirements

The package is ESM and its components are Svelte 5 components: an app compiles them with the Svelte plugin, and `hmplot/vite`'s plugin is optional. `svelte`, `three`, `@threlte/core` and `@threlte/extras` are peer dependencies; jax-js is bundled (as `hmplot/jax`), and apache-arrow, hyparquet and the video encoder load only when used. Drawing needs WebGPU in the browser. See docs/USAGE.md, "Browser and build requirements".

## hmplot/tiles

Page: /reference/svelte/package-tiles.md

Load, place and style vector tiles yourself; the VectorTile mark does all of it for you.

### Example

```svelte
import { tileAt, tileBounds, loadVectorTiles, DEFAULT_TILES } from "hmplot/tiles";

const tile = tileAt([-73.99, 40.73], 12);   // [12, 1206, 1539]
const [west, south, east, north] = tileBounds(tile);
const features = await loadVectorTiles(DEFAULT_TILES.url, [tile]);
```

### Exports

- `tileAt([longitude, latitude], z)` (`[z, x, y]`): The tile that contains a point at zoom z (an integer, 0 to 30); latitudes past Web Mercator's ±85.05° clamp.
- `tileBounds([z, x, y])` (`[west, south, east, north]`): A tile's box in degrees.
- `loadVectorTiles(url, tiles, {signal, init, clip, layers})` (`Promise<FeatureCollection>`): Fetches and decodes Mapbox Vector Tiles into one GeoJSON FeatureCollection in degrees, each feature's source layer in properties.layerName; VectorTile's data= takes it. url: a {z}/{x}/{y} template or a function of { z, x, y }. clip (default true) cuts geometry at each tile's edge; layers(name) chooses source layers. An HTTP error names the status and URL; a 204 or an empty body is an empty tile.
- `localPlane(origin, unitsPerMeter)` (`([lon, lat]) => [x, y]`): A local plane around origin ([longitude, latitude]): meters east and north of it, times unitsPerMeter (default 1). Within a few tens of kilometers, lengths are off by well under 1%.
- `DEFAULT_TILES` (`{ url, attribution, maxZoom }`): The tiles VectorTile draws without a url: VersaTiles' OpenStreetMap tiles (Shortbread schema, zoom 0 to 14, no key), with the credit their licenses ask for.
- `vectorTileScheme(theme)` (`scheme`): VectorTile's part styles from a theme's colors (background, palette, text), as a theme's vectorTile section or VectorTile's scheme= takes them.

### Usage

The [VectorTile](vector-tile) mark loads, decodes, places and styles tiles itself, from `tile`, `tiles` or a `bounds` box, or following the view. These helpers are for doing a part of that yourself: finding the tiles for a place (`tileAt`, `tileBounds`), loading them once and passing the result as VectorTile's `data` or to a GeoJSON mark (`loadVectorTiles`), placing other data in the meters of a local map (`localPlane`), or styling a basemap from a theme (`vectorTileScheme`).

Tile coordinates are the standard XYZ ("slippy map") ones: zoom, then the column from the west and the row from the north, in Web Mercator. `DEFAULT_TILES` needs no key and allows any origin; show its `attribution` wherever the tiles are shown, as their licenses ask. Another tile server's `url` is a template with `{z}`, `{x}` and `{y}`, as in its documentation. See docs/VECTOR-TILES.md.

These helpers are JavaScript only. In Python, VectorTile takes `tile`, `tiles` and `bounds` the same way, and exported pages embed the tiles they drew.

### Related examples

- [Vector tiles that follow the view](/HMPlot/examples/vector-tiles.md)

## hmplot/video

Page: /reference/svelte/package-video.md

A plot's animation encoded as MP4 in the browser with WebCodecs, loaded on first use.

### Example

```svelte
// A Plot handle loads this module itself: plot.exportVideo({ duration: 3000, fps: 30 }).
import { exportVideo } from "hmplot/video";

const blob = await exportVideo(plot, { duration: 3000, fps: 30, scale: 2 });
```

### Exports

- `exportVideo(handle, {duration, fps, start, scale})` (`Promise<Blob>`): An MP4 (H.264 where the browser has it, else VP9) of a Plot handle's animation: one PNG export per frame at a frozen clock time, from start (ms, default 0) for duration ms at fps (default 30) and scale (PNG pixels per CSS pixel, default 1); the clock returns to its time and frozen state afterwards. A browser without VideoEncoder is an error.
- `frameTimes({duration, fps, start})` (`number[]`): The frames' clock times in milliseconds: start + i × 1000 / fps before start + duration, at least one (the frames Python's export_mp4 steps through).
- `encodeFrames(frames, {fps})` (`Promise<Blob>`): Encodes image frames (PNG Blobs or ImageBitmaps, all one size, from an iterable or async iterable) at fps into an MP4. A frame has no alpha: it goes over white.
- `muxMp4({samples, width, height, fps, entry, codec, description})` (`Uint8Array`): The MP4 bytes of already encoded samples ({ data, key }) at a constant frame rate; encodeFrames uses it.

### Usage

A [Plot handle](plot-handle)'s `exportVideo({ duration, fps, start, scale })` imports this module the first time it runs, so a page that never exports video does not carry the encoder; import it yourself to encode frames of your own, or to know the frames' times. The video has the plot's animation clock frozen at each frame's time, so `@time` channels, transitions, playing Playbacks and running Simulates all advance by exactly one frame per frame, however long the export takes.

Encoding uses the browser's WebCodecs `VideoEncoder`: Chrome and Edge have it, and other browsers may not, in which case the export is an error. Odd frame sizes are padded to even ones, and frames are drawn over white, since MP4 video has no alpha. Python's `export_mp4(..., encoder="browser")` uses this encoder in the notebook view or the export browser; its default encoder is ffmpeg, which needs no WebCodecs. See docs/DOCUMENT-EXPORT.md, "Video in the browser".

### Related examples

- [animate, enter/exit, and @time](/HMPlot/examples/animation-engine.md)

## hmplot/vite

Page: /reference/svelte/package-vite.md

A Vite plugin that makes an app's own @jax-js/jax imports hmplot's jax-js, so arrays pass straight in.

### Example

```svelte
// vite.config.js
import { defineConfig } from "vite";
import { sveltekit } from "@sveltejs/kit/vite";
import { hmplotJax } from "hmplot/vite";

export default defineConfig({ plugins: [hmplotJax(), sveltekit()] });
```

### Exports

- `hmplotJax()` (`Vite plugin`): Resolves the app's imports of @jax-js/jax to hmplot's bundled jax-js (hmplot/jax), so the app and its plots share one jax-js and one GPU device. Without it, arrays from the app's own copy are read back and uploaded again, with a warning.

### Usage

A jax-js array belongs to the jax-js copy that made it, and each copy has its own GPU device. hmplot bundles its own jax-js ([hmplot/jax](package-jax)); an app that also imports `@jax-js/jax` has a second copy, whose arrays hmplot reads back to the CPU and uploads again (once per array, with a warning). Add the plugin before the Svelte plugin to give the app hmplot's copy instead, so arrays pass straight in. The app's own jax-js code then runs hmplot's jax-js version, whose API is upstream jax-js 0.1.25's.

In TypeScript, point `@jax-js/jax` at hmplot's types too, as the two copies' classes are separate types:

```json
{ "compilerOptions": { "paths": { "@jax-js/jax": ["./node_modules/hmplot/dist/jax.d.ts"] } } }
```

With another bundler, alias `@jax-js/jax` to `hmplot/jax`. An app that builds its arrays with `hmplot/jax` alone needs no plugin. See docs/USAGE.md, "Apps that use jax-js themselves".

## hmplot/jax

Page: /reference/svelte/package-jax.md

The jax-js that hmplot runs on, for building GPU arrays that plots read without a copy.

### Example

```svelte
import { initializePlot } from "hmplot";
import { numpy as np } from "hmplot/jax";

await initializePlot();
const points = np.array([[0, 0], [0.5, 0.5]]);
```

### Exports

- `everything jax-js exports` (`jax-js`): numpy, the transformations and the rest of jax-js's API, as upstream jax-js 0.1.25 documents it (hmplot's patches change compilation, not the API).

### Usage

`hmplot/jax` is [jax-js](https://github.com/ekzhang/jax-js) 0.1.25 (MIT, by Eric Zhang), bundled as `@hmplot/jax` with patches that keep GPU programs from compiling again for every new array length or constant. It exports everything jax-js does, with the same API; see jax-js's own documentation for it rather than this reference. The patches are listed in `vendor/jax-js/PATCHES.md` in the repository.

Plots take plain JavaScript arrays and typed arrays without any of this. Build jax-js arrays with this module when the data is computed on the GPU, so the arrays belong to the same jax-js, and the same GPU device, as the plots that read them: then a plot reads them in place. Call [initializePlot](initialize-plot) first, in the browser (in `onMount` or an event, not during server rendering); it selects WebGPU as jax-js's default backend. Dispose arrays you own when you are done with them; marks keep the inputs they still need.

An app that imports `@jax-js/jax` directly gets a separate copy of jax-js, whose arrays are copied through the CPU: use [hmplot/vite](package-vite) to make it this one.

## hmplot/scene
