The heads are Points, sized as Points are: `size` is a head's diameter in CSS pixels (5 by default), and the stems default to 1.5 CSS pixels wide. `size` and the head-only properties (`fill`, `shape`, `select`, `hover`, `brush`) apply to the heads, while `visible`, `opacity`, `respond`, `identity`, `enterEffect`/`exitEffect`, and the animation switches apply to both, and the mark's one legend entry toggles both.

Lollipop is a built-in template (TODO 130.3): BarGeometry places each stem's base and tip, a Segments draws the stems and Points the heads. It is importable from `hmplot/charts`; "Writing a pattern" in docs/USAGE.md has a hand-written lollipop as a worked example.

### Related examples

- [Lollipop chart](/HMPlot/examples/lollipop.md)

## charts.Pie

Page: /reference/python/pie.md

A pie or donut chart: a sector per row, its angle its value's share of the total.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"region": ["North", "East", "South", "West"], "sales": [42, 18, 27, 13]}
with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300) as plot:
    hm.charts.Pie(value="sales", category="region")
plot
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Plot } from "hmplot";
import { Pie } from "hmplot/charts";
  const data = { region: ["North", "East", "South", "West"], sales: [42, 18, 27, 13] };
</script>

<Plot {data} height={300}>
  <Pie value="sales" category="region" />
</Plot>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

#### Options

- `value` (`channel`): Each sector's size: a numeric column or expression. A negative value is an error; a zero or missing one draws nothing.
- `category` (`column`): The sectors' categories: they fill the sectors unless fill is given, so the legend lists them.
- `by` (`column | column[]`): One pie per group, drawn as concentric rings that each sum to their own total, each ring's sectors aligned to the inner ones they sum (in row order; sort sorts each ring on its own and breaks that); for pies side by side, use a Facet.
- `sort` (`"none" | "asc" | "desc" | category[]`): The sectors' order clockwise from start_angle: row order, by value, or a list of categories (the others after them). Default: `"none"`.
- `start_angle` (`number`): Where the pie starts, clockwise from 12 o'clock. Default: `0` degrees.
- `end_angle` (`number`): Where the pie ends, clockwise from 12 o'clock; below start_angle the sectors run counter-clockwise. Default: `360` degrees.
- `pad_angle` (`number`): A gap between sectors, taken from their shares as d3.pie's pad_angle is; with by, from each sector's own share (at most half its width, so a very small sector gets a narrower gap), so the rings stay aligned. Default: `0` degrees.
- `inner_radius` (`number`): The hole's radius as a fraction of the disk's: above 0 makes a donut. Default: `0`.
- `outer_radius` (`number`): The pie's radius as a fraction of the disk's. Default: `1`.
- `sector_label` (`"category" | "value" | "percent" | column | expression`): Text at each sector's centroid: its category, its value, its percent of its pie, a column, or an expression; a label that would overlap a larger sector's is hidden.
- `sector_label_format` (`string`): A d3-format string for numeric sector labels. Default: ".0%" for "percent", ",.7~r" otherwise.
- `text_color` (`color`): The sector labels' color. Default: `"#ffffff"`.
- `font_size` (`number`): The sector labels' font size. Default: `12` px.
- `placement` (`{anchor, size}`): Where the pie goes in a Cartesian plot: anchor in data coordinates, size in pixels. In a polar plot the pie fills the disk. Default: centered in the frame, across 90% of its shorter side.
- `data` (`table`): A table for this mark alone: a mark with data displays on its own, in a Plot of its own.

#### Appearance

- `fill` (`channel`): The fill color: a CSS color, or a column of numbers or categories mapped to colors. Default: the category column.

Also these options the marks share (described on Mark options): `color`, `opacity`, `outline_color`, `outline_opacity`, `outline_width`.

#### Scales

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `fill_scale`, `color_scale`, `colormap`, `outline_color_scale`, `opacity_scale`.

#### Display

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `label`, `legend`, `visible`, `domains`, `blend`, `glow`, `shade`, `options`, `name`.

#### Interaction

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `identity`, `select`, `hover`, `tooltip`, `nearest`, `respond`, `selection_opacity`, `enter_effect`, `exit_effect`.

#### Animation

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `animation`, `animation_duration`, `animation_easing`.

#### Legend settings

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `legend_font_size`, `legend_font_family`, `legend_text_color`, `legend_tick_format`.

#### Color settings

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `quantize`, `levels`.

#### Limits

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `max_elements`.

#### The mark's own axes

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `x_transform`, `x_invert`, `xbounds`, `xrange`, `y_transform`, `y_invert`, `ybounds`, `yrange`, `z_transform`, `z_invert`, `zbounds`, `zrange`.

#### Shading

- `lit` (`boolean`, setting): Shade the mark with the plot's lights. Default: `False`.
- `transparent` (`boolean`, setting): Draw the mark in the transparent pass, blended in depth order with other transparent marks. Default: `False`.

#### Advanced renderer options

- `max_instances` (`number | null`): The most rows drawn; past it the rows are sampled (null draws them all), though SVG and PDF exports draw every row. Default: `None`.

### Usage

A sector per row, its angle its `value`'s share of the total, clockwise from 12 o'clock (d3.pie's convention, with angles in degrees). `category` fills the sectors, so `<Legend for={pie} channel="fill">` (Python `hm.Legend(target=pie, channel="fill")`) lists the categories. `innerRadius` above 0 makes a donut; `startAngle` and `endAngle` make a partial pie; `padAngle` separates the sectors; `sort` orders them by value or by a list of categories. `sectorLabel` writes each sector's `"category"`, `"value"`, `"percent"`, a column, or an expression at its centroid; a label that would overlap a larger sector's is hidden.

In a polar Plot or Frame the pie fills the disk. In a Cartesian one (the default Plot) the Pie places a polar Frame of its own: centered in the frame's domain and across 90% of its shorter side, or where `placement` puts it (`anchor` in data coordinates, `size` in pixels), so a pie can sit beside other marks as an inset.

A negative value is a data error naming its row; a zero, missing or hidden value draws nothing. Put a `key` on the data and turn on `animation` to tween the sectors when the values change. `by` draws one pie per group as concentric rings; in row order, a ring's sectors start and end where the inner sectors whose values they sum do (a sunburst), each sector's `padAngle` coming out of its own share (at most half its width, so a very small sector gets a narrower gap). A `sort` sorts each ring on its own, which breaks that alignment. For pies side by side, put the Pie in a Facet:

See the [complete example](/HMPlot/examples/pie-facet.md).

Pie is a built-in template (TODO 130.3): the PieGeometry transform, a Rect for the sectors and a Text for their labels, importable from `hmplot/charts`. See "Writing a pattern" in docs/USAGE.md.

> **SVG and PDF export**
>
> **Vector, except** in a 3D view, where SVG and PDF exports draw the pie (a polar frame) with all of that view's marks as one image and `mode="vector"` refuses it. A `fill` column of numbers or categories stays vector. See [what is not exported as vector](/HMPlot/docs/export.md).

### Related examples

- [Pie chart](/HMPlot/examples/pie.md)
- [Donut chart](/HMPlot/examples/donut.md)
- [Pies in a Facet](/HMPlot/examples/pie-facet.md)

## charts.RuleX

Page: /reference/python/rule-x.md

A vertical reference line at x across the frame: one per row, or one at a value or the pointer.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"x": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], "y": [3, 4, 2, 5, 6, 5]}
with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True) as plot:
    hm.Line(x="x", y="y")
    hm.charts.RuleX(x=3.5)
plot
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Plot, Line } from "hmplot";
import { RuleX } from "hmplot/charts";
  const data = { x: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], y: [3, 4, 2, 5, 6, 5] };
</script>

<Plot {data} height={300} axes2d>
  <Line x="x" y="y" />
  <RuleX x={3.5} />
</Plot>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

#### Options

- `y0` (`channel`): Where the rule starts in y: a number or a column. Default: the bottom of the frame's visible domain.
- `y1` (`channel`): Where the rule ends in y: a number or a column. By default the rule spans the frame as it pans and zooms. Default: the top of the frame's visible domain.
- `dash` (`boolean | number | [number, number]`): Dash the rule: true (4 px dashes and gaps), a dash length (gaps as long), or [dash, gap], measured along the drawn rule. In px.
- `data` (`table`): A table for this mark alone: a mark with data displays on its own, in a Plot of its own.

#### Position

- `x` (`channel`): Where the rule stands: a number, a time or a category draws one rule, a column one per row, and "@pointer_x" follows the pointer.

#### Appearance

- `color` (`color`): The rule's color. Default: `"#8a949e"`. Default: the theme's rule gray.
- `width` (`number`): The rule's width. Default: `1` px. Default: 1.
- `opacity` (`number`): The rule's opacity, 0 to 1. Default: `1`.

#### Display

- `legend` (`boolean`): Whether the mark has a legend entry. Default: `False`.
- `visible` (`boolean`): Whether the rule is drawn. Default: `True`.
- `name` (`string`): The rule's name in the settings pane.

Also these options the marks share (described on Mark options): `label`, `blend`, `glow`, `shade`.

#### Interaction

- `identity` (`identity`): Whose rows these are for selections: an identity() shared by tables that show the same things. Default: its data's.
- `select` (`boolean | selection`): Click a rule to select its row: true uses its data's selection, or give a selection().
- `hover` (`boolean | selection`): Mark the rule under the pointer as @hovered, without fading the others: true uses its data's hover, or give a selection().
- `respond` (`boolean | "selected" | "brushed" | "hovered" | "nearby" | selection | array`): Which interaction states fade the rules outside them. Default: the states it sets, except hover.

#### Animation

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `animation`, `animation_duration`, `animation_easing`.

#### Legend settings

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `legend_font_size`, `legend_font_family`, `legend_text_color`, `legend_tick_format`.

#### Color settings

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `quantize`, `levels`.

#### Limits

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `max_elements`.

#### The mark's own axes

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `x_transform`, `x_invert`, `xbounds`, `xrange`, `y_transform`, `y_invert`, `ybounds`, `yrange`, `z_transform`, `z_invert`, `zbounds`, `zrange`.

#### Shading

- `transparent` (`boolean`, setting): Draw the mark in the transparent pass, blended in depth order with other transparent marks. Default: `False`.

#### Advanced renderer options

- `max_instances` (`number | null`): The most rows drawn; past it the rows are sampled (null draws them all), though SVG and PDF exports draw every row. Default: `None`.

### Usage

RuleX draws a vertical rule at `x` across the frame: at a constant or a time (a release date), at each row of a column (one rule per event), or at the pointer (`x="@pointer_x"`). By default it spans the frame's visible domain in y (`"@view_y_min"` to `"@view_y_max"`), so it reaches the frame's edges as the plot pans and zooms; `y0` and `y1` give other ends, numbers or columns.

The rule follows the frame's coordinates: a spoke in a polar frame, a meridian on a map or a globe. On a band axis, `x` is a category. Rules never widen automatic domains.

RuleX is a built-in template, built from transforms and simpler marks: import it from `hmplot/charts`.

> **SVG and PDF export**
>
> **Vector, except** in a 3D view that holds a mark with no vector form there (Points3D, Surface or another 3D mark, a Heatmap or Image, a lit or additive mark, a globe or polar frame): then SVG and PDF exports draw all of that view's marks as one image, and `mode="vector"` refuses it. In other 3D views the rules are vectors too, drawn back to front by depth (approximate where marks cross closely). `dash` and a `color` column stay vector. See [what is not exported as vector](/HMPlot/docs/export.md).

For Plotly users, this is the `add_vline` pattern. For a shaded interval, use [BandX](/HMPlot/reference/svelte/band-x.md) (the corresponding `add_vrect` pattern).

### Related examples

- [Crosshair and rules](/HMPlot/examples/crosshair.md)

## charts.RuleY

Page: /reference/python/rule-y.md

A horizontal reference line at y across the frame: one per row, or one at a value or the pointer.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"x": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], "y": [3, 4, 2, 5, 6, 5]}
with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True) as plot:
    hm.Line(x="x", y="y")
    hm.charts.RuleY(y=4)
plot
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Plot, Line } from "hmplot";
import { RuleY } from "hmplot/charts";
  const data = { x: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], y: [3, 4, 2, 5, 6, 5] };
</script>

<Plot {data} height={300} axes2d>
  <Line x="x" y="y" />
  <RuleY y={4} />
</Plot>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

#### Options

- `x0` (`channel`): Where the rule starts in x: a number or a column. Default: the left of the frame's visible domain.
- `x1` (`channel`): Where the rule ends in x: a number or a column. By default the rule spans the frame as it pans and zooms. Default: the right of the frame's visible domain.
- `dash` (`boolean | number | [number, number]`): Dash the rule: true (4 px dashes and gaps), a dash length (gaps as long), or [dash, gap], measured along the drawn rule. In px.
- `data` (`table`): A table for this mark alone: a mark with data displays on its own, in a Plot of its own.

#### Position

- `y` (`channel`): Where the rule stands: a number, a time or a category draws one rule, a column one per row, and "@pointer_y" follows the pointer.

#### Appearance

- `color` (`color`): The rule's color. Default: `"#8a949e"`. Default: the theme's rule gray.
- `width` (`number`): The rule's width. Default: `1` px. Default: 1.
- `opacity` (`number`): The rule's opacity, 0 to 1. Default: `1`.

#### Display

- `legend` (`boolean`): Whether the mark has a legend entry. Default: `False`.
- `visible` (`boolean`): Whether the rule is drawn. Default: `True`.
- `name` (`string`): The rule's name in the settings pane.

Also these options the marks share (described on Mark options): `label`, `blend`, `glow`, `shade`.

#### Interaction

- `identity` (`identity`): Whose rows these are for selections: an identity() shared by tables that show the same things. Default: its data's.
- `select` (`boolean | selection`): Click a rule to select its row: true uses its data's selection, or give a selection().
- `hover` (`boolean | selection`): Mark the rule under the pointer as @hovered, without fading the others: true uses its data's hover, or give a selection().
- `respond` (`boolean | "selected" | "brushed" | "hovered" | "nearby" | selection | array`): Which interaction states fade the rules outside them. Default: the states it sets, except hover.

#### Animation

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `animation`, `animation_duration`, `animation_easing`.

#### Legend settings

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `legend_font_size`, `legend_font_family`, `legend_text_color`, `legend_tick_format`.

#### Color settings

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `quantize`, `levels`.

#### Limits

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `max_elements`.

#### The mark's own axes

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `x_transform`, `x_invert`, `xbounds`, `xrange`, `y_transform`, `y_invert`, `ybounds`, `yrange`, `z_transform`, `z_invert`, `zbounds`, `zrange`.

#### Shading

- `transparent` (`boolean`, setting): Draw the mark in the transparent pass, blended in depth order with other transparent marks. Default: `False`.

#### Advanced renderer options

- `max_instances` (`number | null`): The most rows drawn; past it the rows are sampled (null draws them all), though SVG and PDF exports draw every row. Default: `None`.

### Usage

RuleY draws a horizontal rule at `y` across the frame: a threshold, one rule per row of a column, or the pointer (`y="@pointer_y"`). By default it spans the frame's visible domain in x; `x0` and `x1` give other ends, so `x1="@pointer_x"` draws a leader from the axis to the pointer.

The rule follows the frame's coordinates: a circle in a polar frame (an arc between `x0` and `x1`), a parallel on a map or a globe. Rules never widen automatic domains.

RuleY is a built-in template, built from transforms and simpler marks: import it from `hmplot/charts`.

> **SVG and PDF export**
>
> **Vector, except** in a 3D view that holds a mark with no vector form there (Points3D, Surface or another 3D mark, a Heatmap or Image, a lit or additive mark, a globe or polar frame): then SVG and PDF exports draw all of that view's marks as one image, and `mode="vector"` refuses it. In other 3D views the rules are vectors too, drawn back to front by depth (approximate where marks cross closely). `dash` and a `color` column stay vector. See [what is not exported as vector](/HMPlot/docs/export.md).

For Plotly users, this is the `add_hline` pattern. For a shaded interval, use [BandY](/HMPlot/reference/svelte/band-y.md) (the corresponding `add_hrect` pattern).

### Related examples

- [Crosshair and rules](/HMPlot/examples/crosshair.md)

## charts.Smooth

Page: /reference/python/smooth.md

A fitted curve through a scatter, with its confidence band.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"x": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8], "y": [2.1, 2.9, 3.2, 4.8, 4.9, 6.1, 6.8, 8.2]}
with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True) as plot:
    hm.Points(x="x", y="y")
    hm.charts.Smooth(x="x", y="y")
plot
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Plot, Points } from "hmplot";
import { Smooth } from "hmplot/charts";
  const data = { x: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8], y: [2.1, 2.9, 3.2, 4.8, 4.9, 6.1, 6.8, 8.2] };
</script>

<Plot {data} height={300} axes2d>
  <Points x="x" y="y" />
  <Smooth x="x" y="y" />
</Plot>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

#### Options

- `method` (`"linear" | "poly" | "log" | "exp" | "pow"`): The model: a line, a polynomial of degree order, y on ln x ("log"), ln y on x ("exp"), or ln y on ln x ("pow"). Default: `"linear"`.
- `order` (`number`): The polynomial's degree for method "poly", 1 to 6. Default: `2`.
- `samples` (`number`): How many points the curve is drawn through, evenly spaced across extent. Default: `100`.
- `extent` (`[number, number]`): The x range the curve spans. Default: the fitted rows' x range. In data units.
- `band` (`number | false`): The confidence level of the band around the fit, or false for no band. Default: `0.95`.
- `data` (`table`): A table for this mark alone: a mark with data displays on its own, in a Plot of its own.

#### Position

- `x` (`column`): The column along x: the fit is of y on x.
- `y` (`column`): The column fitted, along y.

Also these options the marks share (described on Mark options): `z`, `position`.

#### Appearance

- `fill` (`channel`): The confidence band's color. Default: `"#547ba2"`.
- `color` (`channel`): The fitted line's color. Default: `"#30343b"`.
- `width` (`channel`): The fitted line's width. Default: `2` px.
- `opacity` (`channel`): The confidence band's opacity, 0 to 1; the line stays opaque. Default: `0.25`.

Also these options the marks share (described on Mark options): `size`.

#### Scales

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `fill_scale`, `color_scale`, `colormap`, `size_scale`, `width_scale`, `opacity_scale`.

#### Display

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `label`, `legend`, `visible`, `domains`, `blend`, `glow`, `shade`, `options`, `name`.

#### Interaction

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `identity`, `select`, `hover`, `tooltip`, `nearest`, `respond`, `selection_opacity`, `enter_effect`, `exit_effect`.

#### Animation

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `animation`, `animation_duration`, `animation_easing`.

#### Legend settings

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `legend_font_size`, `legend_font_family`, `legend_text_color`, `legend_tick_format`.

#### Color settings

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `quantize`, `levels`.

#### Limits

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `max_elements`.

#### The mark's own axes

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `x_transform`, `x_invert`, `xbounds`, `xrange`, `y_transform`, `y_invert`, `ybounds`, `yrange`, `z_transform`, `z_invert`, `zbounds`, `zrange`.

#### Shading

- `transparent` (`boolean`, setting): Draw the mark in the transparent pass, blended in depth order with other transparent marks. Default: `False`.

#### Advanced renderer options

- `sampling` (`"random" | "uniform-x"`): Which rows a Line keeps when it has more than max_instances: a random sample, or the extremes across even steps of x. Default: `"random"`.
- `max_instances` (`number | null`): The most rows drawn; past it the rows are sampled (null draws them all), though SVG and PDF exports draw every row. Default: `None`.

### Usage

This mark has no separate outline channel. Use `color` and `width` for its line stroke.

Regression, then an Area for the band and a Line for the fit, as a Violin is a Density and an Area. `color` and `width` style the line, `fill` and `opacity` the band. Under `<Filter where="@brushed" inactive="all">` it fits the brushed rows, and all of them with no brush.

Place under Plot or a Frame with the scatter it summarizes. Fix the axes' domains when the fit may be refitted to few rows: its band widens, and automatic domains would follow it.

Smooth is a built-in template, built from transforms and simpler marks: import it from `hmplot/charts`.

### Related examples

- [A fitted curve that refits under a brush](/HMPlot/examples/smooth.md)

## charts.Swarm

Page: /reference/python/swarm.md

A beeswarm: points along a categorical axis, moved aside so none overlap.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {
    "group": ["A", "A", "A", "A", "A", "B", "B", "B", "B", "B", "C", "C", "C", "C", "C"],
    "value": [3.0, 3.1, 3.1, 3.2, 3.5, 4.1, 4.2, 4.2, 4.3, 4.8, 2.5, 2.6, 2.6, 2.7, 3.0],
}
with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True) as plot:
    hm.charts.Swarm(x="group", y="value")
plot
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Plot } from "hmplot";
import { Swarm } from "hmplot/charts";
  const data = {
    group: ["A", "A", "A", "A", "A", "B", "B", "B", "B", "B", "C", "C", "C", "C", "C"],
    value: [3.0, 3.1, 3.1, 3.2, 3.5, 4.1, 4.2, 4.2, 4.3, 4.8, 2.5, 2.6, 2.6, 2.7, 3.0],
  };
</script>

<Plot {data} height={300} axes2d>
  <Swarm x="group" y="value" />
</Plot>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

#### Options

- `orientation` (`"horizontal" | "vertical"`): A vertical swarm spreads its points sideways from categories on x; a horizontal one spreads them up and down from categories on y. Default: from which of x and y is categorical.
- `padding` (`number`): The gap kept between neighboring points. Default: `1` px.
- `seed` (`number`): The seed of the random order the points are placed in: another seed arranges the same points differently. Default: `42`.
- `data` (`table`): A table for this mark alone: a mark with data displays on its own, in a Plot of its own.

#### Position

- `x` (`column`): The categories along x for a vertical swarm, or the values for a horizontal one.
- `y` (`column`): The values for a vertical swarm, or the categories along y for a horizontal one.

Also these options the marks share (described on Mark options): `z`, `position`.

#### Appearance

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `fill`, `color`, `size`, `width`, `opacity`, `outline_color`, `outline_opacity`, `outline_width`.

#### Scales

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `fill_scale`, `color_scale`, `colormap`, `size_scale`, `width_scale`, `outline_color_scale`, `opacity_scale`.

#### Display

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `label`, `legend`, `visible`, `domains`, `blend`, `glow`, `shade`, `options`, `name`.

#### Interaction

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `identity`, `select`, `hover`, `tooltip`, `brush`, `nearby`, `nearest`, `respond`, `selection_opacity`, `drag`, `enter_effect`, `exit_effect`.

#### Animation

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `animation`, `animation_duration`, `animation_easing`.

#### Symbol rotation

- `rotation` (`number`): The symbol's rotation. Default: `0` degrees.

#### Symbol

- `shape` (`string | column | string[]`): The point symbol: a shape name, a column of categories mapped to shapes, or one name per row. Default: `"circle"`.
- `shape_scale` (`scale`): A categorical() scale from the shape column's categories to shape names.

#### Size units

- `size_units` (`"px" | "data"`): What size measures: CSS pixels whatever the zoom, or units of the x axis, so zooming scales the points. Default: `"px"`.

#### Legend settings

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `legend_font_size`, `legend_font_family`, `legend_text_color`, `legend_tick_format`.

#### Color settings

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `quantize`, `levels`.

#### Limits

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `max_elements`.

#### The mark's own axes

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `x_transform`, `x_invert`, `xbounds`, `xrange`, `y_transform`, `y_invert`, `ybounds`, `yrange`, `z_transform`, `z_invert`, `zbounds`, `zrange`.

#### Geometry

- `detail` (`number`, setting): How finely a point's or a surface's geometry is divided (sphere segments, grid cells).

#### Shading

- `lit` (`boolean`, setting): Shade the mark with the plot's lights. Default: `False`.
- `transparent` (`boolean`, setting): Draw the mark in the transparent pass, blended in depth order with other transparent marks. Default: `False`.

#### Advanced renderer options

- `max_instances` (`number | null`): The most rows drawn; past it the rows are sampled (null draws them all), though SVG and PDF exports draw every row. Default: `None`.

### Usage

The categorical axis determines displacement direction. Size is a point's diameter in CSS pixels; padding is the gap between glyphs. Uses Dodge and preserves original row identities. Screen-space collision layout is Cartesian 2D.

Swarm is a built-in template, built from transforms and simpler marks: import it from `hmplot/charts`.

### Related examples

- [Swarm plot](/HMPlot/examples/swarm.md)

## charts.Violin

Page: /reference/python/violin.md

Violin plots: each group's distribution as a mirrored density curve.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {
    "group": ["A", "A", "A", "A", "A", "B", "B", "B", "B", "B", "C", "C", "C", "C", "C"],
    "value": [2.1, 2.9, 3.4, 3.8, 5.2, 4.4, 5.1, 5.6, 6.3, 7.4, 3.1, 3.5, 3.9, 4.1, 4.6],
}
with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True) as plot:
    hm.charts.Violin(x="group", y="value")
plot
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Plot } from "hmplot";
import { Violin } from "hmplot/charts";
  const data = {
    group: ["A", "A", "A", "A", "A", "B", "B", "B", "B", "B", "C", "C", "C", "C", "C"],
    value: [2.1, 2.9, 3.4, 3.8, 5.2, 4.4, 5.1, 5.6, 6.3, 7.4, 3.1, 3.5, 3.9, 4.1, 4.6],
  };
</script>

<Plot {data} height={300} axes2d>
  <Violin x="group" y="value" />
</Plot>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

#### Options

- `orientation` (`"horizontal" | "vertical"`): Vertical violins stand on categories along x; horizontal violins sit on categories along y. Default: from which of x and y is categorical.
- `scale` (`"width" | "count" | "area"`): How the violins' sizes compare: equally wide ("width"), equal in area ("area"), or with areas in proportion to their groups' rows ("count"). Default: `"width"`.
- `side` (`"left" | "right" | "both"`): Draw the density on both sides of its category, or on one side only (a half violin). Default: `"both"`.
- `bandwidth` (`number | "auto"`): The width of the Gaussian kernel; "auto" picks it by Scott's rule. Default: `"auto"`. In data units.
- `resolution` (`number`): How many points along the measurement axis the density is evaluated at. Default: `256`.
- `band_fraction` (`number`): The share of its category's band each violin may fill, 0 to 1; on a numeric axis, a width in data units. Default: `0.8`.
- `data` (`table`): A table for this mark alone: a mark with data displays on its own, in a Plot of its own.

#### Position

- `x` (`channel`): The groups along x, a violin each, or the measurements for horizontal violins.
- `y` (`channel`): The measurements for vertical violins, or the groups along y for horizontal ones.

Also these options the marks share (described on Mark options): `z`, `position`.

#### Appearance

- `fill` (`channel`): The fill color: a CSS color, or a column of numbers or categories mapped to colors. Default: `"#547ba2"`.
- `opacity` (`channel`): The opacity, 0 to 1: a number, or a column (categories map through opacity_scale). Default: `0.35`.
- `outline_color` (`channel`): The outline's color: a CSS color, or a column of categories mapped through outline_color_scale. Default: `"#30343b"`.
- `outline_width` (`channel`): The outline's width in CSS pixels, drawn inside the mark's edge (a point's at most its radius). Default: `1` px.

Also these options the marks share (described on Mark options): `color`, `size`, `outline_opacity`.

#### Scales

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `fill_scale`, `color_scale`, `colormap`, `size_scale`, `outline_color_scale`, `opacity_scale`.

#### Display

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `label`, `legend`, `visible`, `domains`, `blend`, `glow`, `shade`, `options`, `name`.

#### Interaction

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `identity`, `select`, `hover`, `tooltip`, `nearest`, `respond`, `selection_opacity`, `enter_effect`, `exit_effect`.

#### Animation

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `animation`, `animation_duration`, `animation_easing`.

#### Legend settings

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `legend_font_size`, `legend_font_family`, `legend_text_color`, `legend_tick_format`.

#### Color settings

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `quantize`, `levels`.

#### Limits

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `max_elements`.

#### The mark's own axes

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `x_transform`, `x_invert`, `xbounds`, `xrange`, `y_transform`, `y_invert`, `ybounds`, `yrange`, `z_transform`, `z_invert`, `zbounds`, `zrange`.

#### Geometry

- `detail` (`number`, setting): How finely a point's or a surface's geometry is divided (sphere segments, grid cells).

#### Shading

- `lit` (`boolean`, setting): Shade the mark with the plot's lights. Default: `False`.
- `transparent` (`boolean`, setting): Draw the mark in the transparent pass, blended in depth order with other transparent marks. Default: `False`.

#### Advanced renderer options

- `max_instances` (`number | null`): The most rows drawn; past it the rows are sampled (null draws them all), though SVG and PDF exports draw every row. Default: `None`.

### Usage

Uses grouped Density. Default scale=width gives groups equal maximum width; area and count change normalization. Supports orientation, side, bandwidth, resolution, fill, and outline. Picking identifies the observation group.

Violin is a built-in template, built from transforms and simpler marks: import it from `hmplot/charts`.

> **SVG and PDF export**
>
> **Vector, except** in a 3D view that holds a mark with no vector form there (Points3D, Surface or another 3D mark, a Heatmap or Image, a lit or additive mark, a globe or polar frame): then SVG and PDF exports draw all of that view's marks as one image, and `mode="vector"` refuses it. In other 3D views the violins are vectors too, drawn back to front by depth (approximate where marks cross closely). A `fill` column stays vector. See [what is not exported as vector](/HMPlot/docs/export.md).

### Related examples

- [Violin plot](/HMPlot/examples/violin.md)

## charts.BandX

Page: /reference/python/band-x.md

A vertical shaded reference interval spanning the visible frame.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"x": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], "y": [3, 4, 2, 5, 6, 5]}
with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True) as plot:
    hm.charts.BandX(x0=2, x1=4, fill="#3478c7")
    hm.Line(x="x", y="y")
plot
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Plot, Line } from "hmplot";
  import { BandX } from "hmplot/charts";
  const data = { x: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], y: [3, 4, 2, 5, 6, 5] };
</script>

<Plot {data} height={300} axes2d>
  <BandX x0={2} x1={4} fill="#3478c7" />
  <Line x="x" y="y" />
</Plot>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

#### Options

- `x0` (`channel`): The interval's starting x coordinate: a number, date or column.
- `x1` (`channel`): The interval's ending x coordinate: a number, date or column.
- `data` (`table`): A table for this band alone.

#### Appearance

- `opacity` (`number`): The band's opacity, 0 to 1. Default: `0.15`.

Also these options the marks share (described on Mark options): `fill`, `outline_color`, `outline_opacity`, `outline_width`.

#### Scales

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `fill_scale`, `outline_color_scale`, `opacity_scale`.

#### Display

- `legend` (`boolean`): Include the band in a legend. Default: `False`.

Also these options the marks share (described on Mark options): `label`, `visible`, `blend`, `glow`, `shade`, `options`, `name`.

#### Interaction

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `identity`, `select`, `hover`, `tooltip`, `nearest`, `respond`, `selection_opacity`, `enter_effect`, `exit_effect`.

#### Animation

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `animation`, `animation_duration`, `animation_easing`.

#### Legend settings

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `legend_font_size`, `legend_font_family`, `legend_text_color`, `legend_tick_format`.

#### Color settings

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `quantize`, `levels`.

#### Limits

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `max_elements`.

#### The mark's own axes

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `x_transform`, `x_invert`, `xbounds`, `xrange`, `y_transform`, `y_invert`, `ybounds`, `yrange`, `z_transform`, `z_invert`, `zbounds`, `zrange`.

#### Shading

- `transparent` (`boolean`, setting): Draw the mark in the transparent pass, blended in depth order with other transparent marks. Default: `False`.

#### Advanced renderer options

- `max_instances` (`number | null`): The most rows drawn; past it the rows are sampled (null draws them all), though SVG and PDF exports draw every row. Default: `None`.

<!-- Generated by scripts/generate-python-signatures.mjs from src/lib/charts/bandX.js; do not edit. -->
### Usage

Use `BandX(x0=2, x1=4, fill="#3478c7")` in Python, or `<BandX x0={2} x1={4} fill="#3478c7" />` from `hmplot/charts`. Bounds are data coordinates (numbers, dates or column names). Constant bounds draw one band; columns draw one per row. The other dimension follows the frame's visible domain as it pans and zooms. Bands do not widen automatic domains and have no legend entry unless `legend=True` is set. Use `fill`, `opacity` and Rect's outline styling; compose Text or Callout for an annotation (`label` is the legend/settings label). Place a band before foreground marks. This is Plotly's `add_vrect` pattern; `RuleX(x=...)` and `RuleY(y=...)` cover `add_vline` and `add_hline`. For a rectangle bounded in both dimensions, use Rect. These are frame-coordinate bands, not screen overlays; in non-Cartesian frames they follow Rect's coordinate mapping.

BandX is a chart: a template over public components, defined in one file, src/lib/charts/bandX.js.

## charts.BulletChart

Page: /reference/python/bullet-chart.md

Actual values, target ticks and supplied qualitative ranges on categorical rows.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"metric": ["Revenue", "Renewals"], "actual": [65, 82], "goal": [80, 90],
        "poor": [50, 60], "fair": [70, 80], "good": [100, 100]}
with hm.Plot(data=data, height=250, axes2d=True, x={"label": "Percent of plan"}) as plot:
    hm.charts.BulletChart(x="actual", y="metric", target="goal", fields=["poor", "fair", "good"],
                          tick={"fill": "#20252b"})

```

```svelte

    poor: [50, 60], fair: [70, 80], good: [100, 100] };
</script>

  <BulletChart x="actual" y="metric" target="goal" fields={["poor", "fair", "good"]}
    tick={{ fill: "#20252b" }} />
</Plot>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

#### Options

- `target` (`channel`): Optional target value for each bullet.
- `fields` (`column[]`): Columns of cumulative qualitative upper bounds, all at or above baseline.
- `baseline` (`number`): The common starting value for actual and range bars. Default: `0`.
- `band_fraction` (`number`): The share of a category band occupied by the actual bar. Default: `0.3`.
- `ranges` (`object`): Props of the background Bar part, such as fill, fill_scale and opacity.
- `tick` (`object`): Props of the target Prism part, such as fill, width and depth.
- `data` (`table`): A table for this chart alone.

#### Position

- `x` (`channel`): The actual value for each bullet.
- `y` (`channel`): Each bullet's category along y.

#### Appearance

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `fill`, `opacity`, `outline_color`, `outline_opacity`, `outline_width`.

#### Scales

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `fill_scale`, `outline_color_scale`, `opacity_scale`.

#### Display

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `label`, `legend`, `visible`, `domains`, `blend`, `glow`, `shade`, `options`, `name`.

#### Interaction

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `identity`, `select`, `hover`, `tooltip`, `nearest`, `respond`, `selection_opacity`, `enter_effect`, `exit_effect`.

#### Animation

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `animation`, `animation_duration`, `animation_easing`.

#### Legend settings

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `legend_font_size`, `legend_font_family`, `legend_text_color`, `legend_tick_format`.

#### Color settings

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `quantize`, `levels`.

#### Limits

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `max_elements`.

#### The mark's own axes

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `x_transform`, `x_invert`, `xbounds`, `xrange`, `y_transform`, `y_invert`, `ybounds`, `yrange`, `z_transform`, `z_invert`, `zbounds`, `zrange`.

#### Shading

- `transparent` (`boolean`, setting): Draw the mark in the transparent pass, blended in depth order with other transparent marks. Default: `False`.

<!-- Generated by scripts/generate-python-signatures.mjs from src/lib/charts/bulletChart.js; do not edit. -->
### Usage

Each row supplies actual `x`, category `y`, and optionally `target`. `fields` is a list of columns containing qualitative upper bounds, such as `["poor", "fair", "good"]`; omit it to omit the ranges. Bounds must be at or above `baseline` and describe cumulative ranges from it. Fold and Sort draw the largest background bar first, with alpha layering distinguishing the smaller ranges; bounds need not be passed in order. Missing bounds are not drawn. Main-part props style the actual horizontal Bar; `ranges={...}` styles its background Bars and `tick={...}` styles the target Prism. The tick is 0.6 category bands high and 0.4% of the visible x span wide; its width/depth can be overridden in the tick part, in data units. Values and bounds are supplied, never estimated. Keep one row per bullet; repeated categories overlap. Use Plot for axis/domain settings.

BulletChart is a chart: a template over public components, defined in one file, src/lib/charts/bulletChart.js.

## charts.Candlestick

Page: /reference/python/candlestick.md

Prices over time as candles: a wick from each period's low to its high, and a body from its open to its close.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {
    "day": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8],
    "open": [100, 103, 101, 106, 104, 108, 107, 111],
    "high": [105, 106, 107, 109, 110, 112, 113, 114],
    "low": [98, 99, 100, 102, 101, 105, 104, 108],
    "close": [103, 101, 106, 104, 108, 107, 111, 113],
}
with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True) as plot:
    hm.charts.Candlestick(x="day", open="open", high="high", low="low", close="close")
    hm.Legend()
plot
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Plot, Legend } from "hmplot";
  import { Candlestick } from "hmplot/charts";
  const data = {
    day: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8],
    open: [100, 103, 101, 106, 104, 108, 107, 111],
    high: [105, 106, 107, 109, 110, 112, 113, 114],
    low: [98, 99, 100, 102, 101, 105, 104, 108],
    close: [103, 101, 106, 104, 108, 107, 111, 113],
  };
</script>

<Plot {data} height={300} axes2d>
  <Candlestick x="day" open="open" high="high" low="low" close="close" />
  <Legend />
</Plot>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

#### Options

- `data` (`table`): A table for this mark alone: a mark with data displays on its own, in a Plot of its own.
- `open` (`column`): The column of each period's opening price.
- `high` (`column`): The column of each period's highest price.
- `low` (`column`): The column of each period's lowest price.
- `close` (`column`): The column of each period's closing price.
- `band_fraction` (`number`): The share of its period's band each body fills, 0 to 1; on a numeric or date axis, the body's width in the axis's units (milliseconds for dates). Default: `0.7`.
- `wick` (`object`): The wicks' own props, as one object: {color: "black", width: 2}. They are a Segments, gray and 1 px wide by default.

#### Position

- `x` (`column`): The column of the periods along x, one candle each.

#### Appearance

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `fill`, `opacity`, `outline_color`, `outline_opacity`, `outline_width`.

#### Scales

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `fill_scale`, `outline_color_scale`, `opacity_scale`.

#### Display

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `label`, `legend`, `visible`, `domains`, `blend`, `glow`, `shade`, `options`, `name`.

#### Interaction

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `identity`, `select`, `hover`, `tooltip`, `nearest`, `respond`, `selection_opacity`, `enter_effect`, `exit_effect`.

#### Animation

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `animation`, `animation_duration`, `animation_easing`.

#### Legend settings

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `legend_font_size`, `legend_font_family`, `legend_text_color`, `legend_tick_format`.

#### Color settings

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `quantize`, `levels`.

#### Limits

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `max_elements`.

#### The mark's own axes

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `x_transform`, `x_invert`, `xbounds`, `xrange`, `y_transform`, `y_invert`, `ybounds`, `yrange`, `z_transform`, `z_invert`, `zbounds`, `zrange`.

#### Shading

- `transparent` (`boolean`, setting): Draw the mark in the transparent pass, blended in depth order with other transparent marks. Default: `False`.

<!-- Generated by scripts/generate-python-signatures.mjs from src/lib/charts/candlestick.js; do not edit. -->
### Usage

Each row is one period: its `x` (a number, a date or a category) and its `open`, `high`, `low` and `close` columns. On a numeric or date axis a body's width is `bandFraction` in the axis's units: for daily dates, milliseconds, so `bandFraction={0.7 * 86400000}`. The body is filled by direction, so a Legend names the rising and falling periods, and `fillScale` picks their colors.

Candlestick is a chart: a template over public components, defined in one file, src/lib/charts/candlestick.js.

## charts.EndLabels

Page: /reference/python/end-labels.md

Labels at the ends of lines: each series' name or value beside its last (or first) point.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"year": [2019, 2020, 2021, 2022] * 3,
        "index": [100, 104, 111, 118, 100, 97, 103, 109, 100, 101, 99, 102],
        "fund": ["Growth"] * 4 + ["Value"] * 4 + ["Bonds"] * 4}
colors = hm.categorical(domain=["Growth", "Value", "Bonds"], range=["#3477b4", "#df7253", "#52997a"])
with hm.Plot(data=data, height=260, legend=False) as plot:
    hm.Line(x="year", y="index", series="fund", color="fund", color_scale=colors)
    hm.charts.EndLabels(x="year", y="index", series="fund", color="fund", color_scale=colors)
plot
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Plot, Line, categorical } from "hmplot";
  import { EndLabels } from "hmplot/charts";
  const data = {
    year: [2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022],
    index: [100, 104, 111, 118, 100, 97, 103, 109, 100, 101, 99, 102],
    fund: ["Growth", "Growth", "Growth", "Growth", "Value", "Value", "Value", "Value", "Bonds", "Bonds", "Bonds", "Bonds"],
  };
  const colors = categorical({ domain: ["Growth", "Value", "Bonds"], range: ["#3477b4", "#df7253", "#52997a"] });
</script>

<Plot {data} height={260} legend={false}>
  <Line x="year" y="index" series="fund" color="fund" colorScale={colors} />
  <EndLabels x="year" y="index" series="fund" color="fund" colorScale={colors} />
</Plot>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

#### Options

- `series` (`column`): The column naming each line, as the Line's series; without it, one label at the data's end.
- `text` (`channel`): What each label says: a column (numbers are written as Text writes them) or a literal. Default: the series' name.
- `format` (`string`): How numbers in the text are written: a d3-format string (",.0f", ".1%"), or a %-pattern for dates.
- `at` (`"last" | "first"`): Which end of each series is labelled. Default: `"last"`.
- `dx` (`number`): How far right of its point each label starts (left of it when negative; at the first end, its default is -6 and the label ends there). Default: 6 at the last end, -6 at the first. In px.
- `data` (`table`): A table for this mark alone.

#### Position

- `x` (`channel`): The line's x: the label sits beside the end point's.
- `y` (`channel`): The line's y.

#### Appearance

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `color`, `size`, `width`, `opacity`, `outline_color`, `outline_opacity`, `outline_width`.

#### Scales

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `color_scale`, `colormap`, `size_scale`, `width_scale`, `outline_color_scale`, `opacity_scale`.

#### Display

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `label`, `legend`, `visible`, `domains`, `blend`, `glow`, `shade`, `options`, `name`.

#### Interaction

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `identity`, `select`, `hover`, `tooltip`, `nearest`, `respond`, `selection_opacity`, `enter_effect`, `exit_effect`.

#### Animation

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `animation`, `animation_duration`, `animation_easing`.

#### Legend settings

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `legend_font_size`, `legend_font_family`, `legend_text_color`, `legend_tick_format`.

#### Color settings

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `quantize`, `levels`.

#### Limits

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `max_elements`.

#### The mark's own axes

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `x_transform`, `x_invert`, `xbounds`, `xrange`, `y_transform`, `y_invert`, `ybounds`, `yrange`, `z_transform`, `z_invert`, `zbounds`, `zrange`.

#### Shading

- `transparent` (`boolean`, setting): Draw the mark in the transparent pass, blended in depth order with other transparent marks. Default: `False`.

<!-- Generated by scripts/generate-python-signatures.mjs from src/lib/charts/endLabels.js; do not edit. -->
### Usage

Draw it beside the Line it labels, with the same `x`, `y` and `series`: each series gets one label at its last row with finite x and y (`at="first"` for its first), in current input order after any enclosing Filter or Sort. The label is the series' name by default; `text` takes a column instead, such as the y values (numbers are written as Text writes them, or in `format`). Give `color` the Line's color column and color scale so each label matches its line. The labels sit `dx` pixels beside their points; in the plot's own frame the room they need is a pixel inset of the plot area, so they never widen the axis or misalign linked plots. Labels of series that end close together are spread apart along y, each by the least that clears its neighbours, again as the view moves.

EndLabels is a chart: a template over public components, defined in one file, src/lib/charts/endLabels.js.

## charts.ForestPlot

Page: /reference/python/forest-plot.md

Point estimates with horizontal confidence intervals on categorical rows.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"study": ["Trial A", "Trial B", "Trial C"], "estimate": [0.8, 1.1, 1.3],
        "low": [0.6, 0.9, 1.0], "high": [1.0, 1.4, 1.6]}
with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True, x={"label": "Risk ratio"}) as plot:
    hm.charts.ForestPlot(x="estimate", y="study", lower="low", upper="high", reference=1,
                         interval={"color": "#5b6470", "cap_size": 8})
plot
```

```svelte

  import { ForestPlot } from "hmplot/charts";

    low: [0.6, 0.9, 1.0], high: [1.0, 1.4, 1.6] };
</script>
```

- `reference_line` (`object`): Props of the optional RuleX part, such as color and width.

#### Position

- `y` (`channel`): Each estimate's category along y.

#### Interaction

#### Animation

#### Limits

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `max_elements`.

#### The mark's own axes

These options the marks share (described on Mark options): `x_transform`, `x_invert`, `xbounds`, `xrange`, `y_transform`, `y_invert`, `ybounds`, `yrange`, `z_transform`, `z_invert`, `zbounds`, `zrange`.

#### Geometry

- `detail` (`number`, setting): How finely a point's or a surface's geometry is divided (sphere segments, grid cells).

#### Shading

- `transparent` (`boolean`, setting): Draw the mark in the transparent pass, blended in depth order with other transparent marks. Default: `False`.

<!-- Generated by scripts/generate-python-signatures.mjs from src/lib/charts/forestPlot.js; do not edit. -->
### Usage

Supply one row per estimate: `x` is the estimate, `y` the category, and `lower`/`upper` are absolute interval endpoints, not error distances. Intervals with missing or reversed bounds are omitted by ErrorBars; the estimate remains a point. `reference` optionally draws a RuleX (for example 0 for differences, 1 for ratios); it does not expand automatic domains. Points is the main part (`getMark()`), and accepts ordinary point props. Style the supporting parts with `interval={color: ..., capSize: ...}` and `referenceLine={color: ..., width: ...}` (Python `reference_line`). All values are supplied; this template computes no confidence intervals. Use Plot's x settings for log axes, titles and domain limits.

ForestPlot is a chart: a template over public components, defined in one file, src/lib/charts/forestPlot.js.

### Usage

Each row supplies task category `y`, start `x0` and end `x1`, in numeric units or datetime columns. The main part is a flat Prism spanning those endpoints, with overlapping intervals rather than stacking; use distinct categories for separate lanes. Equal endpoints have zero area. Reversed endpoints still span their two values; the template does not validate schedules. `milestone` optionally supplies one point per task (missing values omit that point); `milestones={...}` styles the Points part, diamond-shaped by default. Main-part props style the interval Prism. Dates preserve their time metadata; set the host Plot's x type to datetime and its origin to the first start for a time axis (as the paired example does). No scheduling or lane-allocation algorithm runs.

## stats.Bin

Page: /reference/python/bin.md

Counts the rows in each interval of x (a histogram), or in each cell of an x-y or x-y-z grid.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"value": [1.2, 2.5, 2.9, 3.1, 3.4, 3.8, 4.2, 4.4, 5.1, 6.3]}
with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True) as plot:
    with hm.stats.Bin(x="value", bins=5):
        hm.Rect(x0="x0", x1="x1", y0=0, y1="count")
plot
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Plot, Rect } from "hmplot";
import { Bin } from "hmplot/stats";
  const data = { value: [1.2, 2.5, 2.9, 3.1, 3.4, 3.8, 4.2, 4.4, 5.1, 6.3] };
</script>

<Plot {data} height={300} axes2d>
  <Bin x="value" bins={5}>
    <Rect x0="x0" x1="x1" y0={0} y1="count" />
  </Bin>
</Plot>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

- `name` (`string`): Names the transform, so a Facet's getTransform(name) reaches its copy in every cell.
- `x` (`channel`): The values to bin along x; each bin's row gets x0 and x1 (its edges) and x (its center).
- `y` (`channel`): The values to bin along y, for a 2D grid of bins; each bin gets y0, y1 and y.
- `z` (`channel`): The values to bin along z, for a 3D grid of bins; each bin gets z0, z1 and z.
- `bins` (`number | expression | number[] | "auto" | "sturges" | "fd" | "scott" | {x, y, z}`): How many equal-width bins span the data, the edges themselves (Dates on a datetime axis), a rule that picks the count as numpy does, or an expression such as `power(count(col.x), 0.5)`; {x, y, z} sets each axis. Default: `30`.
- `interval` (`string | {x, y, z}`): For a datetime column, the calendar interval each bin spans, such as "1 month", "1 week" or "6 hours" (weeks start on Sunday); {x, y, z} sets each axis. Default: the interval axis ticks would use for `bins` bins.
- `tz` (`string | {x, y, z}`): The time zone of a datetime column's calendar bins: an IANA name, "UTC" or "Local"; {x, y, z} sets each axis. Default: the column's own, else UTC.
- `mode` (`"aggregate" | "assign"`): "aggregate" gives one row per bin, with its count; "assign" keeps the input rows and adds each row's bin: binX (its index), binX0 and binX1 (its edges), and likewise for y and z. Default: `"aggregate"`.
- `shared_bins` (`boolean`): In a Facet, gives every cell the same edges, with a rule or expression resolved over all the cells' rows; false bins each cell on its own. Default: `True`.
- `empty` (`boolean`): Show the bins no row falls in; false hides them. Default: `True`.
- `normalization` (`"count" | "proportion" | "density"`): Gives a histogram's bars, binning x alone (or y alone): each bin also gets y0 (0), y1 and y (x0, x1 and x for bins along y) holding its rows' count, their share of all the rows ("proportion"), or that share divided by the bin's width ("density"), so one Rect x0="x0" x1="x1" y0="y0" y1="y1" draws either orientation.
- `columns` (`{[name]: expression}`): Columns to compute over each bin's rows besides count, each a reduction expression as in Calculate: {mean_y: mean("y")}, Python {"mean_y": hm.mean("y")}. Every reduction reduces the bin's visible rows; an empty bin's column is missing.
- `as_` (`{[column]: string}`): New names for the output columns, such as {count: "n", x0: "left"}.
- `weight` (`column`): A column, or one number per row, that scales each row's contribution to count(), sum(x) and mean(x) columns (other columns leave out rows of weight 0; with a column weight, a sum, mean or count inside a larger expression is an error). An interaction column such as "@brushed" counts only those rows, and every row while there are none.

### Usage

Outputs centers, lower/upper bounds per dimension, count, and `columns`: reduction expressions as in Group (`columns={{ mean_y: mean("y") }}`), missing for an empty bin. Defaults to 30 bins; bins may instead supply explicit edges. Aggregate mode includes empty rectangular bins; assign mode keeps original rows. Bins are half-open except for the last upper boundary.

For a histogram over x alone (or y alone), `normalization` gives each bin its bar along the other axis: `y0` (0), `y1` and `y` hold its count (`"count"`), its share of all the rows (`"proportion"`), or that share divided by the bin's width (`"density"`); binning y gives `x0`, `x1` and `x` instead. So `<Rect x0="x0" x1="x1" y0="y0" y1="y1" />` draws the bars either way round, as [Histogram](histogram) does.

`bins` also takes a rule name — `"auto"`, `"sturges"`, `"fd"`, or `"scott"`, computed from the data exactly as numpy does — or an expression evaluated against this transform's input, such as `power(count(col.x), 0.5)`. Either way the count is resolved before binning, and re-resolved whenever the data changes. Changing a bin count changes the number of rows, so marks snap to the new bins rather than animating between them.

Inside a Facet, bins are shared across the cells by default, so a rule name or an expression is resolved once over the rows of every cell together and each cell gets the same edges. Set `sharedBins={false}` to resolve the count per cell, against that cell's rows.

To let the viewer change a setting, read an input in it: `bins={input("bins")}` (Python `bins=hm.input.bins`), where `bins` is a [Slider](slider).

### Related examples

- [Histogram bins](/HMPlot/examples/histograms.md)

## stats.Normalize

Page: /reference/python/normalize.md

Rescales a column to z-scores, to 0 to 1, or relative to its sum, first value or maximum, over all rows or per group.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {
    "day": [1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 3, 4],
    "stock": ["A", "A", "A", "A", "B", "B", "B", "B"],
    "price": [10, 12, 11, 14, 50, 52, 57, 60],
}
with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True) as plot:
    with hm.stats.Normalize(field="price", method="first", by="stock"):
        hm.Line(x="day", y="normalized", series="stock")
plot
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Plot, Line } from "hmplot";
import { Normalize } from "hmplot/stats";
  const data = {
    day: [1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 3, 4],
    stock: ["A", "A", "A", "A", "B", "B", "B", "B"],
    price: [10, 12, 11, 14, 50, 52, 57, 60],
  };
</script>

<Plot {data} height={300} axes2d>
  <Normalize field="price" method="first" by="stock">
    <Line x="day" y="normalized" series="stock" />
  </Normalize>
</Plot>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

- `name` (`string`): Names the transform, so a Facet's getTransform(name) reaches its copy in every cell.
- `field` (`column`): The numeric column to normalize.
- `method` (`"deviation" | "extent" | "sum" | "first" | "max"`): "deviation" gives z-scores (0 for a constant column), "extent" maps the minimum to 0 and the maximum to 1, and "sum", "first" and "max" divide by the column's sum, first value or maximum. Default: `"deviation"`.
- `by` (`column | column[]`): Normalize within each group of these columns instead of over all the rows.
- `as_` (`string`): The name of the normalized column it adds. Default: `"normalized"`.

### Usage

Retains source columns and adds the as column. Methods are deviation (default), extent, sum, first, and max. by sets groups. Constant-feature deviation normalization produces zero.

To let the viewer change a setting, read an input in it: `method={input("method")}` (Python `method=hm.input.method`), where `method` is a [Select](select) of methods.

This is a template over [Calculate](calculate), not a separate normalization kernel. The
`deviation` method expands to `(field - mean(field)) / where(std(field) > 0, std(field), 1)`;
`extent` uses the minimum and maximum, and `sum`, `first`, and `max` divide by that reduction.
Reductions ignore hidden and nonfinite values. With `by`, the runner prepares the grouping keys
once for the expression, including numeric keys. The caller's children read the resulting column.

### Related examples

- [Signal and uncertainty](/HMPlot/examples/layered-signal.md)

## stats.Window

Page: /reference/python/window.md

A moving average (or other reduction) over each row and its neighbors.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"x": [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8], "y": [2, 5, 3, 6, 4, 7, 5, 8]}
with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True) as plot:
    with hm.stats.Window(field="y", size=3):
        hm.Line(x="x", y="smoothed")
plot
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Plot, Line } from "hmplot";
import { Window } from "hmplot/stats";
  const data = { x: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8], y: [2, 5, 3, 6, 4, 7, 5, 8] };
</script>

<Plot {data} height={300} axes2d>
  <Window field="y" size={3}>
    <Line x="x" y="smoothed" />
  </Window>
</Plot>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

- `name` (`string`): Names the transform, so a Facet's getTransform(name) reaches its copy in every cell.
- `field` (`column`): The numeric column to reduce; windows run over the rows in their order, so Sort them first if they are not.
- `size` (`number | expression`): How many rows each window spans; windows at the ends use the rows there are. Default: `5` rows.
- `reduce` (`"mean" | "sum" | "count" | "min" | "max" | "first" | "last" | "variance" | "std" | "any" | "all"`): What to compute over each window. Default: `"mean"`.
- `align` (`"trailing" | "center" | "leading"`): Where each row sits in its window: at its end (the row and the ones before it), in its middle, or at its start. Default: `"trailing"`.
- `by` (`column | column[]`): Window each group of these columns separately.
- `as_` (`string`): The name of the column it adds. Default: `"smoothed"`.

### Usage

Adds a derived column without sorting observations. Defaults to a trailing mean over five observations. align supports trailing, center, or leading; by separates groups. Sort explicitly before Window when time order is required.

To let the viewer change a setting, read an input in it: `size={input("size")}` (Python `size=hm.input.size`), where `size` is a [Slider](slider).

`any` and `all` reduce logical booleans or finite numeric truth values; empty/all-missing windows
yield false and true respectively. The `window(value, {size, reduce, align, by, orderBy})`
expression uses the same kernels and restores results to original rows after local ordering.
Python uses `hm.window(value, size=..., order_by=...)`. See [Reductions](reductions).

This template expands to [Calculate](calculate) with
`columns={smoothed: window(field, {size, reduce, align, by})}` (using the name passed as `as`).
It reuses the window expression's kernels and the ordinary transform lifecycle, including input
controls, status subscriptions, updates, and error recovery.

### Related examples

- [Signal and uncertainty](/HMPlot/examples/layered-signal.md)

## stats.Hexbin

Page: /reference/python/hexbin.md

Counts the points in each hexagon of a hexagonal grid over x and y.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {
    "x": [1, 1.4, 2, 2.2, 2.5, 2.7, 3, 3.1, 3.5, 4, 4.2, 5],
    "y": [2, 2.6, 3, 2.8, 3.2, 3.1, 3, 3.5, 2.9, 4, 3.8, 4.5],
}
with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True, aspect="equal") as plot:
    with hm.stats.Hexbin(x="x", y="y", bins=4):
        hm.Prism(x="x", y="y", width="width", depth="depth", rotation="rotation", shape="hexagon",
                 z0=0, z1=0, fill="count")
plot
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Plot, Prism } from "hmplot";
import { Hexbin } from "hmplot/stats";
  const data = {
    x: [1, 1.4, 2, 2.2, 2.5, 2.7, 3, 3.1, 3.5, 4, 4.2, 5],
    y: [2, 2.6, 3, 2.8, 3.2, 3.1, 3, 3.5, 2.9, 4, 3.8, 4.5],
  };
</script>

<Plot {data} height={300} axes2d aspect="equal">
  <Hexbin x="x" y="y" bins={4}>
    <Prism x="x" y="y" width="width" depth="depth" rotation="rotation" shape="hexagon"
      z0={0} z1={0} fill="count" />
  </Hexbin>
</Plot>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

- `name` (`string`): Names the transform, so a Facet's getTransform(name) reaches its copy in every cell.
- `x` (`channel`): The x values to bin; each hexagon's row gets x, its center's x.
- `y` (`channel`): The y values to bin; each hexagon's row gets y, its center's y.
- `bins` (`number | expression`): How many hexagons span the x extent (or the x of `bounds`). Default: `30`.
- `radius` (`number | expression`): The hexagons' radius, instead of the one bins gives. Each row's width and depth columns give a Prism with shape="hexagon" this size. Default: from bins. In data units.
- `bounds` (`{x, y}`): A fixed grid: the hexagons covering these x and y ranges, one row per hexagon with the occupied ones shown, so filtering the input never changes the output's length. Points outside fall in no hexagon. In data units.
- `orientation` (`"pointy" | "flat"`): Whether the hexagons point up or have flat tops; each row's rotation column (30 or 0 degrees) turns a Prism's hexagon to match. Default: `"pointy"`.
- `shared_bins` (`boolean`): In a Facet, gives every cell the same hexagon grid; false sizes each cell's grid from its own rows. Default: `True`.
- `columns` (`{[name]: expression}`): Columns to compute over each hexagon's rows besides count, each a reduction expression as in Calculate: {mean_v: mean("v")}, Python {"mean_v": hm.mean("v")}. With bounds, a count, sum or mean of a column keeps the fixed grid; any other column groups the hexagons.
- `as_` (`{[column]: string}`): New names for the output columns, such as {count: "n"}.

### Usage

Outputs occupied-cell centers, width, depth, rotation, count, and `columns`: reduction expressions as in Group (`columns={{ mean_v: mean("v") }}`). Defaults to 30 cells across X and pointy orientation. radius chooses an explicit cell radius. Facets share the lattice unless sharedBins is false.

The cells are regular hexagons in data units: a Plot that fills its box scales x and y independently and stretches them. Give the Plot `aspect="equal"` (as the example does) when the cells should look regular, with one data unit as long on x as on y.

To let the viewer change a setting, read an input in it: `bins={input("bins")}` (Python `bins=hm.input.bins`), where `bins` is a [Slider](slider).

### Related examples

- [Facets & transforms](/HMPlot/examples/facets.md)

## stats.Summary

Page: /reference/python/summary.md

An estimate per group, the mean or median, with an interval around it: the numbers behind error bars.

### Example

```python
import hmplot as hm

data = {"group": ["a", "a", "a", "b", "b", "b"], "value": [1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 5]}
with hm.Plot(data=data, height=300, axes2d=True) as plot:
    with hm.stats.Summary(field="value", by="group", interval="standard-error"):
        hm.charts.ErrorBars(x="group", y="estimate", lower="lower", upper="upper")
plot
```

```svelte
<script>
  import { Plot } from "hmplot";
import { Summary } from "hmplot/stats";
import { ErrorBars } from "hmplot/charts";
  const data = { group: ["a", "a", "a", "b", "b", "b"], value: [1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 5] };
</script>

<Plot {data} height={300} axes2d>
  <Summary field="value" by="group" interval="standard-error">
    <ErrorBars x="group" y="estimate" lower="lower" upper="upper" />
  </Summary>
</Plot>
```

### Options

Keywords are snake_case.

- `name` (`string`): Names the transform, so a Facet's getTransform(name) reaches its copy in every cell.
- `field` (`column`): The numeric column summarized; the output also has its `count`, `standardDeviation` and `standardError`.
- `by` (`column | column[]`): The columns that group the rows: an output row per group, with its keys (one row without it).
- `estimate` (`"mean" | "median"`): What the `estimate` column holds: each group's mean or median. Default: `"mean"`.
- `interval` (`"none" | "deviation" | "standard-error" | "normal" | "bootstrap"`): The `lower` and `upper` columns: one standard deviation or standard error either side of the mean, a normal confidence interval, or a bootstrap one (missing for "none"). Only a bootstrap takes the median. Default: `"none"`.
- `confidence` (`number`): The confidence level of a normal or bootstrap interval, between 0 and 1. Default: `0.95`.
- `samples` (`number`): How many resamples a bootstrap interval draws. Default: `1000`.
- `seed` (`number`): The bootstrap's random seed, an integer: the same seed gives the same interval. Default: `42`.
- `as_` (`{estimate, lower, upper, count, standardDeviation, standardError}`): New names for the output columns.

### Usage

Outputs estimate, lower, upper, count, standardDeviation, and standardError. Default estimate is mean and interval is none. Analytic intervals require mean; bootstrap supports mean or median with 1,000 replicates and seed 42 by default. A singleton has no defined sample variability.

To let the viewer change a setting, read an input in it: `interval={input("interval")}` (Python `interval=hm.input.interval`), where `interval` is a [Select](select) of interval names.

### Related examples

- [Quantiles and group summaries](/HMPlot/examples/quantile-aggregate.md)
